| Defaulted | Data                                      | Reason                                                                                                                                                       |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Yes       | Version of CrewAI                         | Assessing the adoption rate of our latest version helps us understand user needs and guide our updates.                                                      |
| Yes       | Python Version                            | Identifying the Python versions our users operate with assists in prioritizing our support efforts for these versions.                                        |
| Yes       | General OS Information                    | Details like the number of CPUs and the operating system type (macOS, Windows, Linux) enable us to focus our development on the most used operating systems.  |
| Yes       | Number of Agents and Tasks in a Crew      | Ensures our internal testing mirrors real-world scenarios, helping us guide users towards best practices.                                                    |
| Yes       | Crew Process Utilization                  | Understanding how crews are utilized aids in directing our development focus.                                                                                 |
| Yes       | Memory and Delegation Use by Agents       | Insights into how these features are used help evaluate their effectiveness and future development.                                                          |
| Yes       | Task Execution Mode                       | Knowing whether tasks are executed in parallel or sequentially influences our emphasis on enhancing parallel execution capabilities.                          |
| Yes       | Language Model Utilization                | Supports our goal to improve support for the most popular languages among our users.                                                                          |
| Yes       | Roles of Agents within a Crew             | Understanding the various roles agents play aids in crafting better tools, integrations, and examples.                                                       |
| Yes       | Tool Usage                                | Identifying which tools are most frequently used allows us to prioritize improvements in those areas.                                                        |
| No        | Goal (Opt-In)                             | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, enabling deeper insight into usage patterns.                                                                  |
| No        | Backstory (Opt-In)                        | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, providing context for task execution and improving user experience.                                           |
| No        | Context (Opt-In)                          | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, essential for understanding how tasks are set up and executed.                                                |
| No        | Output (Opt-In)                           | Part of detailed crew and task execution data, offering insights into the final results of task execution.                                                   |
| No        | Human Input (Opt-In)                      | Captures whether human input was required during task execution, helping to improve human-agent interaction mechanisms.                                      |
| No        | Agent Verbosity (Opt-In)                  | Indicates whether agents were set to verbose mode, providing insights into detailed logging and communication preferences.                                    |
| No        | Max Iterations (Opt-In)                   | Records the maximum number of iterations allowed for agents, aiding in the analysis of task complexity and agent efficiency.                                 |
| No        | Max RPM (Opt-In)                          | Tracks the maximum RPM (Requests Per Minute) settings, useful for understanding performance constraints and resource allocation.                              |
| No        | Tools Names (Opt-In)                      | Identifies the specific tools used by agents during tasks, helping to prioritize tool development and support.                                                |
| No        | Tool Reuse (Opt-In)                       | Logs repeated usage of tools by agents, helping to identify potential areas for tool optimization or additional support.                                      |
| No        | Task Description (Opt-In)                 | Logs the description of each task, providing context for understanding task objectives and expected outcomes.                                                |
| No        | Expected Output (Opt-In)                  | Captures the expected output for tasks, useful for comparing against actual outcomes and measuring task success.                                              |
| No        | Task Output (Opt-In)                      | Records the actual output of tasks, enabling the assessment of task completion and quality of results.                                                       |
                                                   

3. There still the issue of the ability to support querying and deletion of data collected and locality. As your not explicitly targeting EU users, you have exemptions but anyone implementing the software for an EU market doesn't. GDPR is always in flux, so I recommend that you include a note to developers to disable telemetry to be GDPR compliant.

comments.author: gardner
comments.body:
After some experimentation, it does appear that the following will disable the telemetry. You can add this in your `main.py` before you instantiate any crewAI classes:

```python
os.environ["OTEL_SDK_DISABLED"] = "true"
```

To test this is working, first remove the above line from your code. Now add this to your `/etc/hosts`:

```
127.0.0.1	telemetry.crewai.com
```

Run your code and observe the timeout errors spamming the console:

```
urllib3.exceptions.NewConnectionError: <urllib3.connection.HTTPSConnection object at 0x100db7c40>: Failed to establish a new connection: [Errno 61] Connection refused

urllib3.exceptions.MaxRetryError: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='telemetry.crewai.com', port=4319): Max retries exceeded with url: /v1/traces (Caused by NewConnectionError('<urllib3.connection.HTTPSConnection object at 0x100db7c40>: Failed to establish a new connection: [Errno 61] Connection refused'))
```

Now add the environment variable at the top of your script:

```python
import os
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process
from crewai_tools import SerperDevTool

os.environ["OTEL_SDK_DISABLED"] = "true"
```

Now when your main.py is run a warning is displayed and no timeout errors are thrown:

```
2024-05-08 21:43:19,654 - 8682764992 - __init__.py-__init__:1198 - WARNING: SDK is disabled.
```

Which I hope this line of code in [opentelemetry/sdk/trace/__init__.py](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/blob/397e357dfad3e6ff42c09c74d5945dfdcad24bdd/opentelemetry-sdk/src/opentelemetry/sdk/trace/__init__.py#L1211).

comments.author: MattFriedman
comments.body:
It is my understanding that telemetry is currently hardwired into the system. If this is incorrect, please let me know.

If there is no way to opt out/in of the system sending information or attempting to send information outside of the business network, the business I work for will have to decline using CrewAI.

The nature of the telemetry information does not matter.

The business I work for gets security audited, and the auditors would not accept this.

I want to emphasize that I really like CrewAI so far (and will likely use it personally), but this issue needs to be addressed if you want security-focused businesses to adopt it.

comments.author: dezoito
comments.body:
> It is my understanding that telemetry is currently hardwired into the system. If this is incorrect, please let me know.

You are correct, but Telemetry can (or at least could) be disabled, by adding the following [snippet](https://github.com/joaomdmoura/crewAI/issues/254#issuecomment-1973042953):

```py
from crewai.telemetry import Telemetry


def noop(*args, **kwargs):
    print("Telemetry method called and noop'd\n")
    pass


for attr in dir(Telemetry):
    if callable(getattr(Telemetry, attr)) and not attr.startswith("__"):
        setattr(Telemetry, attr, noop)
```

I am NOT running this in production or anywhere with confidentiality requirements and would not suggest anyone to do so.

comments.author: MattFriedman

We have been talking and dwelling on adding the ability to disable it given it could extremely hinge our ability to improve the library effectively if enough people disable it, versus the fact it's anonymous and we making it more secure. Not saying we wont add it, just pondering for now.

Hello João,
@joaomdmoura 

Thanks for the security upgrades coming with HTTPS and the planned extra encryption layer.

In secure environments, users will likely disable telemetry anyway, even without an explicit option. By not offering this out of the box, it might actually push some users to avoid the library entirely for security reasons.

I think having an option to disable telemetry would build more trust and transparency. It would acknowledge the security needs of users and could help more people feel comfortable using the library.

Thanks for considering this!
Matt

title: CI: consider adding npm dependency caching to setup-node step
security_topic: caching disabled due to missing lockfile and potential CI cache pollution
qa_summary: The developer asked if npm dependency caching can be added to the CI workflow and whether it poses a security risk; the maintainer answered that caching must be disabled without a lockfile per the actions/setup-node documentation (see the advanced‑usage docs) and noted potential cache‑pollution attacks.

comments.author: eddieteall
comments.body:
I was exploring the CI workflow as part of my university project on GitHub Actions and noticed that the setup-node step doesn't currently include dependency caching.

The current setup-node step looks like this:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'

Adding cache: 'npm' would allow GitHub Actions to cache node_modules between runs, which can reduce install time on repeated builds:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'
    cache: 'npm'

I tested this on my own Node.js project and it worked without any other changes needed. I appreciate this may already be a considered decision, so happy to hear if there's a reason it's been left out.

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
I looked at the history and caching is not mentioned anywhere in #5599, which reworked the CI. The older Appveyor CI did [cache `node_modules`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c96c690dc087d121137c97318215e03a432395c5/appveyor.yml#L22-L23), so maybe everyone just missed this.

The "Install dependencies" step does not take a lot of time (7-15 seconds on ubuntu runners; 20+ on windows), but I think it's enough for cache to make it faster. GitHub only stores cache for [7 days](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy:~:text=GitHub%20will%20remove%20any%20cache%20entries%20that%20have%20not%20been%20accessed%20in%20over%207%20days%2E) and there have been periods when CI did not run for more than this[^1]. Saving cache will make the execution time a bit longer, but in my opinion it is not something that we should care about.

Finally, cache can allow compromising CI though cache pollution (evict cache and then make GitHub save your version with malicious additions, which will then be used to install dependencies). This is also not a problem for us, because running actions requires maintainer approval (though I'm not completely sure about this) and workflows that could use cache ([ci](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L16-L17) and [legacy](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/legacy.yml#L18-L19)) have read-only [`contents` permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#permissions).

[^1]: Adding [scheduled runs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) would allow avoiding cache expiry and, more importantly, help us faster detect regressions caused by dependency updates.

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
I guess I found out why we don't use cache for CI. Express does not have a `package-lock.json`[^1] (https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/4619, https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/3963#issuecomment-493460138) and the `actions/setup-node` [documentation](https://github.com/actions/setup-node/blob/670825a89dc0abd596e7a3abd0f5e3f6e5faf37c/docs/advanced-usage.md#running-without-a-lockfile) says:

> If you choose not to use a lockfile, you must ensure that **caching is disabled**. The `cache` feature relies on the lockfile to generate a unique key for the cache entry.

[^1]: enforced by [`.npmrc`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f873ac23124ffcff8c040b4bd257b32c29828d53/.npmrc) and [`.gitignore`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f873ac23124ffcff8c040b4bd257b32c29828d53/.gitignore#L3)

human_note: the question is valid because it concerns CI dependency caching behavior, which directly affects supply-chain integrity and reproducibility, and the answer is acceptable because it cites authoritative GitHub Actions documentation explaining the lockfile requirement and the security-relevant risk (cache key ambiguity leading to potential cache misuse or inconsistency) when enabling caching without a lockfile.

comments.author: gabrieel1007
UlisesGascon
comments.body:
In this case, the reported vulnerability in `qs` (CVE-2025-15284) is already addressed by default in Express. Current Express releases depend on patched versions of `qs`:

- **Express 4** specifies `"qs": "~6.14.0"`, which resolves to `>=6.14.0 <6.15.0` and therefore pulls in the patched `6.14.1` release by default. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f62378e1bc776259c0a471476c2dc043a02ac762/package.json#L56

- **Express 5** specifies `"qs": "^6.14.0"`, which also pulls in the patched versions automatically. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c2fb76e99f7379b706a5510b4b2dd08a1b710b7b/package.json#L55

As a result, users installing Express without overriding dependency resolutions already receive a version of `qs` that includes the fix, and the reported issue does not represent an unpatched vulnerability in Express itself.

title: location function does not validate potentially malicious URLs
security_topic: validation of Location header schemes
qa_summary: The developer asked whether res.location should validate and reject malicious URL schemes such as javascript: to prevent XSS, and the maintainer replied that per the Express Threat Model (see ThreatModel.md) it is the application's responsibility and non‑HTTP schemes are permitted.

comments.author: xzyingxiashubro
SantiagoCecena
comments.body:
Hi,

I'm interested in working on this issue.

The current behavior of `res.location()` allowing `javascript:` or `data:` schemes in the `Location` header poses a significant **XSS vulnerability**, as browsers might execute such malicious URLs. While `encodeUrl` handles URL encoding, it doesn't validate the safety of the URL scheme itself.

I'd like to propose adding a **scheme validation** step within the `res.location` function. This would involve checking if the provided URL starts with safe schemes like `http://`, `https://`, or is a relative path (`/`). Any other schemes (e.g., `javascript:`, `data:`) would be rejected or handled safely to prevent this type of attack.

I believe this enhancement would significantly improve the **default security of Express** for all users.

Would it be possible for me to pick this up and submit a pull request? I'm happy to discuss the implementation details further.

Thanks,
Santiago

comments.author: ctcpip
comments.body: Hi, please note our [threat model](https://github.com/expressjs/security-wg/blob/main/docs/ThreatModel.md#the-express-threat-model) is clear that it is the application's responsibility to control what is passed to methods, including `res.location()`.  Furthermore, there are perfectly valid use cases for non http schemes in location headers.

human_note: the question is valid because it raises a legitimate security concern about potential XSS/open-redirect risks from allowing malicious URL schemes (e.g., javascript:) in res.location, and the answer is acceptable because it provides a concrete authoritative reference to the Express threat model clarifying the framework’s security boundary and explicitly explains that validation responsibility belongs to the application while preserving valid non-HTTP use cases.

title: res.redirect cannot carry the request header I set
security_topic: custom request headers are not preserved across HTTP redirects
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if custom headers (e.g., an id header) can be preserved or altered during an HTTP redirect, and the answer cites RFC 9110 §15.4 (and the Firefox source list) indicating redirects cannot add or remove custom headers except for security‑sensitive ones like Authorization or Cookie.

comments.author: YJGGZHK
comments.body: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/91c14e66-f7ce-4046-9b14-df73beda90f2)

comments.author: YJGGZHK
comments.body:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/30a7972c-ed24-4b6b-875a-3795fcfbb8ae)
I can ensure that the id is set in the header before forwarding

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
Do you want to:

1. perform (or not) a redirect when a certain header is set,
2. remove a header from redirected request, or
3. add a header to redirected request?

1\. is easy:

```js
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    // redirect if id header is truthy
    if (req.headers.id) res.redirect('https://...');
    else next();
}
```

2\. and 3. as far as I know are impossible. Redirections are described in RFC 9110 in section [15.4. _Redirection 3xx_](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.3xx). The RFC says (emphasis mine):
> When automatically following a redirected request, **the user agent SHOULD resend the original request message** with the following modifications:
>
> 1. Replace the target URI with the URI referenced by the redirection response's [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field value after resolving it relative to the original request's target URI.
> 2. Remove header fields that were automatically generated by the implementation, replacing them with updated values as appropriate to the new request. This includes:
>    1. (...)
> 3. Consider removing header fields that were not automatically generated by the implementation (i.e., those present in the request because they were added by the calling context) where there are security implications; this includes but is not limited to [Authorization](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.authorization) and Cookie.
> 4. Change the request method according to the redirecting status code's semantics, if applicable.
> 5. If the request method has been changed to GET or HEAD, remove content-specific header fields, including (but not limited to) [Content-Encoding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-encoding), [Content-Language](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-language), [Content-Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-location), [Content-Type](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-type), [Content-Length](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-length), Digest, [Last-Modified](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.last-modified).

In general, the user agent (e.g. browser) sends the original request, but changes some necessary automatically generated headers (e.g. `Host`) and **removes headers that may have security implications such as `Authorization` and `Cookie`**. The list of removed headers will probably depend on the user agent - [here is the list from Firefox](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/6cc05c6620814bf3eb05278ccf3b1f49690b7740/netwerk/protocol/http/HttpBaseChannel.cpp#123-148).\
The RFC does not offer a way of adding or removing custom headers when redirecting a request - whatever was in the original request is in the redirected one (with the exceptions mentioned above).

comments.author: YJGGZHK

human_note: he question is a viable security question because it asks whether HTTP redirects can preserve or alter request headers in a way that impacts security-sensitive headers (e.g., Authorization, Cookie), and the answer directly addresses redirect security behavior defined in RFC 9110.

The reason for this is mainly security around DOS protection. There is no way to support path segment regular expression matching while also avoiding major performance regressions. See more here: https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/

comments.author: UlisesGascon
comments.body:
> This is why I am hesitant do add an action for this as I would rather ask GitHub for better spam management tooling.

Agree with @wesleytodd. The issue is quite complex because the moderation in GitHub is not an easy thing:
- Many people (those that are watching the repo) will receive a notification in their email or in the app/web once a new PR is created. This will occur even before a Github Action is triggered. 
- Closing PRs is an easy action (1 click), so that is not a big time consumer
- Detecting invalid PRs is not the big issue because you can easily to spot them with the practice.
- Reporting issues/users is complex because the UI requires many steps to do it for each user, so that is a blocker for many maintainers.
- Nuke button like @CBID2 suggested is great when the community needs to slow down due a discussion/flame in certain moments, but is not the long term solution as it will prevent other users from contributing (PRs) that are legit or need help (issues) while using Express.

So, I think that we are quite limited on how much we can do with GitHub actions in this case. There are other scenarios that are less frequent but more prone to use GitHub Actions to moderate, for example when people do comments that include offensive content or heavily language. In most projects that I am involved the moderation is done by the humans behind the project or a specific team that volunteer to do it, it is a heavy job. The same way as it is hard to keep a slack/discord/gitter community channel a safe space by moderating content.

title: Can express req.headers[x] be an array?
security_topic: array values in request headers for Express/Node.js
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether Express can include array‑valued headers such as set‑cookie and how to safely combine them, and the answer cites the Node.js HTTP documentation (https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders) which states that only the set‑cookie header is an array and should not be merged into a string.

comments.author: RobertSandiford
dougwilson
comments.body:
Hello, so the `req.headers` object is just from Node.js HTTP itself; Express.js doesn't set anything there. This means the rules are types are that of the version of Node.js you are running on. Here is their documentation:

https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders

And notably I see this about array values:

> set-cookie is always an array. Duplicates are added to the array.

I don't think `set-cookie` can be safely combined into a string, which is why it seems the only one that Node.js will put as an array.

I hope that helps.

Edit: also, it is pretty much non-existent that `set-cookie` header would even be in a request to a server like express, as that is a response header, not a request header.

human_note: Accepted because the question is about header typing and runtime behavior in Express/Node, which is valid framework-level behavior. The answer is valid since it correctly states that Express does not transform headers (they come from Node.js), and accurately identifies that set-cookie is the only header that Node may represent as an array in req.headers, while also correctly noting it is primarily a response header rather than a request header.

Instead of using ` res.cookie() ` I've resorted to using the native ` res.setHeader() ` coupled with the [jshttp cookie](https://www.npmjs.com/package/cookie).

const cookie = require('cookie')

        maxAge: 86400,

title: Basic auth `realm` is REQUIRED but handled as optional
security_topic: requirement of realm parameter for HTTP Basic authentication
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether the `realm` parameter in HTTP Basic auth is required by the spec, and the answer cites RFC 7617 and RFC 7235 (including Appendix A) showing that the realm is now optional.

comments.author: tvogel
comments.body:
According to https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 , specification of the `realm` parameter is REQUIRED, so making `realm` optional here

https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/643d2845de09a437b955a163ab25eb0887bfd0e1/fastapi/security/http.py#L195

and at related places, is misleading and makes it easy to create non-conforming APIs. It bit me when a Shelly device refused (rightfully) to authenticate against the API which was using the default (missing) `realm` behavior.

comments.author: tvogel
comments.body: Ah, good that this is already in the works! However, the fix to default it to "global" is questionable to me because that is a string that in general gets presented to users as a prompt to provide credentials, so shouldn't have a rather meaningless default. A good framework should make the framework user provide relevant detail like the realm. If they use basic auth, they need to define a realm.

comments.author: YuriiMotov
comments.body:
I think we should close this issue.

As Sebastian mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/13786#pullrequestreview-3501695067), `realm` seems to be not required in latest version of RFC.

> I also noted that the spec says that the realm is now optional, but only in a footer note (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A). 😂 Anyway, we are good with that now.


I checked this and agree:

The https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 states:

> The authentication parameter 'realm' is REQUIRED ([RFC7235], Section 2.2).

But if we go to Section 2.2 of RFC7235, we have:

> [2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2.2).  Protection Space (Realm)
> 
>    The "realm" authentication parameter is reserved for use by
>    authentication schemes that wish to indicate a scope of protection.
> 
>    A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme
>    and authority components of the effective request URI; see [Section](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)
>    [5.5 of [RFC7230]](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)) of the server being accessed, **in combination with**
>    **the realm value if present.** ...

So, current version of RFC7235 doesn't say that `realm` is required.

Moreover, it's mentioned in [Appendix A](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A):

>    The "realm" parameter is no longer always required on challenges;
>    consequently, the ABNF allows challenges without any auth parameters.
>    ([Section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2))

human_note: Standards interpretation issue affecting HTTP Basic authentication behavior (realm optionality, RFC 7235 vs RFC 7617 evolution)

comments.body:
Hey @Kludex, what do you think about raising a `HTTP 400 BAD REQUEST` for cases where the authentication scheme is not correctly 'bearer'?

[From RFC 6750 Section 3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750#section-3.1):

```
invalid_request
         The request is missing a required parameter, includes an
         unsupported parameter or parameter value, repeats the same
         parameter, uses more than one method for including an access
         token, or is otherwise malformed.  The resource server SHOULD
         respond with the HTTP 400 (Bad Request) status code.

invalid_token
         The access token provided is expired, revoked, malformed, or
         invalid for other reasons.  The resource SHOULD respond with
         the HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) status code.  The client MAY
         request a new access token and retry the protected resource
         request.
```

My reading of this text is that:

- when the server understands the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is correct) but the token itself is malformed we should return a `401`
- when the server does **not** understand the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is wrong), then we should return a `400`

comments.author: sehraramiz
comments.body:
[Dependant](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L15) object has a cache_key attribute which the dependency resolver of fastapi uses it to cache dependencies and use the already resolved dependencies (get_session in this case).
according to [this line](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L58) of Dependant class the cache_key is generated using the **dependency function reference** and **security scopes**.
when you use get_authenticated_user as a security dependency every param in get_authenticated_user gets the security scopes of the parent api (user_activate).
so when resloving dependencies from user_activate with scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ('activate'))```
when resloving dependencies from user_activate with no scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ())```

i think this behavior might be a security feature.

it might help you to read [this part of the doc](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/?h=dependenc#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times) on dependency cache
and [this part](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/security/oauth2-scopes/?h=dependency#dependency-tree-and-scopes) about dependency tree and scopes.

human_note: Security-relevant dependency injection caching behavior where OAuth2 scopes affect FastAPI dependency resolution keys.

comments.author: csrgxtu
comments.body:
@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body:
@araujo88 It can't be using `self.stream()`, for per request, only one time can use `self.stream()`.  
Or you will hang forever because of `await self.event_message.wait()`  
[You can see here: uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fedf67e68d3f81c846bf3740c8ae21fa133000a4/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543)  
This is because that when `self.stream()` done, there are no action to notify `self.event_message`
This `asyncio.Event` will be notified of four actions:
- when Connection Lost
- when body_data received
- when body_data readed done
- when write reponse data done

And you can try this:
```
async for chunk in request.stream():
    print(chunk)
await request.json()
```

I guess that he meant that yellow warning sign.
If you use `SameSite=none`, it is required to set `secure` attribute aswell as described [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite).

title: jsonable_encoder alters json_encoders of Pydantic objects
security_topic: global encoder mutation causing secret value leakage
qa_summary: The developer needed to know why jsonable_encoder mutates the Pydantic model’s json_encoders causing secret values to be exposed, and the answer provides a concrete fix by merging encoders with `{**encoder, **custom_encoder}` anchored in commit 39cc2925 (see the diff).

### Commit to Help

- [X] I commit to help with one of those options 👆

### Example Code

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder


class Credentials(BaseModel):
    password: SecretStr


ENCODERS = {SecretStr: lambda v: v.get_secret_value() if v is not None else None}

creds = Credentials(password="helloworld")

a = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(a)  # {'password': '**********'}, as expected
b = jsonable_encoder(creds, custom_encoder=ENCODERS)
print(b)  # {'password': 'helloworld'}, as expected
c = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(c)  # gives {'password': 'helloworld'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?


creds = Credentials(password="123456789")

d = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(d)  # gives {'password': '123456789'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?
```


### Description

* I'm using `jsonable_encoder` at multiple locations in the code, sometimes with `custom_encoder` and sometimes without.
* My understanding is that passing `custom_encoder` should only affect the current call and not modify any global state.
* What actually happens is that it modifies `__config__.json_encoders`, and as a result, public API endpoints might suddenly start returning secret values that should be filtered.

0.78.0

Python 3.9.2

Using Pydantic version 1.9.1.

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body: I see that it use `__config__.json_encoders` and also pass to next call with `encoder`, so could we use `encoder = encoder.copy()` to avoid  modifies `__config__.json_encoders`?

comments.author: slackner
comments.body:
Yes, copying `encoder` before modifying it fixes the issue. Since FastAPI requires at least Python 3.6 merging the dictionaries could also be done with `{**a, **b}`, so an alternative fix would look like this:

```diff
diff --git a/fastapi/encoders.py b/fastapi/encoders.py
index 4b7ffe31..39cc2925 100644
--- a/fastapi/encoders.py
+++ b/fastapi/encoders.py
@@ -52,7 +52,7 @@ def jsonable_encoder(
     if isinstance(obj, BaseModel):
         encoder = getattr(obj.__config__, "json_encoders", {})
         if custom_encoder:
-            encoder.update(custom_encoder)
+            encoder = {**encoder, **custom_encoder}
         obj_dict = obj.dict(
             include=include,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
             exclude=exclude,  # type: ignore # in Pydantic
```

Note that I'm not sure yet if the change has any negative side effects. Would be good to know to know if there was a reason why `.update()` was used in the first place. :thinking:

comments.author: slackner
comments.body: For reference, the code in question was initially added in https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/715. There is no explanation why the pydantic config itself is updated, so it probably was meant to be a copy in the first place.

```

This appears to be an issue where the default FastAPI handler for HTTPExceptions always returns content even for status codes (304, 204), where no content should be specified.

comments.author: aboubacs
comments.body:
Hi,

The default handler for HTTPException will always construct a JSONResponse with content. https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/22528373bba6a654323de416ad5c867cbadb81bb/fastapi/exception_handlers.py#L9-L16

This behavior is documented in the tip here: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/handling-errors/#the-resulting-response

This is incompatible with returning HTTP status codes that shouldn't have any content. Whether or not fastapi should choose whether to send a JSONResponse or not based on the status code is debatable, but since this behavior isn't implemented today, you can build it with your own exception handler. If you have to use exceptions instead of returning the response directly, some sample code would be:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
from starlette.requests import Request

app = FastAPI()


class NotModifiedException(Exception):
    pass


@app.exception_handler(NotModifiedException)
async def not_modified_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: NotModifiedException):
    return Response(status_code=304)


@app.get('/foo')
async def route(request: Request):
    raise NotModifiedException()

```

comments.author: adriangb
comments.body:
Can't you just include the header in your tests?

```python
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

router = APIRouter()

security = HTTPBearer()


async def validate_firebase_token(token: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> None:
    ...


@router.get("/", dependencies=[Depends(validate_firebase_token)])
def endpoint() -> None:
    ...



def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    app = FastAPI()
    app.include_router(router)
    return app


from fastapi.testclient import TestClient


def test_endpoint() -> None:

    test_token = "foo"
    
    async def validate_fake_token(token: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> None:
        assert token.credentials == test_token

    app = create_app()
    app.dependency_overrides[validate_firebase_token] = validate_fake_token

    client = TestClient(app)

    resp = client.get("/", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {test_token}"})
    assert resp.status_code == 200


test_endpoint()
```

title: HTTP backend: TLS config defaults to TLS 1.0, allows protocol downgrade
security_topic: TLS minimum version default and downgrade risk
qa_summary: Whether the HTTP backend really permits a TLS downgrade is answered by Go's crypto/tls documentation showing Config.MinVersion defaults to TLS 1.2, not TLS 1.0.

comments.author: SebTardif
comments.body:
### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v1.16.0-dev (main branch, HEAD)
```

### Terraform Configuration Files

This is an internal code issue in the HTTP backend TLS configuration, not triggered by a specific user config. Any configuration using the HTTP backend with TLS client certificates is affected:

```terraform
terraform {
  backend "http" {
    address        = "https://example.com/state"
    client_cert_file = "/path/to/cert.pem"
    client_key_file  = "/path/to/key.pem"
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

No debug output needed. The issue is visible in the source code at `internal/backend/remote-state/http/backend.go` in the `configureTLS` function: the `tls.Config` is created without setting `MinVersion`, which defaults to TLS 1.0.

### Expected Behavior

The HTTP backend should enforce TLS 1.2 as the minimum protocol version, consistent with the OCI backend (`internal/backend/remote-state/oci/auth.go:323`) and the deprecation of TLS 1.0/1.1 per [RFC 8996](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8996) (March 2021).

### Actual Behavior

The `tls.Config` created by `configureTLS` uses Go's default `MinVersion` of 0, which permits TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections. This allows protocol downgrade attacks against state data in transit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Review `internal/backend/remote-state/http/backend.go`, function `configureTLS`
2. Note that `tls.Config{}` is created without `MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12`
3. Compare with OCI backend at `internal/backend/remote-state/oci/auth.go:323` which correctly sets `MinVersion`

### Additional Context

The omission was introduced in #34806 (2024-03-05) during the `helper/schema` refactoring. I intend to submit a fix for this issue and have a working implementation on my fork.

### References

- #34806 (introduced the omission)
- [moby/moby#32056](https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/32056) (Docker/Moby added TLS minimum version enforcement for the same class of downgrade risk)
- Previously submitted as #38546 (closed; resubmitting with issue-first workflow per Contributing.md)
- Fork branch with fix: [`SebTardif/terraform@fix/http-backend-tls-minversion`](https://github.com/SebTardif/terraform/tree/fix/http-backend-tls-minversion)

comments.author: dbanck
comments.body:
Thanks for the report! We are actively looking into the issue.

https://www.hashicorp.com/.well-known/pgp-key.txt contains two keys. While the first one expired on 2026-04-18, the second one is valid and can be used to validate release. But many tools, including [hashicorp/hc-install](https://github.com/hashicorp/hc-install/issues/370) only decode the first block and never try the second key. Any downstream tooling that is using hc-install, is affected as well.

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @fancybear-dev, Terraform is behaving as documented in this instance: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/provider-network-mirror-protocol#authentication

Specifically:

> Terraform does not send credentials when retrieving the archives whose URLs are given in the "List Available Installation Packages" response below. If a particular mirror considers the distribution packages themselves to be sensitive then it must use cryptographically-secure, user-specific, and time-limited URLs in the metadata response. Strategies for doing so are out of scope of this protocol documentation.

The next version of Terraform (v1.11) will support using a `.netrc` file to support adding credentials to the follow up requests, which may work for you in the short term: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.11.x/providers#private-providers

In the longer term, please follow this enhancement requests for updates on this issue more generally: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/29349

Thanks!

Hey @BroMattMiller,

Thank you for reporting this! The S3 backend is managed by the AWS Provider team at HashiCorp, and this issue has been added to their triage queue. Thanks again!

comments.author: bschaatsbergen
comments.body:
Based on your debug logs, I noticed references to object locking. Could you confirm if S3 Object Lock is enabled on your bucket, and if default retention is enabled, as this is often used to prevent deletion and overwriting of files? AFAIK, the `Content-MD5` or `x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header is required for any request to upload an object with a retention period configured using Object Lock.

Please note that the lock file is expected to be written to the S3 bucket and deleted when the lock is cleaned up, which could potentially conflict with how Object Lock is configured on the S3 bucket.

I haven’t been able to replicate this issue with an S3 bucket that has Object Lock enabled but default retention disabled. I’ll take some time to set up an S3 bucket with both Object Lock and default retention enabled to investigate further and get back to you as soon as I have an update.

**Update**: I can replicate the issue with an S3 bucket configured with Object Lock and default retention set to Governance for X days.

comments.author: BroMattMiller
comments.body: Yes, I have enabled Object Lock, per AWS Security Hub control S3.15, "S3 general purpose buckets should have Object Lock enabled." The retention mode is Governance and the retention date is 30 days. The credentials used by Terraform do have the necessary privileges to override this.

comments.author: bschaatsbergen
comments.body:
For some additional context, when S3 Object Lock is enabled on a bucket with a retention period, Amazon S3 requires the `Content-MD5` or` x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header for object uploads via PutObject to ensure data integrity during the upload process. For more details, see [Uploading objects to an Object Lock enabled bucket](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock-managing.html#object-lock-managing-events).

It appears that the default behavior of the `skip_checksum` flag for the lock file was not maintained when writing the lock file to S3 Object Lock-enabled buckets.

To clarify the default behavior of `skip_checksum`: by default, if this argument is not set in the backend, we set the S3 checksum algorithm behavior to SHA256. This causes the underlying S3 AWS SDK V2 serializers to automatically append the that required `x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` header. For more details, see the relevant code in the [AWS SDK v2 serializers](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/blob/8939ed049c8b3490f9a3dbd4e4d3d56cf22a27f2/service/s3/serializers.go#L7494-L7497).

I think it should be possible to swap out the current base S3 client with the [s3manager](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/tree/8939ed049c8b3490f9a3dbd4e4d3d56cf22a27f2/feature/s3/manager) to handle writing lock files to S3 Object Lock-enabled buckets the same way as we write state, and perserve the default behavior of `skip_checksum` when writing a lock file too.

A vulnerability was identified in Consul and Consul Enterprise (“Consul”) such that using Headers in L7 traffic intentions could bypass HTTP header based access rules.

Installed version: v1.13.0 

Fixed version: 1.20.1

CVE-2024-51744 - github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v4

golang-jwt is a Go implementation of JSON Web Tokens. Unclear documentation of the error behavior in `ParseWithClaims` can lead to situation where users are potentially not checking errors in the way they should be. Especially, if a token is both expired and invalid, the errors returned by `ParseWithClaims` return both error codes. If users only check for the `jwt.ErrTokenExpired ` using `error.Is`, they will ignore the embedded `jwt.ErrTokenSignatureInvalid` and thus potentially accept invalid tokens. A fix has been back-ported with the error handling logic from the `v5` branch to the `v4` branch. In this logic, the `ParseWithClaims` function will immediately return in "dangerous" situations (e.g., an invalid signature), limiting the combined errors only to situations where the signature is valid, but further validation failed (e.g., if the signature is valid, but is expired AND has the wrong audience). This fix is part of the 4.5.1 release. We are aware that this changes the behaviour of an established func

Installed version: v4.4.2

Fixed version: v4.5.1

### Actual Behavior

As shown in the debug output, Terraform failed to download the file because it's not using the credential I have specified. I also confirmed that the server side didn't receive any bearer token. It seems Terraform _assumes_ the download URLs are publicly accessible.

Also notice, the previous calls for service discovery and getting version (e.g. `GET https://ar-terraform-registry.us-central1.run.app/v1/providers/tf-registry-backend/random/3.6.3/download/darwin/arm64`) were all successful because Terraform used the auth token in those requests. It's only the **download** call that's impacted.

I can't make the service accessible to you. But I'd expect any other custom private registry will have the same problem if the download URLs require authentication.

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @yolocs, thanks for filing this.

I can confirm that Terraform isn't attaching authentication to the follow up requests when retrieving the `downloadUrl` and the `shasumUrl`. This is because both the public and private registries return publicly available URLs for these attributes. This means that it is difficult for us to change this without breaking our primary points of integration.

I do agree that this behaviour isn't documented, I've tagged this issue as a documentation improvement and raised with the internal docs team.

Could you attach temporary credentials to the returned URLs? Or copy the behaviour of the private registry which returns temporary unauthenticated endpoints?

Thanks!

comments.author: wieso-itzi
comments.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.9.7
on linux_amd64
```


### Use Cases

Terraform stores the values of variables inside the terraform.tfstate file in plain-text, no matter if they are sensitive or not. The reasoning behing this is that Terraform needs to be aware of changes to these variables in order to properly handle e. g. a terraform apply after changing a variable.

However I believe that if for sensitive variable the text in the tfstate file wasn't the plain-text variable but something like a hash digest of the actual value, it would increase security drastically and this would still allow Terraform to check for changes since different input variables lead to different digests.

### Attempted Solutions

I haven't yet tried or looked into how this could be implemented, but I would be glad to work on the proposed solution.

title: Terraform Test wrongly removing sensitive marks and warning now Terraform Core can handle sensitive inputs
security_topic: sensitive value handling between Terraform test runs
qa_summary: Whether Terraform Test was incorrectly stripping sensitive marks from inputs between run blocks, and the maintainer says it was fixed in Terraform 1.8.0 with PR #34414 and commit fc756571130af35fc33e4f5651c9db487df6d861.

comments.author: seblatre
liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @seblatre, thanks for filing this! This has been fixed in the 1.8.0 release series, are you able to upgrade to the newly released v1.8.0? We're not currently planning any more releases to the v1.7 series.

Thanks!

comments.author: seblatre
comments.body:
Hello @liamcervante, I updated to the latest version and I can confirm that it's working now.
Any link to the original bug fix around this?
Thanls anyway for your very quick answer!

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Hi @seblatre, we don't have a specific issue for this as it seems to have been fixed by a change made to add additional support for an unrelated feature.

The PR that fixed it is #34414, with this being the more specific commit: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/fc756571130af35fc33e4f5651c9db487df6d861

In the current code the line that removes the marks you can see are being complained about in the error is here: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/terraform/context_plan.go#L287.

comments.author: liamcervante
comments.body:
Actually, I will reopen this. Within the test framework specifically we are checking for sensitive marks as a way to warn if they are being lost: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/backend/local/test.go#L1249-L1269

However, we are not checking the embedded values within complex types so that is probably the actual root cause of this issue originally. The fact the plan functionality now handles marked values does not address the bug in the test framework.

As it is I think we don't need to print that warning anymore, as the plan can now handle sensitive marks on inputs properly. I'll leave this open as a bug, and we can stop stripping the sensitive marks from inputs within the test framework.

This is what Overall/Manage permission is for: https://www.jenkins.io/jep/223

### What Operating System are you using (both controller, and any agents involved in the problem)?

Fedora 43

### Reproduction steps

   1. Initialize a clean Jenkins installation using `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm` as the security realm.
   2. Ensure no user accounts have been created yet (initial setup state).
   3. Simultaneously send multiple concurrent POST requests to the `/securityRealm/createFirstAccount` endpoint with different usernames and valid account details.
   4. Verify the number of users created and their permissions.


### Expected Results

Only the very first request should succeed in creating an account. All subsequent concurrent requests should fail with a 401 Unauthorized error (or similar) because a user already exists or is being created, preventing the creation of multiple initial administrator accounts.

### Actual Results

A race condition exists in `HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.doCreateFirstAccount`. The `hasSomeUser()` check is non-atomic and unsynchronized. In testing with 20 concurrent threads, 20 different user accounts were created, and all 20 were granted administrative privileges via `tryToMakeAdmin(u)`.

### Anything else?

The vulnerability is a classic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition in `core/src/main/java/hudson/security/HudsonPrivateSecurityRealm.java` between lines 366-376. While impact is limited to the initial setup phase, it allows an attacker to gain admin access if they can time requests during the window before the first user is fully persisted.

### Are you interested in contributing a fix?

Yes, the fix involves adding a static lock object to synchronize the `doCreateFirstAccount` method. This ensures the `hasSomeUser()` check and subsequent user creation are atomic.

title: Security Scan Report: Object Deserialization Can Lead to Remote Code Execution
security_topic: unsafe Java object deserialization risk in Keycloak components
qa_summary: Whether the reported unsafe Java object deserialization in TwitterIdentityProvider or KerberosSerializationUtils actually poses an RCE risk, and the maintainer’s answer points to DelegatingSerializationFilter and says the auth notes cannot be directly manipulated.

comments.author: AnupWellpro
comments.body:
### Description

During a recent SAST security scan of our **keycloak** deployment, the scanner flagged **4 findings** (2 Critical, 2 Medium) with a severity score of **94/100** related to **Unsafe Java Object Deserialization**.

Deserializing entire Java objects is dangerous because malicious actors can craft Java object streams with unintended consequences. If an attacker can control the data being deserialized, this can lead to **Remote Code Execution (RCE)** — one of the most severe vulnerability classes.

### Value Proposition

- **Prevent RCE:** Unsafe deserialization is a top OWASP vulnerability (A8:2017) that can give attackers full server control
- **Compliance:** Eliminate Critical findings from security pipelines (SOC2, HIPAA audit readiness)
- **Reduce blast radius:** Even in test frameworks, deserialization gadget chains can be leveraged if test utilities are accidentally exposed or reused in production paths


### Goals

- [ ] Replace `ObjectInputStream` usage in `SerializationUtil.java` (both test-framework and testsuite copies) with safer alternatives — use JSON serialization (Jackson/Gson) or implement an `ObjectInputFilter` allowlist (Java 9+) to restrict deserializable classes
- [ ] Add `ObjectInputFilter` to `KerberosSerializationUtils.java` to restrict deserialization to known Kerberos credential types only
- [ ] Refactor `TwitterIdentityProvider.java` to deserialize the Base64-decoded data using JSON instead of Java object streams
- [ ] If `ObjectInputStream` must be retained, implement HMAC signature verification on the data stream before deserializing to ensure integrity and authenticity
- [ ] Add unit tests validating that crafted malicious object streams are rejected

### Non-Goals

- [ ] Rewriting Keycloak's entire serialization infrastructure — changes should be targeted to the 4 flagged locations
- [ ] Removing Kerberos support — `KerberosSerializationUtils` needs deserialization but should be hardened with filters, not removed
- [ ] Addressing test-only findings as P0 — the `SerializationUtil.java` files are in test frameworks, so while they should be fixed, they are lower operational risk than production code
- [ ] Fixing vulnerabilities outside the `keycloak` repository scope

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
We don't need to worry about hardening the test code, KerberosSerializationUtils does utilized a filter (see DelegatingSerializationFilter), and auth notes cannot be directly manipulated so there is not currently a risk from deserializaion there. 

If you narrow this enhancement to just be a task for a hardening of the TwitterIdentityProvider, it could be considered for the backlog. Otherwise we can just close this.

title: Keycloak makes network requests to addresses in login certificates before verifying them
security_topic: certificate revocation check ordering and SSRF-style internal network access
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak’s certificate-revocation lookup can be abused for SSRF by making network requests to addresses embedded in an untrusted certificate, and the answer rests on the issue comment and fix direction in the thread, including the mutual-TLS trust-store guidance and the stated plan to change revocation order.

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
## Description

When Keycloak is configured to allow login using digital certificates (like smart cards or X.509 certificates), it can be set to check if those certificates have been canceled (revoked). It does this by looking for an address inside the certificate called a "CRL Distribution Point" and connecting to it to get a list of canceled certificates.

The issue is that Keycloak tries to connect to this address **before** it checks if the certificate was even issued by a trusted source. This allows anyone to create a fake certificate, put a private or secret internal network address inside it, and send it to Keycloak. Keycloak will then try to connect to that secret address. This allows an outsider to use the Keycloak server as a "bridge" to see into or interact with private parts of a company's network that are usually hidden.

## Version affected

Keycloak 26.5.2 and earlier.

## Expected behavior

Keycloak should first verify that a certificate is signed by a trusted authority. If the certificate is not trusted, the system should stop immediately and should **not** try to connect to any web addresses listed inside that certificate.

## Actual behavior

Keycloak attempts to connect to the address listed in the certificate (using HTTP or LDAP) immediately upon receiving it, without checking if the certificate itself is valid or trusted.

## Steps to reproduce

1. **Enable Certificate Login:** Set up a Keycloak realm to use X.509 client certificate authentication and turn on the setting to check "CRL Distribution Points."
    
2. **Create a Fake Certificate:** Create a self-signed certificate. In the "CRL Distribution Point" settings of the certificate, put an address for a private internal server (for example, `http://192.168.1.50:8080/admin`).
    
3. **Log in:** Try to log in to Keycloak using this fake certificate.
    
4. **Check the logs:** You will see the Keycloak server trying to reach out to the private address you provided in the certificate, even though the certificate isn't trusted.

title: Brute-force detection: Authenticated session token refresh resets lockout counter
security_topic: brute-force lockout counter reset via authenticated session refresh
qa_summary: Whether authenticated token refresh or SSO re-auth was incorrectly resetting brute-force lockout state, with the fix anchored in the maintainer comment describing the moved `logSuccess()` call.

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
## Description

When brute-force detection locks an account after repeated failed login attempts, a token refresh from an already-authenticated session on the same account resets the lockout state. This allows an attacker to resume password guessing before the lockout period expires, provided the legitimate user is actively using their account during the attack window. The attacker still must guess the correct password — this is a counter reset, not a bypass of password verification.

## Version affected

26.5.7, 26.6.2

## Expected behavior

A successful cookie-based or token-refresh authentication from an existing session should not alter the brute-force lockout state. The lockout counter and timer should only be affected by explicit password-based authentication attempts. Existing sessions should remain active (locking them would enable attacker-triggered DoS), but they should be neutral with respect to lockout state.

## Actual behavior

When the locked account's legitimate user performs an action that triggers a token refresh (e.g., page reload in an already-authenticated browser), the "Temporarily locked" flag is cleared in the admin console and the lockout period is effectively cancelled. A subsequent login attempt from a different browser succeeds with the correct password despite the lockout window not having expired.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure brute-force detection on a realm (e.g., max login failures: 5, lockout duration: 15 minutes).
2. In Browser A, authenticate as the target user and remain logged in.
3. In Browser B, submit failed login attempts for the same account until the lockout threshold is reached.
4. In Browser B, confirm the account is locked by attempting to log in with the correct password — login is denied.
5. In Browser A, perform any action that triggers a token refresh (e.g., reload the page).
6. In Browser A, verify in the admin console that the "Temporarily locked" toggle is now disabled.
7. In Browser B, attempt to log in again with the correct password — login succeeds despite the lockout period not having expired.


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

comments.author: niels-van-nerum
comments.body: Hi! I would like to resolve this as my first OSS-contribution. I am currently writing a test to verify the behavior, after that I will implement the fix. Could this be assigned to me?

comments.author: niels-van-nerum
comments.body:
I checked the `refresh_token` flow first, but couldn't produce a failing test for this issue, checked the code out some more, and saw a lead that make me think it was related to cookie-based SSO re-auth. So wrote a test for it and it failed!

When an already logged in user triggerd a SSO re-auth, it was resetting the brute-force detection counter, and removing the temporary lockout.

Fixed it by moving the call to `logSuccess()` to the if-else statement just above it that checks if the login is coming from SSO. After this my failing test was passing.

title: OIDC: Token introspection audience check validates azp instead of authenticating client when dynamic-scopes is enabled
security_topic: token introspection audience-check regression with experimental scopes
qa_summary: Whether the token introspection audience check regression caused by dynamic-scopes/parameterized-scopes was fixed, anchored by linked PR #48981 and the backport PR #50297 (with the maintainer noting it was previously fixed in issue #48980).

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
## Description

The audience check added to the token introspection endpoint in PR #49131 (fixing CVE-2026-37979) does not work correctly when the `dynamic-scopes` experimental feature is enabled. In `AccessTokenIntrospectionProvider.introspectionChecks()`, the call to `transformAccessToken()` triggers dynamic-scopes scope resolution which calls `session.getContext().setClient(<azp client>)`, repointing the request context's client to the token's issued-for client. When `verifyAudience()` then reads `session.getContext().getClient()`, it gets the token's `azp` instead of the client that authenticated to the introspection endpoint.

This causes two problems: legitimate resource-server introspection returns `active:   false` (because the check becomes `azp in aud` instead of `authenticating-client in aud`), and confidential clients not in the token's audience can still read full claim sets from lightweight access tokens when `azp` happens to be in `aud`.

With dynamic-scopes disabled, the audience check works correctly.

## Version affected

26.6.2 (regression introduced by PR #49131, not present in 26.5)

## Expected behavior

The introspection audience check should validate that the authenticating client (the one presenting credentials to the `/introspect` endpoint) is in the token's `aud`, regardless of whether `dynamic-scopes` is enabled.

## Actual behavior

When `dynamic-scopes` is enabled, the check validates whether the token's `azp` is in `aud` instead. The event log confirms the wrong client is checked:

type="INTROSPECT_TOKEN_ERROR" error="invalid_token" reason="Client '<azp/frontend>' is not in the token audience"

The client named in `reason` is the token's `azp`, not the client that authenticated.

| token `aud` contains | introspecting client | `dynamic-scopes` | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **on** | `active: false` |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **off** | `active: true` |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start Keycloak with `KC_FEATURES=dynamic-scopes`.
2. Create a realm with two clients: `frontend` (public) and `api` (confidential).
3. Obtain an access token via `frontend`. Ensure `api` is in the token's `aud` (e.g., via an audience mapper).
4. Call the introspection endpoint authenticating as `api` with the access token.
5. Observe `active: false` with the event reason naming `frontend` (the `azp`), not `api` (the authenticating client).
6. Disable `dynamic-scopes` and repeat — observe `active: true`.


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
@u3r I understand this is frustrating, but let me clarify what "experimental" means in Keycloak, as defined in our [feature development process](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/main/docs/features.md):

**Experimental features:**
- Are **not supported for production use-cases**, only for evaluation purposes
- Do **not have to be feature complete**
- Do **not have to provide backwards compatibility for APIs, nor migration support**

And specifically regarding breaking changes:

> *"Experimental features have no contract in terms of breaking changes. That means breaking changes can be introduced at any point, without new versions, deprecations, or any other warning. Additionally, no migration support is required."*

The duration a feature has been in experimental status does not change these guarantees — or the lack thereof. Features remain experimental until they meet the criteria for graduation to preview, which includes being feature complete, passing a security review, and resolving open feedback. The fact that parameterized scopes has been evolving (including the rename from dynamic scopes) is exactly why it is still experimental — it is under active development.

As @rmartinc confirmed, this appears to be already fixed on `main`. We encourage you to verify with the [nightly build](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/nightly). But backporting fixes for experimental features is not something we commit to — that is the trade-off of using them.

If you rely on this in production, that is at your own risk, and we strongly recommend waiting for the feature to graduate to at least preview status.

You should still rely on the rest of Keycloak to work. If we don't guarantee this, nobody will ever activate an experimental feature on a production instance even for evaluation only and we will not get any feedback on it.

Yes, I agree. It's unfortunate that enabling some experimental feature may break some other parts, but as you mentioned, it's quite hard to verify it in the CI. You should never run the experimental feature in production, which is emphasized in docs/logs properly (I believe). IMO, the intention of using the experimental feature is to enable it in some dev/test environment, try only the specific functionality, and gather some feedback. So, it means that no harm should be done to your business or your real business data.

We'll try our best to keep the experimental features as "isolated" as possible, but for some features, it might be very challenging. Even with this issue and your insights, we got the necessary feedback, so we can react to it via these backports! 🚀  Thanks for that! :))

comments.author: vramik
comments.body:
The regression was introduced in commit 249d4e35b4a  fixing #46606.

This commit added a new Admin Console-specific endpoint `RoleMappingDeleteResource` at `rest/admin-ui-ext/src/main/java/org/keycloak/admin/ui/rest/RoleMappingDeleteResource.java` and switched the Admin Console from using the standard Admin REST API `DELETE /role-mappings/realm` to the new `POST /ui-ext/role-mapping-delete/users/{id}`.

comments.author: trixpan
comments.body:
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

core

### Describe the bug

The configureTruststore Quarkus build step lacks a dependency on CryptoProviderInitBuildItem, making its execution order relative to setCryptoProvider non-deterministic. In 26.5.7, the build step DAG coincidentally scheduled crypto provider initialization first. Changes in 26.6.1 (removal of UserProfileBuildItem steps, new createHttpAccessLogDirectory step, added @Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class) on health/resteasy steps) altered the DAG enough that configureTruststore now executes before the BouncyCastle FIPS provider is registered, causing KeyStore.getInstance("BCFKS") to fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException.

### Version

26.6.1

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

FIPS compliant BCFKS works

### Actual behavior

KeyStore.getInstance("BCFKS") fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException

### How to Reproduce?

Start in FIPS mode with 

JAVA_OPTS="$JAVA_OPTS -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreType='BCFKS'"

### Anything else?

_No response_

comments.author: slaskawi
comments.body:
When reading this ticket, I see two separate issues:

1. DAG execution order change - the BouncyCastle Provider loading and setting up truststore executes shifted places leading to a failure. 
2. Hardcoded inclusion of the default Trust Store. 

## DAG execution order change

### Summary

It looks like Keycloak 26.5.7 scheduled `setCryptoProvider` earlier than `configureTruststore`. This changed in `26.6.1`, where `configureTruststore` runs earlier than `setCryptoProvider` leading to a failure

### Details

The `KeycloakProcessor.java` defines these methods in the following way:

``` java
@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)
@Produce(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)
@BuildStep
@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
void setCryptoProvider(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}

@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
@BuildStep
@Consume(ConfigBuildItem.class)
void configureTruststore(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}
```

`configureKeycloakSessionFactory` properly consumes `CryptoProviderInitBuildItem`. `configureTruststore` does not. No happens-before edge in DAG → topo-sort order between them depends on what else changed.

`git diff 26.5.7..26.6.1 -- quarkus/deployment/.../KeycloakProcessor.java` indicated the following changes leading to this behavior:

1. **New `createHttpAccessLogDirectory` step**
2. **`UserProfileBuildItem` steps removed** — `parseDefaultUserProfileConfig` + `setDefaultUserProfileConfig` deleted
3. **`@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)` added on `disableHealthCheckBean` + `configureResteasy`**


### Related PRs

* [#45991](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45991)
* [#45994](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45994)
* [#46076](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/46076)
* [#48008](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/48008)

### Potential fix

The fix seems to be simple - add `@Consume(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)` to `configureTruststore` build step in `KeycloakProcessor.java`

## Hardcoded default Trust Store issue

### Summary

After the new Kubernetes Trust Store detection has been merged ([#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506)), Keycloak always adds the default Trust Store on the default execution path. This leads to the following failures:

  - **fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)**: `NoSuchMethodError: CryptoServicesRegistrar.checkConstraints` - non-FIPS BC instantiated against FIPS-flavored bcprov classes.
  - **fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12**: `NPE: No password supplied for PKCS#12 KeyStore` while loading `/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk/lib/security/cacerts`.

### Details

The [#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506) indeed refactored adding the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores by default. However, the if none of these are present, the code returns exactly the same way as previously:

```java
//Pre-#44506 escape code path:
} else if (truststores.length == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure — JDK default used directly
}

//The current version of it:
else if (truststores.size() == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure, we'll just use the system default
}
```

The automatic inclusion of the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores can be activated with the `--truststore-kubernetes-enabled=false` option (@trixpan which I would recommend as a workaround here).

Analyzing the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` case, I have an impression that we don't have any checks for this case - FIPS disabled but the BC libraries are present on the classpath. This probably requires a separate fix.

The `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` seems to be another corner case when using the Default/System Trust Store, we should assume PKCS12 format. 

### Proposed fix

There are a few smaller things we could do here:

1. Introduce a check if BC is present in the `setCryptoProvider` and fail if it does and the FIPS mode is disabled. 
2. When loading the System Trust Store, we could first check the default password we use (`changeit`) and then the blank one. This might mitigate the NPE in password problem. 

But I honestly think the fixes here are more of a hardening compared to the `DAG execution order change` problem. 

## Final recommendation

At first, use the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/49359 as a reproducer for the described problem. Ensure this fails correctly and fix the DAG dependency issue (potentially following the recommendation). Once this gets merged, consider opening follow up, focused issues for the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` and `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` cases.
