title: Welcome page admin bootstrap bypasses local-only check when behind a same-host proxy without forwarding headers
security_topic: same-host proxy bypass of local-only admin bootstrap check
qa_summary: Whether the welcome-page admin bootstrap bypass via a same-host proxy is a real security issue and how it was addressed, anchored by the issue discussion and follow-up #49162.

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
### Description

The initial admin creation form on the welcome page is guarded by `WelcomeResource.isLocal()`, which checks that both the remote and local addresses are loopback and that no `X-Forwarded-For` or `Forwarded` headers are present. When Keycloak is deployed behind a reverse proxy or TCP forwarder running on the same host that connects to a loopback-bound Keycloak listener without injecting forwarding headers, the check is satisfied for remote requests. A remote user can access the bootstrap form and create the initial admin account.

### Version affected

All current versions.

### Expected behavior

The welcome page admin creation form should not be accessible to remote users, regardless of whether a same-host proxy is in the request path. In production mode, dynamic admin creation via the welcome page should either be disabled entirely or require additional verification beyond network locality.

### Actual behavior

When a same-host reverse proxy or TCP forwarder connects to Keycloak over loopback without adding `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-For` headers, the `isLocal()` check passes for remote requests. The welcome page serves the admin creation form to any remote user accessing through the proxy.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a fresh Keycloak instance with no existing master admin user, bound to `127.0.0.1:8080`
2. Place a same-host reverse proxy or TCP forwarder in front of it, exposed on a remotely reachable interface, without configuring it to add `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-For` headers
3. From a remote machine, request the proxied `/` welcome page
4. Observe that Keycloak serves the "Create an administrative user" form instead of the "Local access required" warning
5. Submit the bootstrap form with a chosen username and password
6. The admin user is created successfully

### Anything else?

The impact is limited: the bootstrap form is only available on an uninitialized Keycloak instance with no sensitive data, and a legitimate admin would notice they are locked out. The team suggests considering disabling dynamic admin creation when starting Keycloak in production mode as a hardening measure. Related discussion: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/48410


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
For the proxy to be involved, yet not set the headers this means that either:
- that the instance is setup for tls passthrough
- or the documentation has not be followed (https://www.keycloak.org/server/reverseproxy - you are told to set the proxy-headers option for non-https passthrough and to have the proxy always set the headers)

In tls passthrough if proxy-protocol is used, the client would still need to be local to pass the isLocal check.

So the security concern here is basically limited to tls passthrough when proxy-protocol is not enabled.

It's been discussed in issues related to #48410 whether we should require proxy-protocol to be used in passthrough, rather than introduce something like a proxy-mode setting.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
@abstractj @vmuzikar @sschu @slaskawi based upon the review comments on the PR and our team discussion, I'm moving back to the issue to discuss the possible strategies here.

In prod mode the absolute safest approach, now that we have the bootstrap-admin command, is to disable by default the ability to create the initial admin via the welcome page. This means we won't have to make any assumptions based upon whether the proxy is setup correctly or the proxy settings are correct. If the option to allow creation via the web interface (e.g. --bootstrap-admin-web=true) was enabled, the check could still try to infer if the connection is local. The option though would document when this strategy may not work. This is however a potentially large breaking change.

The middle-ground, as shown on the PR, is to assume that the proxy and proxy settings are configured appropriately, which will limit when it's possible for the isLocal detection to not work as expected. However that could still be seen as breaking as without an additional option of some kind, a setup with tls passthrough and proxy-protocol not enabled won't be able create an admin via the welcome page. Note that if proxy-protocol were enabled, users can't currently use a standard browser to create the admin user as browser won't perform the proxy protocol - there is some overlap here with #48741

WDYT? Or should this be widened to all of keycloak-security?

And while it doesn't have to be done as part of this hardening, it seems like in dev mode the isLocal check could just return true.  This will improve usability when running in a container as the incoming connection is ofter not coming from localhost, but a different interface that keycloak has bound to within the container.

comments.author: sschu
comments.body: @shawkins I am fine with the current approach. I also don't really see it as breaking because we don't really touch any existing installation but just change how you setup a new installation.

comments.author: slaskawi
comments.body:
Thanks for tagging me @shawkins !

> In prod mode the absolute safest approach, now that we have the bootstrap-admin command, is to disable by default the ability to create the initial admin via the welcome page.
> [...]
> If the option to allow creation via the web interface (e.g. --bootstrap-admin-web=true) was enabled, the check could still try to infer if the connection is local.
> [...]
> This is however a potentially large breaking change.

I like the general idea of introducing a switch, and making it possible to disable/enable the Welcome Page on demand. 

I also agree, this is a large breaking change. Some platforms, like [UDS Core](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/uds-core), heavily rely on it. But I also do appreciate there are other installations that do not care about it so much. 

In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`. The "Configuring Keycloak for production" guide could clarify that disabling this option provides more hardened configuration.

> The middle-ground, as shown on the PR, is to assume that the proxy and proxy settings are configured appropriately, which will limit when it's possible for the isLocal detection to not work as expected. However that could still be seen as breaking as without an additional option of some kind, a setup with tls passthrough and proxy-protocol not enabled won't be able create an admin via the welcome page

Regardless to the path forward, I believe we should have a switch that will ignore additional checks. Otherwise it will be a breaking change for someone. 

Maybe we could consider something like: `--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]`, where the `auto` mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior. 

> And while it doesn't have to be done as part of this hardening, it seems like in dev mode the isLocal check could just return true.

Sounds reasonable!

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally. 

We have two additional options based upon this:
- as mentioned in the PR, only do the new check if it's an https request. This allows users who have set --http-enabled=true to then create the initial admin over http
- allow sni to be enabled (which needs to be done in general), such that we can check the host used to access the server.

cc @vmuzikar

> Maybe we could consider something like: --bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto], where the auto mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior.

@slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:

--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]

auto (default in prod): allow the first "local" user to create the bootstrap admin
true (default in dev): in dev mode this would be any access, in prod mode it would be the prior / relaxed notion of isLocal 
false: never allow the creation of the initial admin over the web interface

comments.author: vmuzikar
comments.body:
> In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`.

-1, this would not solve the issue. If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

I feel we're overthinking this here a bit with the `--bootstrap-admin-web` option. There's a security issue but the predicate here is misconfigured proxy (not using headers or PROXY protocol). Similar issue when proxy is misconfigured (and Keycloak can't reliably get the actual remote address) is affecting more areas like brute force detection. Maybe we should instead focus  on the root cause – can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it? I think we can, at least for locally running proxy (on the same host as Keycloak). We could reject requests with localhost as the remote address in non dev modes, when proxy headers or protocol are not configured. YEs, it is a breaking  change but it's a security fix which might be strong enough justification.

comments.author: slaskawi
comments.body:
> One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally.

+1 - that seems like a good idea. 

@shawkins @vmuzikar I also wanted to suggest that we make it an explicit requirement that this feature works correctly with `kubectl port-forward` as this is the primary way Kube folks are expected to use it. 

> @slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:
> If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

@shawkins Yes, I think so, but at the same time @vmuzikar has a very good point here as well. 

> can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it

This sounds like a very interesting idea! However it might be a broader topic as we might want to at least have the "audit configuration" mode where Keycloak will allow these requests to pass through and "enforcing mode" where Keycloak would reject requests with an incorrect configuration. The Kubernetes [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/) could be a good source of inspiration how to design these type of features.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
@vmuzikar sorry for introducing some additional confusion. We can absolutely focus on the hardening first, then circle back to whether a new option makes sense.

On the hardening, we can:
1. Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.
 
2. The more I think about this, the more it seems related to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48741 / #47453. Along those lines we could think about adding the ability to create the initial user via the management port, which we never expect to be proxied, nor do we accept proxy settings for. Via the management port there would be no need for the isLocal check. If we go this route, we may also want to allow the management port to be independently enabled from health / metrics and eventually perhaps remove the ability of creating the initial admin user from main interface.

comments.author: vmuzikar
comments.body:
> create the initial user via the management port

If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
> If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?

I don't think that is what @slaskawi is implying - there's no expectation that the main interface is being publicly exposed to create the initial admin. How ever they are doing it, it would still have to satisfy the isLocal check.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
> Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.

#49162 is now up-to-date with this, and I believe can close this issue.

The possible follow-ups are:
- relax isLocal for dev mode
- bootstrap-admin-web option, which could overlap with relaxing the isLocal check
- add the ability to create the initial admin on the management port, which would definitely be usable by port forwarding as well

human_note: This is a security-relevant authentication bootstrap issue in Keycloak involving initial admin account creation bypass, which is a high-impact security control (privileged access setup).

title: [Security] CVE‑2026‑42581/42584/42579 – Netty 4.1.125/4.1.130 (used by Quarkus 3.27.x) still vulnerable in Keycloak 26.x
security_topic: whether a Netty vulnerability affecting Quarkus 3.27.x is already fixed in Keycloak
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak 26.x remains vulnerable because its Quarkus 3.27.x runtime still pulls in Netty versions affected by CVE-2026-42581/42584/42579, with the maintainer saying #48805 covers it and closes this as a duplicate.

comments.author: martakat
comments.body:
### Description

### Summary
Keycloak 26.x (including the latest 26.6.1) depends on Quarkus 3.27.x, which pulls in Netty 4.1.125.Final and 4.1.130.Final.  
Both versions contain three critical Remote‑Code‑Execution vulnerabilities:

| CVE | CVSS | Brief description |
|-----|------|-------------------|
| CVE‑2026‑42581 | 9.8 | HTTP‑1.0 TE + CL smuggling bypass – arbitrary code execution. |
| CVE‑2026‑42584 | 9.1 | Race condition in `DefaultEventLoop` – remote code execution. |
| CVE‑2026‑42579 | 9.1 | `ChannelOutboundBuffer` overflow – remote code execution. |

Quarkus uses `quarkus‑netty` as its default HTTP server, so any client that can reach the service’s HTTP port can trigger these bugs.

### Upstream status
* Netty fixed the issues in **4.1.131.Final** (2026‑04‑02).  
* Quarkus upgraded to Netty 4.1.131.Final in **Quarkus 3.28.0** (2026‑04‑23).  
* Keycloak 26.x still ships with Quarkus 3.27.x, therefore the vulnerable Netty versions remain in the runtime artifact.

### Request

- Is there an estimated timeline or keycloak version which will include the updated quarkus version?

 _It would be great if the updated quarks version could be back-ported to Keycloak 26.5_

Thank you for your attention to this issue.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body: CVE‑2026‑42581 is covered by #48805, since all the issues are fixed by the same release, I'm closing this as a duplicate.

title: Investigate what is required for cookies to be PQC ready
security_topic: post-quantum readiness of cookie cryptography
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak’s cookie signing and hashing scheme is sufficiently post-quantum safe, with the answer anchored in the maintainer’s cookie-type inventory and the linked follow-up issues #49858 and #49860.

comments.author: stianst
comments.body:
### Description

Cookies in Keycloak are currently signed by `HS512` by default. This should be PQC ready, but as part of this issue we should investigate to make sure all cookies are indeed PQC safe, or if some improvements are required.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

If any issues are discovered as part of this investigate a refined sub-issue should be added to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690 with applicable sub-tasks.

comments.author: rmartinc
comments.body:
The cookies that we are using in keycloak are the following (file `CookieType.java`):

| Java | Cookie | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
|AUTH_DETACHED | KC_STATE_CHECKER | internal encoded token signed with HS512 |
|AUTH_RESTART | KC_RESTART | internal encoded token signed with HS512 and encrypted using AES128 |
|AUTH_SESSION_ID_HASH | KC_AUTH_SESSION_HASH | SHA256 hash of the authentication session ID |
|AUTH_SESSION_ID | AUTH_SESSION_ID | Base64 of the auth session ID and signature using HS512 signer context (id.signature) |
|IDENTITY | KEYCLOAK_IDENTITY | internal encoded token signed with HS512 |
|LOCALE | KEYCLOAK_LOCALE | locale plain string ("en" or "es") |
|LOGIN_HINT | KEYCLOAK_REMEMBER_ME  | Just plain "username: " + urlencoder of the username |
|SESSION | KEYCLOAK_SESSION | Base64Url of the SHA-256 of the ID of the session |
|WELCOME_CSRF | WELCOME_STATE_CHECKER | Just base64url of 256 random bits (32 bytes) |

So keycloak is using HS512, AES128 and SHA256. The three of them are sufficient for post-quantum cryptography. In the case of AES128 and SHA256 it seems that there is a Grover's Algorithm that reduce the effective security in half, but as SHA256 only hashes the random generated session IDs (session and auth session ID) and AES is only used to encrypt the KC_RESTART we are safe. So better if we improve those two to use AES256 and SHA384/SHA512. Issues created for both:

* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49858
* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49860

title: Investigate and plan what is needed for SAML 2.0 to be PQC ready
security_topic: PQC readiness for SAML 2.0 signatures and encryption
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak’s SAML 2.0 flow needs PQC/hybrid signature support to avoid downgrade attacks, anchored by the RFC9231bis draft and the linked W3C strategy issue plus the implementation milestone #50292.

comments.author: stianst
comments.body:
### Description

Many of the algorithms used by SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions are not considered PQC-safe. We need to investigate what new algorithms we need to support, including reviewing if some hybrid signing algorithms are required. This should cover all usage of cryptography in Keycloak in SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions, including server-side (both when Keycloak acts as the server, and when Keycloak acts as the client, for example identity brokering) as well as all client libraries provided by Keycloak

It should go without saying that the approach should be based on standards and specifications; this is vital for interoperability as well as from a security perspective.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

The outcome of this investigation should be a refined issue added to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690, including adding sub-issues as applicable.

comments.author: stianst
comments.body:
Some notes from previous discussions:
* SAML for clients and identity brokering  
  * There is an initiative to add new PQC algorithms for XML/SAML (see this [W3C issue](https://github.com/w3c/strategy/issues/484)). The new RFC is in progress in [rfc9231bis](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-eastlake-rfc9231bis-xmlsec-uris-06). It seems that the idea is adding this new four PQC algorithms (three for signatures and one for key derivation/encryption):  
    * HSS/LMS: Hierarchical Signature System / Leighton-Micali Signatures (Supported in JDK 21 and BC 1.79)  
    * ML-DSA: Module Lattice \- Digital Signature Alorgithm (Supported in JDK 24 and BC 1.79)  
    * SLH-DSA: Stateless Hash-based \- Digital Signature Alorgithm (BC 1.79)  
    * ML-KEM: Module-Lattice Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (Supported in JDK 24 and BC 1.79)  
* There is also a paper from the past year [Post-quantum XML and SAML Single Sign-On](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/828) that used java, BC, apache santuario and opensaml to implement a PoC about SAML/XML/PQC integration. The paper forked santuario and added some of the algorithms (previous names, this is a mess). Reading it very quickly I think that only signatures are implemented. This is the [repo](https://github.com/PQSAML/index) that links to other repos.  
* So, there are gaps and missing points (not even the names for the algorithms are defined in rfc9231bis now). But probably the general idea is clear:  
    * The rfc9231 is going to add the new algorithms for XML signature and encryption. There are some missing parts like how to define the *\<KeyInfo\>* element for the new keys.  
    * We need to expand (contribute to) apache santuario/xmlsec to support one signature and one derivation for PQC (for example ML-DSA and ML-KEM).  
    * Integrate the new algorithms in Keycloak to be selected.

comments.author: pskopek
comments.body:
### Hybrid approach

We can use dual hybrid approach to maintain backward compatibility while in transition period.

Dual hybrid architecture means we will include booth legacy and quantum safe signatures.
We have to consider downgrade attack when attacker removes quantum safe signature. This has to be configured on the validator side.

### Santuario support for signing an ecryption quantum safe algorithms

Nobody seems to be working on support of quantum safe algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA and ML-KEM) in Apache Santuario.

Apache Santuario supports use of custom keys for signing and encryption. We need to implement key registration while initializing Santuario in `XMLSignatureUtil` and `XMLEncryptionUtil`  classes.

comments.author: pskopek
comments.body: Implementation milestone with sub tasks is [#50292](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/50292)

The [Github advisory has a CVSS3.1 score of 5.8 / Moderate](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xxqh-mfjm-7mv9).
But [NIST/NVD's own scoring is 9.8 / Critical](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42581).

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
The short answer is: the real-world risk here is significantly lower than the NVD 9.8 suggests.

The core issue in this CVE is about HTTP request smuggling when Netty acts as a proxy, forwarding requests between a client and a backend. Keycloak doesn't do that. It's an end-application server, not a proxy. On top of that, all of Keycloak's backchannel HTTP calls (SAML artifact resolution, OAuth2/OIDC token exchange, etc.) go through Apache HttpClient, not Netty, so those paths aren't affected either.

The one scenario where this could matter is if Keycloak sits behind a reverse proxy that happens to accept HTTP/1.0, reuses backend connections, and handles the Transfer-Encoding/Content-Length conflict differently than Netty does. In practice, most modern proxies like nginx, HAProxy, or Envoy either reject HTTP/1.0 with chunked encoding or normalize the headers before forwarding, so this is a pretty narrow window.

With that in mind, my personal take is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N 5.4 Medium. The 9.8 on NVD is accurate for Netty used in proxy mode, but that's not how Keycloak uses it.

### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

authorization-services

### Describe the bug

Currently set up with Keycloak with the following:
- Realm with LDAP user storage.
- Service client(s) that containerized workloads authenticate with using client id and client secret
- Client that protects resources (for this set up it is kafka topics and consumer groups). The authorization uses a mix of Group policies and Client policies to grant write/read access to various topics and consumer groups.

Finding in the logs, when the service client is requesting access to the protected resource via the uma ticket flow to get a RPT token, the logs with LDAP debugging on show that and LDAP query is being done with the user storage with the UUID of the service account for the client. Example log below:

2026-04-29 14:27:07,221 DEBUG [org.keycloak.storage.ldap.idm.store.ldap.LDAPOperationManager.perf] (executor-thread-792)
LdapOperation: search

 filter: (&(mail=c501b859-2de6-464b-be33-6da20f3f162c)(objectclass=person)(objectclass=organizationalPerson)(objectclass=user))
 searchScope: 2

took: 131 ms

26.6.1

- [ ] The issue is a regression

Keycloak during the UMA ticket flow process to try to determine what authorization should be granted to the resource tries to query LDAP with the internal UUID of a service account during the process causing wasted LDAP queries.

### How to Reproduce?

1. Set up Keycloak with the following:
- Realm with LDAP User storage
- Service account client
- Client with Authorization turned on and a mix of client policies and group policies protecting resources.

2. Turn on LDAP debugging in Keycloak.
3. Obtain a token from the Service account client.
4. With the token from the Service account, obtain a RPT token from the client that is protecting resources. The Keycloak logs will show the LDAP search with the UUID of that service account occurring before being granted access to the resource.

title: Keycloak issues tokens via implicit and hybrid flow when DPoP is enforced for the client
security_topic: DPoP enforcement bypass in implicit and hybrid OIDC flows
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak’s DPoP enforcement gap for implicit and hybrid OIDC flows is a security issue, anchored by the issue’s stated bearer-token bypass and the maintainer’s acknowledgment of a security researcher report.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
### Area

oidc

### Describe the bug

When a client is configured with dpop.bound.access.tokens=true ("Require DPoP bound tokens"), Keycloak still issues front-channel bearer access tokens for OIDC:
 
 * implicit flow (response_type=token)
 * hybrid flow (response_type=code token)

The issued access tokens are active bearer tokens (token_type=Bearer) with no cnf binding claim. This bypasses the configured DPoP requirement for those response types.

### Acknowledgement

We acknowledge the security researcher Evan Hendra - Slvrqn and thank them for submitting this via our bug bounty program. 

### Version

26.5.3

### Expected behavior

No tokens should be issued as DPoP isn't supported for these flows.

### Actual behavior

Keycloak issues tokens. It then later rejects those tokens as they are not DPoP bound. 
Other resource providers are expected to reject those tokens as well assuming they are enforcing DPoP. 

### How to Reproduce?

Try creating a new workflow

### Anything else?

Next actions: 

* Add to the documentation that DPoP is not supported for the Implicit Flow.
* Block Implicit Flow requests if "Require DPoP bound tokens" is enabled on the client.



---

title: Add option to specify the CA Subject DN in the Client X.509 Authenticator
security_topic: mTLS truststore deprecation and server-level truststore necessity
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak should require and verify the CA Subject DN for X.509 client authentication, with the discussion anchored in the issue description and comments about mTLS trust-store behavior and the existing https-trust-store-file settings.

comments.author: rmartinc
comments.body:
### Description

Right now the X.509 client authenticator only allows to specify the Subject DN for the client certificate. As the trust-store (or mTLS store) is common for all the keycloak setup (same for all the realms), we can enhance this to also add the Root CA Subject DN. This way keycloak can check if the client certificate is issued by the expected CA. A very raw idea of the implementation:

* We need to re-verify the certificate in the app side and obtain the root CA (using the keycloak trust-store).
* If trusted (it should be as it was previously verified by the mTLS, but it can be more complicated when using proxies), check the Root CA has the correct and configured Subject DN.
* Check how the certificate chain is obtained in proxies. We need to obtain the full chain passed by the client.
* Document this and add a note for adding intermediate CAs if the chain is not passed by proxies.
* Add an option to disable the new working or just maintain the same old behavior if the CA DN is not specified but make it compulsory. Secure by default but old configurations maintain the old behavior. We can think about this when doing the implementation.

For the moment this issue is just for the client X.509 authentication. We will need a follow up for the user authenticator (but in that case we will need to setup a list of valid CA DNs, as maybe there are several valid CAs).

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
@rmartinc @vmuzikar @michalvavrik not sure what the best place is to start a discussion on this, but I wanted to see if a goal  is to eventually deprecate the https-trust-store-file-* settings again - which was the initial intent when first doing the truststore changes (undone by https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/33172). It seems like once we have support like this for both clients and users, and it's required, then the https-trust-store-file may no longer be needed.

The other rationales for keeping https-trust-store-file as undeprecated:
- it's currently reloadable, but the one created by the truststores feature won't be until at least quarkus 3.36 along with some additional refinements.
- if is there an expectation that the https-trust-store-file is being used for mTLS level access restriction, and not for authentication.

title: UMA IS_ADMIN filter breaks ticket finding
security_topic: UMA admin filter causing cache poisoning across resource servers
qa_summary: Whether the IS_ADMIN UMA ticket filter could let cache poisoning hide or mis-handle granted tickets across resource servers, and the answer is anchored by the maintainer’s acknowledgment plus fix PR #48385.

comments.author: erdoganege
comments.body:
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

_No response_

### Describe the bug

Hello, 

I think this new `IS_ADMIN` UMA permission ticket filter broke the caching functionality. 
The MR: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47210
I'm talking about specifically this change: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47210/changes#diff-1e921492f31a55b4f93aaafdc92b2107801175e16b15e895108b213b9211d037R90

We have the following use case in our project as an ADMIN API: We want to retrieve all granted tickets within the system independently from their owner, requester, resource servers or anything else. This is what we do:

1. We retrieve all Resource Servers in the system
2. Iterate over the Resource Servers, and pull their tickets with (filters include `IS_ADMIN=true`, because we want to retrieve all tickets with the current user which is not either owner or requester):
`ticketStore.find(rs, filters, null, null)`

The above change causes Keycloak to pull **ALL tickets independently from their actual resource servers**, because it **does not** put this one: 

`predicates.add(builder.equal(root.get("resourceServer").get("id"), resourceServer.getId()));`

Then, if the first resource server is not the ticket's corresponding resource server, cache sets this ticket id as "not existing". So, when the actual resource server is queried in the next iteration, cache directly returns `null`, so we don't receive the ticket from this function call.

I think this should have been kept without touched:

```
if (resourceServer != null) {
            predicates.add(builder.equal(root.get("resourceServer").get("id"), resourceServer.getId()));
```

And, all other `IS_ADMIN` logic should be inside a separate if check.

### Version

26.5.7

### Regression

- [ ] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

Expected behavior is:
filter contains IS_ADMIN=true

When I run ticketStore.find(rs, filter, null, null), it should **only** care about the tickets that belong to that RS, not all tickets. So that, it won't do some caching for tickets that do not belong to that RS. In other words,

This should be added regardless of IS_ADMIN filter when resource server is not null:

`predicates.add(builder.equal(root.get("resourceServer").get("id"), resourceServer.getId()));`

### Actual behavior

filter contains IS_ADMIN=true

When I run ticketStore.find(rs, filter, null, null), the `StoreFactoryCacheSession` sets a ticket as non-existing ticket in case resource servers are not matched.

### How to Reproduce?

1. Create two resource servers
2. Grant a permission which belongs to first resource server (RS**1**)
3. Set filters Granted=True and IS_ADMIN=True
4. Call ticketStore.find(RS**2**, filter, null, null)
5. Call ticketStore.find(RS**1**, filter, null, null)


You won't see the granted ticket.

### Anything else?

_No response_

comments.body:
@pedroigor sorry for the delayed response. You can find the Python script to reproduce the issue in the attachment (mostly Claude code :D). 

**PREREQUISITE:** To simulate `IS_ADMIN=true` filter, you should add this line to "GET /permission/ticket" API call ib the "services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/protection/permission/PermissionTicketService.java" file:

`filters.put(PermissionTicket.FilterOption.IS_ADMIN, Boolean.TRUE.toString());`

**What does below script to (It assumes you have a running Keycloak with the above change):**
1.  Bootstrap – create a realm, two independent resource-server clients
    (RS1 and RS2), a plain requesting client, a resource-owner user (Alice),
    and a requesting user (Bob).
2.  Obtain a PAT for RS1 and register a protected resource owned by Alice.
3.  Create a UMA permission ticket for that resource.
4.  Bob exchanges the ticket for an RPT → exchange fails as expected
    (access not yet granted), and Keycloak persists a pending permission
    request that Alice can later approve.
5.  RS2 queries the pending tickets for the same resource ID. RS2 has no
    relation to this resource, so the result should be empty – but this call
    pollutes the cache under RS2's IS_ADMIN context.
6.  RS1 queries its own pending tickets for the same resource ID. This
    SHOULD return the single pending ticket from step 4, but due to the
    cache pollution in step 5 it returns an empty list  ← BUG.

**To verify correctness:** Set cache_poison to False in main(cache_poison=False) and re-run. RS1 will correctly return Bob's pending ticket.

[uma_submit_bug_final.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27010575/uma_submit_bug_final.py)

title: [ABCA] Doublecheck how to configure valid keys for client attestation authentication
security_topic: configuration of trusted keys for client attestation authentication
qa_summary: How ABCA client attestation should be configured to trust valid keys, using identity providers as the source of trusted keys via PR #48869 and the `OIDCIdentityProvider`/`DefaultTrustIdentityProvider` mechanism.

comments.author: mposolda
comments.body:
### Description

This is tracker issue for how to properly configure valid keys for ABCA. Since the initial PR https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47962 , it uses option on the client authenticator.

This issue is to review this.

Configuration on the authenticator doesn't work as it is for whole realm, however various clients in the realm can possibly trust different keys (different client attesters). Also it is not possible with the `CLIENT_AUTH_FEDERATED`.

It can be probably good to use identity providers as a source of trusted keys.

Identity providers were originally introduced to Keycloak as "way for authenticate users" different way than by username/password and delegate authentication to other OIDC/SAML/social provider. But now they are intended to be used as more generic "trust relationship".

The feature `CLIENT_AUTH_FEDERATED` already uses identity providers as a way for check signature on the JWT provided during federated client authentication. The key is provided by underlying identity provider (could be OIDC, Spiffe or Kubernetes identity provider as of now). It seems that ABCA can likely use same mechanism?

Initially, we can maybe sufficient with the `OIDCIdentityProvider`, which means keys would be provisioned either from `jwks URL` or configured directly on the side of OIDC provider.

As a follow-up, it may be possible to introduce additional identity provider implementations (specific to OID4VCI or other use-cases).

comments.author: mposolda
comments.body:
This is addressed now by using identity providers as source of trusted keys.

Linked PR https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/48869 added support for clients with ABCA to have ability to configure trusted identity provider. This identity identity provider should provide the trusted keys. IDentity provider can link either using the keys from specified `OIDCIdentityProvider` (JWKS Keys) or PR introduced dedicated identity provider implementation `DefaultTrustIdentityProvider` .

human_note: This is a clear security-relevant authentication configuration and trust-management issue in Keycloak involving client attestation (ABCA) and trusted key provisioning, which directly impacts authentication integrity and trust boundary enforcement.

title: [CVE-2026-37977] CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflected from unverified JWT azp claim on UMA token endpoint
security_topic: CORS origin reflection from unverified JWT claims on token endpoint
qa_summary: Whether CVE-2026-37977 is a real cross-origin data exposure risk from CORS being set from an unverified JWT azp claim on the UMA token endpoint, anchored by the issue’s CVE and the discussion referencing the PermissionGrantType/CorsErrorResponseException behavior.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
## Description

CVE-2026-37977: When using the UMA token endpoint, Keycloak sets the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header based on the `azp` claim from a client-provided JWT before validating the JWT signature. While the token grant itself is correctly rejected during validation, the CORS header has already been set in the response.

This allows a client to control which origin can read the error response cross-origin. The impact is limited to reading error messages - no tokens or user data are exposed.

**Prerequisites:**
- Client must be configured with `webOrigins: ["*"]` (non-default configuration)
- Only affects error responses, not successful token grants

## Version Affected

26.5.6 and potentially other versions

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a Keycloak client with `webOrigins: ["*"]`
2. Create a JWT with the `azp` claim set to any origin (e.g., `https://example.com`)
3. Sign the JWT with any key (signature validation will fail later)
4. Send a POST request to `/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/token` with:
   - `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:uma-ticket`
   - Include the crafted JWT
5. Inspect the response headers

## Expected Behavior

The `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header should only be set after JWT signature validation, or should be based on the client's configured origins rather than the unverified `azp` claim.

## Actual Behavior

The `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header reflects the value from the `azp` claim before signature verification, allowing the error response to be read cross-origin from any specified domain.

## Additional Context

This issue has been assigned CVE-2026-37977 for tracking purposes.

The practical impact is limited because:
- Only error responses are affected
- No tokens or user data are exposed
- Requires non-default client configuration
- The token grant itself is correctly rejected

---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @ahus1.*

@pedroigor - please schedule this in your team. 

I've assigned you to this issue for the time being to do additional labeling and planning.

Resuming from:

The only thing I'm not sure about this one is that the client making the request can be a SPA and, as such, it does not have any CORS setup. It is not the backend.

In such a scenario, the public client is obtaining permissions from another client (the audience, the resource server) to access its protected resources. In this case, shouldn't the token endpoint return the CORS requirements from the resource server? Wouldn't it be a way to allow a resource server to enforce specific requirements for cross-origin requests, including which clients/domains are allowed? If so, the behavior herein described is valid.

However, I also understand the point from the reporter. You might want to expose only the CORS requirements for the client (e.g.: SPA) making the request. Perhaps suggesting allowing management of CORS configuration from a client/resource server?

> stianst:
Actually, the way CORS works for other endpoints is that the RP gets the permitted web-origins in the access token, and it's configured in the app, not the backend service. Our adapters just used to take the web-origin claim from the access token.
```

title: [OID4VCI] Self-Signed x5c Bypasses Key Attestation Validation
security_topic: self-signed certificate handling for key attestation validation
qa_summary: Whether self-signed x5c certificates can bypass Key Attestation validation in Keycloak OID4VCI, based on the reported CWE-295 issue and the described fix that rejects self-signed certificates.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
## Summary

`AttestationValidatorUtil.verifierFromX5CChain()` skips PKIX certificate chain validation when `x5c[0]` is self-signed (`subject == issuer`). An attacker generates a software key, creates a self-signed cert, and forges a key attestation JWT claiming hardware-level security (VAN.5). Keycloak accepts it and issues a Verifiable Credential.

**Affected:** Keycloak <= 26.5.6 (latest stable), all versions with `oid4vc-vci` feature
**CWE:** CWE-295 (Improper Certificate Validation)

Acknowledgement: The Keycloak Security team acknowledges Trung Nguyen from CyStack Security for reporting this. 
As OID4VCI is in experimental mode, this is handled as a regular bug in upstream, and not a CVE. 
The automated reproducer is not attached to the public issue. 

## Vulnerable Code

`services/.../oid4vc/issuance/keybinding/AttestationValidatorUtil.java:332-347`

```java
// Check if this is a self-signed certificate (for test environments)
X509Certificate firstCert = certChain.get(0);
boolean isSelfSigned = firstCert.getSubjectX500Principal()
    .equals(firstCert.getIssuerX500Principal());

// Only validate the certificate chain if it's not a self-signed certificate in a test environment
if (!isSelfSigned) {
    CertPathValidator validator = CertPathValidator.getInstance("PKIX");
    PKIXParameters params = new PKIXParameters(getTrustAnchors());
    params.setRevocationEnabled(false);
    validator.validate(certPath, params);
}

PublicKey publicKey = certChain.get(0).getPublicKey();  // attacker's key trusted
```

Comment says "for test environments" but there is no runtime check. Bypass is always active.

## Execution Path

```
POST /protocol/oid4vc/credential
  AttestationProofValidator.validateProof()
    AttestationValidatorUtil.validateAttestationJwt()
      validateJwsHeader()          -- alg/typ check passes (ES256)
      verifierFromX5CChain()       -- PKIX SKIPPED for self-signed cert
      verify JWT signature         -- passes (attacker signed with own key)
      validateAttestationPayload() -- nonce/resistance checks pass
    return attested_keys           -- attacker's software JWK
  credential issued
```

No secondary defense: no SPI intercept, no realm-level trust store, no event listener.

## Confirmed

| Test | x5c cert | HTTP | Result |
|------|----------|------|--------|
| Self-signed (`subject == issuer`) | `CN=Fake WSCD` / `CN=Fake WSCD` | **200** | Credential issued |
| Non-self-signed (`subject != issuer`) | `CN=Leaf` / `CN=Fake CA` | **400** | PKIX rejects |

Tested on Keycloak **26.5.6** (latest stable) and **nightly** (2026-03-30). Both `jwt_vc_json` and `dc+sd-jwt` formats exploitable.

## Impact

Key attestation proves a credential holder's private key resides in secure hardware. This bypass allows:

- **Forge hardware attestation** -- Software key claims `iso_18045_high` (VAN.5). Server cannot distinguish from genuine hardware.
- **Clone credentials** -- Software key is exportable. Hardware-backed keys are not.
- **Identity fraud** -- In eIDAS 2.0 / EU Digital Identity Wallet, government-issued credentials (national ID, driving licence) can be obtained with forged hardware guarantees, then cloned and shared.
- **LoA bypass** -- Relying parties requiring "high" assurance accept forged credentials.

## Fix

```java
if (isSelfSigned) {
    throw new VCIssuerException(ErrorType.INVALID_PROOF,
        "Self-signed certificates are not accepted for key attestation");
}
CertPathValidator validator = CertPathValidator.getInstance("PKIX");
PKIXParameters params = new PKIXParameters(getTrustAnchors());
params.setRevocationEnabled(false);
validator.validate(certPath, params);
```



---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @ahus1.*

title: [CVE-2026-4874] Server-Side Request Forgery via OIDC token endpoint manipulation
security_topic: validation of client-controlled host used in backchannel logout URL construction
qa_summary: Whether CVE-2026-4874 is exploitable via client-controlled `client_session_host` during backchannel logout, with the answer anchored by the issue description and the maintainer comment proposing validation against administrator-configured allowlisted values.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
## Description

CVE-2026-4874: When processing refresh token requests, Keycloak accepts a `client_session_host` parameter and stores it in the client session without validation. If a client is configured with a backchannel logout URL that includes the `application.session.host` placeholder, Keycloak will substitute this stored value when constructing the logout callback URL.

This means that during logout operations, Keycloak may attempt to send HTTP POST requests to URLs that were provided by the client during token refresh, rather than using only administrator-configured URLs.

**Prerequisites:**
- User must have valid credentials to obtain a refresh token
- Client must be configured with `backchannel.logout.url` attribute containing the `application.session.host` placeholder
- Logout must be triggered (by admin action, user logout, or session timeout)

## Version Affected

26.5.2 and potentially other versions

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy Keycloak with a realm and create a user account
2. Create a public client with:
   - `directAccessGrantsEnabled` set to true
   - `backchannel.logout.url` attribute set to `http://${application.session.host}/callback`
3. Set up an HTTP listener on the same network as Keycloak (e.g., using Python's http.server on port 9999)
4. Obtain tokens via password grant by sending POST to `/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/token` with `grant_type=password`, client_id, username, and password
5. Refresh the token with a custom host by sending POST to `/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/token` with:
   - `grant_type=refresh_token`
   - The refresh_token value
   - `client_session_host=custom-listener:9999`
6. Trigger logout via admin API: POST to `/admin/realms/{realm}/users/{user_id}/logout`
7. Observe that Keycloak sends an HTTP POST request to the custom listener address

## Expected Behavior

The backchannel logout URL should only use administrator-configured values. Client-provided parameters should either be validated against allowed patterns or not be used in URL construction.

## Actual Behavior

Keycloak accepts and uses the client-provided `client_session_host` value when constructing backchannel logout URLs, allowing clients to influence which URLs Keycloak will contact during logout operations.

## Additional Context

This issue has been assigned CVE-2026-4874 for tracking purposes.

The practical impact is limited because:
- Requires valid user credentials
- Requires specific non-default client configuration
- Only affects logout callback URLs
- The feature using placeholders is being considered for deprecation

---

title: FreeMarker templates allow instantiation of new objects and even running OS commands
security_topic: FreeMarker template object instantiation and command execution hardening
qa_summary: Whether Keycloak should disable FreeMarker `?new()` because templates can instantiate arbitrary classes and run OS commands, with the answer anchored in `DefaultFreeMarkerProvider` using `TemplateClassResolver.ALLOWS_NOTHING_RESOLVER` and the FreeMarker resolver docs.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
### Area

login/ui

### Describe the bug

The default FreeMarker configuration allows the `?new()` built-in to
instantiate arbitrary Java classes, including
`freemarker.template.utility.Execute`, which runs shell commands. 

This was reported to the Keycloak security team by Kelvin Mbogo. This was later classified as a hardening issue, and not a CVE. Due to that, it is handled publicly.

Changing Freemarker template file is something only trusted users should be allowed to do, similar to changing any other file (like JavaScript sources or adding extensions). 

### Version

26.2.0 and later

### Expected behavior

The functionality to instantiate new instances is not used by Keycloak's original templates, and therefore it should be disabled.

### Actual behavior

It is enabled. 

### How to Reproduce?

See internal issue.

### Anything else?

Suggested fix: One line added to DefaultFreeMarkerProvider.java after the Configuration is
constructed:

configuration.setNewBuiltinClassResolver(TemplateClassResolver.ALLOWS_NOTHING_RESOLVER);

This tells FreeMarker to reject all ?new() calls in templates, which is the
right default for a server-side template engine processing potentially
untrusted theme content.

Alternatively, SAFER_RESOLVER could be used if any legitimate theme needs
to instantiate specific approved classes, but ALLOWS_NOTHING_RESOLVER is
the safer default.

The documentation should be updated to clarify that Freemarker templates should only be changed by trusted users.  

---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @ahus1.*

comments.author: rmartinc

human_note: This is a clear template engine security hardening issue in Keycloak involving FreeMarker ?new() class instantiation, which can lead to arbitrary object creation and potential OS command execution (Execute utility)—a well-known high-risk template injection class.

title: Email Verify loop when mapping uppercase SAML attribute values to email
security_topic: case-sensitive email comparison causing unwanted re-verification
qa_summary: Whether the SAML email case-mismatch bug that keeps re-adding Verify Email is fixed by PR #39885 and how to avoid it before upgrading to 26.x.

comments.author: ShawnOwczarzak
comments.body:
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

saml

### Describe the bug

When a SAML identity provider has an `Attribute Importer` mapper that maps to `email`, a SAMLResponse attribute value that is identical to the user's email address (except it contains uppercase characters) will trigger a `Verify Email` required action, without any change to the user's email address.

Example: 
User Email: john.doe@domain.com
Incoming Attribute: John.Doe@domain.com 
Mapper Sync Override Mode: Force
Identity Provider Trust Email: Off

Result: 
- User's email remains the same
- User has a `VerifyEmail` required action added to their account




### Version

23.0.5

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

The user does not have a `Verify Email` required action assigned to them when the email from an incoming SAML Response is the same, just with different casing.

### Actual behavior

The user is assigned the `Verify Email` required action even though their email did not change.

### How to Reproduce?

### On Keycloak Side
Setup a SAML Identity Provider.
- Trust Email = Off
- Sync Mode = Force

Setup Attribute Importer on SAML Identity Provider
- Sync Mode = Force
- Attribute Name = TestClaim
- User Attribute Name = email

Setup a user:
- Email: john.doe@domain.com
- Manually link user to IdP configuration (simplifies a bit)

### On IdP Side
Setup attributes:
- TestClaim = JOHN.DOE@domain.com

### Perform SSO Login
- User is assigned a Verify Email required action

### Anything else?

_No response_

comments.author: bkoragan
comments.body:
@ShawnOwczarzak  Seems not a bug on latest release. This was fixed in PR #39885, targeting release was 26.x.

**What changed:** The fix ensures that a case-only difference in the email is no longer treated as a change, so the verification status is left untouched.

**on v23.0.5**: The SAML Attribute Importer mapper used a case-sensitive comparison to decide whether the incoming email differed from the stored one. Since Keycloak stores emails in lowercase, an uppercase value like JOHN.DOE@domain.com was treated as "different" from john.doe@domain.com. This triggered the email update path, which with Trust Email disabled — always set the email to unverified. Combined with the realm's Verify Email setting being enabled, this resulted in the user being assigned a Verify Email required action on every login, even though no actual email change occurred.

If you need this resolved before upgrading to 26.x, I would think of, these two workarounds:
1. Ensure the IdP sends email attribute values in lowercase — this avoids the case mismatch entirely or
2. Enable Trust Email on the Identity Provider — this causes the email to be marked as verified after each brokered login (only if acceptable for your security model)

**I would wait for other reviewers to confirm if any other workarounds and more insights..**

comments.author: ShawnOwczarzak
comments.body:
Thank you @bkoragan! Very helpful. 

Workaround 1 should be enough while we work to get on 26+.

Appreciate the thorough response! 🙂👍

human_note: This is a clear authentication identity-matching issue in Keycloak involving SAML attribute mapping and email verification logic, which directly affects user account state and authentication flows.

title: Log Injection and Audit Forgery in OIDC Authorization Endpoint (client_id parameter)
security_topic: log injection in OIDC authorization endpoint parameters
qa_summary: Whether the OIDC authorization endpoint still allows log injection and audit-forgery via unsanitized parameters, with the answer anchored by the linked PRs/issues #46743, #46740, and #46736 plus the maintainer’s note that #46743 only partially addresses it.

comments.author: Dweep018
comments.body: ### Before reporting an issue - [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them. ### Area oidc ### Describe the bug A log injection vulnerability exists in the OIDC authorization endpoint where the `client_id` parameter is recorded in server logs without neutralization of ANSI escape sequences and control characters. An unauthenticated attacker can inject malicious strings that manipulate the visual output of the Keycloak audit trail. This allows for "Visual Evasion," where critical security warnings (WARN/ERROR) can be disguised as successful information events (INFO/SUCCESS) within a terminal-based monitoring environment. ### Version 26.5.3 ### Regression - [ ] The issue is a regression ### Expected behavior User-provided strings from the OIDC flow, specifically the `client_id`, should be sanitized before being passed to the logging subsystem. All non-printable ASCII characters (0-31) and ANSI escape sequences should be stripped or escaped to ensure the integrity of the audit log and prevent terminal-based manipulation. ### Actual behavior Keycloak reflects the raw, unsanitized `client_id` input into the `org.keycloak.events` log. 1. Visual Evasion: The logging system fails to neutralize ANSI escape codes. An attacker can inject color-coded strings (e.g., green text) into a WARN level log. This contradicts the actual system status (e.g., error="client_not_found") and can deceive security analysts during real-time monitoring. 2. Metadata Corruption: The injected payload successfully breaks the logical structure of the clientId field. By inserting a forged "Success" message directly into the metadata, the attacker compromises the readability and reliability of the audit trail. 3. Search Index Poisoning: Because the raw escape sequences (such as \u001b) are preserved in the log data, keyword-based searches in SIEM platforms (Splunk, ELK) will fail to match the affected strings, allowing malicious activity to evade automated alerting. ### How to Reproduce? 1. Setup: Start a standard Keycloak instance (Quarkus distribution) on Windows from terminal. 2. On any web browser visit `http://localhost:8080/realms/myrealm/account` and you will be redirected to `http://localhost:8080/realms/myrealm/protocol/openid-connect/auth` with necessary client id and parameters. 3. Input payload `fake_client%0D%0A%1b[32m[FORGED+INFO]+User+admin+logged+in+successfully%1b[0m` in the `client_id` parameter and just send the request. 4. Observe the console output. 5. Many different payloads can be tried. Sample Log Output: `2026-04-01 17:35:39,996 WARN [org.keycloak.events] (executor-thread-37) type="LOGIN_ERROR", realmId="84e00b4b-56a5-40a0-b4bf-0531c3c3951b", realmName="myrealm", clientId="fake_client [FORGED INFO] User admin logged in successfully", userId="null", ipAddress="0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1", error="client_not_found"` - `[FORGED INFO] User admin logged in successfully` appears green in terminal. POC: ### Anything else? This issue is a confirmed instance of CWE-117: Improper Output Neutralization for Logs. While the use of structured logging (JSON) may prevent some physical line-breaking issues, it does not resolve the underlying problem of Semantic Poisoning. The presence of non-printable characters in the log "message" or "clientId" fields corrupts the data integrity of the system's security events. This issue exists in every realm including master realm. Suggested Remediation: - Apply a strict validation regex to the client_id parameter and implement a global log formatter that strips all ANSI and control characters before outputting to stdout or log files ## Additional details This issue is partially addressed by https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/46743 , but not fully. See https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/47681#issuecomment-4236505636 for the details on remaining stuff to be fixed.

comments.body: Update: Further testing confirms that the `scope` and `response_type` parameters are also vulnerable to the same. Steps to Reproduce: 1. Same as `client_id` except this time add payloads to `scope` and `response_type` one by one in different requests. 2. Payload tested: `%1B[31mTHIS_IS_RED%1B[0m` Snippet from Terminal:

A common filtering approach sounds like the right direction given the shared input handling across these parameters. Happy to review or test any of the draft PRs if that would be helpful.

@ahus1 Thanks for linking the issue. Just a note that https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/46743 seems to address only query parameters, but OIDC authorization endpoint is not limited to GET request. It could be sent also via POST or some other means (like `request` object or PAR).

So that PR alone is likely not sufficient for addressing this particular issue. But this one should be likely done as a follow-up to that other issue.

> It's my impression that the main reason we need to do this so that security auditing tools won't flag a problem?

Security is usually happier when you remove as much as possible to reduce the attack surface, and that includes publicly available information which includes the map files. Even if we don't know yet how it can be exploited, it is better to not serve them, just in case. 

There is a small possibility that people build their own themes, and then those map files might reveal information that shouldn't be revealed, so this makes it more than "just in case". A comment in the code left there by a developer could be [OSINT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_intelligence) in the hands of an attacker. 

With Claude recently revealing their source code in map files, this is now something all security researchers are looking for.  It would be a tedious task to explain to all of them why keeping the map files is ok. So it is simpler to remove them. 

So this all adds up to "please don't serve map files in production".

### Area

### Version

The confirmation claim should be set in the returned access code.

### Actual behavior

The confirmation claim is missing.

comments.author: graziang
comments.body:
@ryanemerson  From 26.6, token exchange with a sender-constrained `subject_token` is not allowed in any case. It would be useful to support this only when the client that issued the `subject_token` is the same client performing the token exchange request.

The required changes are:

- In `StandardTokenExchangeProvider`, the request should be rejected only if `isSenderConstrainedToken` is true and the token azp is different from the requester client ID. Currently, it is always rejected when `isSenderConstrainedToken` is true.
- If the token is sender-constrained, we need to validate that a DPoP proof or a client certificate is present and it matches the thumbprint of the token. For DPoP, we can use `DPoPUtil.validateBinding`; for mTLS, we can use `MtlsHoKTokenUtil.verifyTokenBindingWithClientCertificate`. Similar checks can be found here:
https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/main/services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/TokenManager.java#L531-L549
- Make sure that the thumbprint is added to the new tokens. For DPoP It should already be handled by the transient mapper. I see you adopted the same approach in the PR https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47315, which looks good to me. But, in other flows for mtls it is added manually (see `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.checkAndBindMtlsHoKToken`).
- For the refresh token, I think it should not be bound, as standard token exchange supports only confidential clients and Keycloak DPoP feature does not bind refresh tokens for confidential clients. For mTLS, I believe it should be the same.
- Add tests for all scenarios and update the documentation. For the doc, you can extend the changes introduced in the recent PR: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47571

As commented before, if the external site is compromised I see no difference between returning a redirect or directly modifying a response, don't know why the redirect is dangerous and the response itself is not (adding a new key for example in a jwks endpoint). Once the site is trusted via the client policy, we are trusting on that site, if the site is compromised, not allowing redirects are not saving us.

IMO we can consider adding some "redirect" options to the HTTP client provider and document them [here](https://www.keycloak.org/server/outgoinghttp) ? That may allow people to avoid redirects if they don't trust their registered clients. It should use same defaults as today.

However it seems to me better to not change the default as I am not sure how much security this really adds... When administrator of client or client-policy trusts some domain, it is his responsibility to make sure that domain is not hacked.

A bit similar case: When client has configured `redirect_uri` as `https://mysite.org` and then `mysite.org` became somehow compromised and would redirected to `https://evil.org` , then there is no option for the browser to avoid redirect. After successful authentication, browser would just redirect to `https://mysite.org`, which would redirect to `https://evil.org` . Keycloak cannot do anything with that.

comments.author: rmartinc
comments.body: @mposolda agree with you, I don't know if some call keycloak is doing requires follow redirects, maybe we should check that before. We can add the option to the http client but this would not be then a CVE.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
This is about blind SSRF which allows testing of Keycloak's network surroundings. 

And the unwanted redirect can happen in multiple ways: 

* A originally valid URL is hacked, and then redirects to for example cloud endpoints. This in security terms would be a scope change, as Keycloak shouldn't be affected by that. 
* A malicious client asks an admin to set them up with their URLs, which are good today, but tomorrow start redirecting to test Keycloak's infrastructure. Very similar to the above. 
* In a dynamic client registration use case, the admin sets up a client policy to allow some client URLs, but then those don't catch the redirect that is happening at runtime. 

If we can't check redirects via client policies, I would vote for a secure-by-default approach: 

* Disable all redirect by default, and note it as a security relevant breaking change in the release notes
* Allow a backwards compatible option that is deprecated to enable redirects, but always log them - this should be possible with a customized redirect policy. This way people can catch up on those redirects, and possibly update URLs.

comments.author: rmartinc
comments.body:
I haven been playing with a different idea that is implementing the restriction directly at `HttpClientProvider` level. This way we can detect and discard any http outgoing connection. I checked and it seems that redirects are managed because they execute again the same client. My dirty test is in this commit https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/commit/8776d4bcfed4011bcfb0994955618401c89a56de. I injected the realm to see if we can access to it, I think that global settings are not OK, we need realm level. My idea would be setting an allow-list (for example another tab in the realm settings -> Security defenses, something like `HTTP outgoing connections` and use a realm attribute to save the permitted list, we should define a syntax, but it can be something like allowed origins, maybe wildcards, I don't know, something like that). I prefer this solution because there are several things that perform outgoing HTTP connections, clients, but also identity providers for sure, and maybe more things. And they have specific permissions (manage-clients and manage-identity-providers respectively). This way we can block anything at the HttpClientProvider level.

The client policy or some other validation can also check the client attributes against the allowed origins defined to return an error at create/update time. This would be a follow-up.

The next thing would be blind connections to other protocols (like ldap or smtp) but I think that those protocols require manage-realm and I think that we are safe with them.

Let me what you think. Probably I'm over-reacting with this.

comments.body:
I think the per-realm settings goes into a good direction. 

Looking at @galarto's commit at https://github.com/galarto/keycloak/commit/650ab0553913690837c99486966903d2ab0bbb17, I see that he's also checking the DNS resolution of the hostname to see if a public DNS hostname could resolve to a denied IP address.

So I'd say checking the resolved IP addresses would be a good additional hardening. 

I'd say allow-lists are usually more secure than deny-lists. But when it comes to denying access to specific subnets, IP addresses might be more common. The commit above has some groups of addresses denied in `validateAddress()` - this could be a checkbox in the UI.

comments.author: mposolda
comments.body:
We can disable all redirects for the HTTP client. However then we still need some backwards compatibility option and hence we should support some kind of "allow list" of the URLs, which would be allowed for redirects. It is very possible that some people even require redirects on purpose due some compatibility or other reasons and hence just disable redirects without any compatibility would be a breaking change.

My vote is to rather configure the allowed redirects at the server level, rather than realm level. It seems it is rather something, which system administrator should approve? Also server level is usually easier (realm level requires admin console changes etc...). I vote for just add an option to `HttpClientProvider` like:
```
allowRedirects = [
  "^https://trusted\\.com.*",
  "^https://trusted2\\.com.*"
]
```
The configuration might be regex (compatibility with `SecureClientUrisPatternExecutor`). WDYT?

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
> So redirects are also checked against the allowed list in the realms just as any other URL.

I don't think this is enough, as a realm-based allow-list is less specific than a per-client allow-list. 

Assuming the following example: 

* `SecureClientUrisPatternExecutor` only allowing `http://example.com/client1/*` for client 1, and `http://example.com/client2/*` for client2
* The realm redirect settings would then need to allow `http://example.com/client1/*` and `http://example.com/client2/*`
* With an IDP idp1 in the realm that might also do redirect, it would also need to allow `http://example.com/idp1/*` for the realm settings.

With this setup, client1 can now redirect also to `http://example.com/client2/*` and `http://example.com/idp1/*` on the realm settings, which is not what an admin wants to achieve.

comments.author: ahus1
comments.body:
> It is very possible that some people even require redirects on purpose due some compatibility or other reasons and hence just disable redirects without any compatibility would be a breaking change.
> My vote is to rather configure the allowed redirects at the server level

If this is disabled by default, and deprecated, I'm ok with that. As it is only about preserving the original behavior, I would be ok to not configure any allow list, but switching the "deny redirect by default" to an "allow redirect and log a warning". With that settings, people can upgrade their setup, analyze the logs for possible violations, and then enable it. 

Side note: "deny redirect by default" should probably log an error message with some meaningful context for admins to follow-up.

title: Make sure that brokering API for retrieve-token can be called only by the confidential clients (new capabilities)
security_topic: client authentication and audience checks for token retrieval endpoint
qa_summary: Whether the brokering retrieve-token API is restricted to confidential clients with client authentication and audience checks, as described in issue #47256 and the linked pull request #47281.

comments.author: mposolda
comments.body:
### Description

As long as feature described in the #47254 is enabled, the brokering API for retrieve-token should be called only by the confidential client and it should require client authentication (currently endpoint is secured only by `Authorization: Bearer` ).

Besides client authentication, it should be checked that access token used for invocation for the token endpoint is either:
- Issued to the client, which invoked the endpoint
- The client, which invoked the endpoint is included in the `aud` claim of the access-token

Besides that, the permissions implemented in #46583 should be checked to make sure that client is permitted to retrieve external tokens of that particular IDP.

Nevertheless I think we can continue with https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/47281 and do the method separation later. That PR fixes the current broken main.
