title: New cffi>=2.0 pin makes cryptography incompatible with other libraries
security_topic: dependency version compatibility affecting security updates
qa_summary: The developer asked if newer cryptography versions (which include security fixes) could be used alongside the existing cffi<2.0 pin, and the answer confirmed that version 46.0.0 works as a workaround.

comments.author: gibsondan
comments.body:
Just flagging that this change https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13448 makes new versions of cryptography incompatible with other packages that pin cffi<2.0 (the specific example that I'm aware of currently is snowflake-connector-python). 

Is there a world in which both versions are allowed?

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
(Pasting this comment here as well since a separate issue is good for this discussion)

Does 46.0.0 work for you? The version bound was only py314 there.

More broadly, I’m not aware of a good answer to this situation, only tradeoffs to choose between. There is no way to express free threaded only dependencies and pip additionally has a constraint where it does not consider pre-release to match >=3.14. Once 3.14 is out we could consider shifting the pin back up to 3.14 but technically that’s still incorrect since we only need it on 3.14t.

Separately, cffi 2.0 is not a semantic versioned library though so compatibility should not be an issue and libraries bounding <2 are under a misapprehension. That said, I imagine you aren’t setting that bound, it’s some other dep.

comments.author: gibsondan
comments.body:
46.0.0 does work, yes - for now there are workarounds, the concern is around having to choose between using snowflake (and whatever other dependencies have strict pins on cffi) and having up to date cryptography fixes going forward. 

(I also filed an issue in the snowflake-connector-python repo, since i'm not sure if they have a good reason for their pin)

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Has an issue/PR been send to snowflake?

As @reaperhulk said, we're kind of between a rock and a hard place here. Would like to find the best solution, but it's probably going to be a compromise either way. The more we can help other libraries raise their bounds, I think the more flexibility we'll have.

(Maybe another way to say this is: no matter what, other libraries that want to be 3.14t compatible will need to raise their bounds.)

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Given that snowflake is the only project we've heard about haaving this issue, and this issue is _really_ on their end (they have a pin for no reason), I'm going to close this from our end.

If there are other projects with upper bounds where this is causing issues, please let us know and we can discuss if it warrants some other action.

title: Add binding for SSL_get0_group_name to support PQC key exchange group detection
security_topic: retrieving negotiated TLS group name for PQC detection
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if adding a binding for SSL_get0_group_name to expose negotiated TLS group names is acceptable, and the maintainers confirmed it by merging cryptography PR #13384 and pyOpenSSL PR #1442.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body:
# Background
I am a developer for a python tool which uses pyOpenSSL to initiate handshakes and probe servers to understand their level of TLS support. I am planning to extend this tool to capture post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness by detecting which key exchange groups are actually negotiated during connections.

Per [OpenSSL docs]( https://docs.openssl.org/3.5/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#history):

> Support for ML-KEM was added in OpenSSL 3.5.
> 
> OpenSSL 3.5 also introduces support for three hybrid ECDH PQ key exchange TLS groups: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024.  

If the conditions are right, one of these hybrid key exchange groups may be used, and I'd like to be able to use pyOpenSSL to capture which group was actually negotiated.

From the [OpenSSL docs](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_CTX_set1_curves/#description), `SSL_get0_group_name` is preferred for this:

> See also [SSL_get0_group_name(3)](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/SSL_get0_group_name/) which returns the name of the negotiated group directly and is generally preferred over SSL_get_negotiated_group().

Here is a link to the openssl source for [SSL_get0_group_name](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/53eb2363a1e6336a40a64b3f7b9f09eca95fabef/ssl/s3_lib.c#L5244) and [PR where it was introduced](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/commit/68668243b176cd2bc53a83c6768d4f39930ba8ed) as of OpenSSL 3.2.

Note: While `SSL_get0_group_name` was introduced in OpenSSL 3.2, the hybrid PQC groups that motivate this request require OpenSSL 3.5.

# Request
I would like to make contributions to both repositories:
1. **cryptography**: Add bindings for `SSL_get0_group_name`. I'm planning to add the binding following the patterns I see for similar functions. My understanding is that it may need appropriate version guards (OpenSSL 3.2+); and looking into how to implement it (looking at things like this which is not quite the same situation as mine): https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5cf5edf1b36afc8400e5b6d3975d0b15380f3eff/src/cryptography/hazmat/backends/openssl/backend.py#L288. 
2. **pyOpenSSL**: Expose this as a new method (e.g., `get_group_name()`) in the SSL module's [Connection class](https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/blob/main/src/OpenSSL/SSL.py#L1948), similar conceptually to `get_cipher_list()`.

# Status

So far, I've:
- followed the [development docs](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/development/) and `nox -e local` succeeds in my local environment
- been reading through c-bindings.rst and ssl.py to understand how I would add a binding given that `SSL_get0_group_name` is only available 
- joined the `#pyca` IRC chat 

# Other discussions

I noticed there have been some similar-ish discussions, for example around setting curves: https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/10797. This was an approach I initially considered.

However, I noticed in the [release notes for OpenSSL 3.5.0](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.5/CHANGES.md#openssl-35) that it appears that at least one of the hybrid PQC groups, `X25519MLKEM768`, is now set by default:

> The default TLS group list setting is now set to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?*X25519:?secp256r1 / ?X448:?secp384r1:?secp521r1 / ?ffdhe2048:?ffdhe3072
> 
> This means two key shares (X25519MLKEM768 and X25519) will be sent by default by the TLS client. GOST groups and FFDHE groups larger than 3072 bits are no longer enabled by default.

I'm a bit new to this area, but either:
a) This means that if a server is configured with `X25519MLKEM768` for the key change group, that my tool will initiate a handshake with it and the group would be negotiated preferentially.
b) Non-PQC groups would need to be excluded by using a setter such as `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list`, in which case I'd need to make contributions for this method as well in both pyOpenSSL and cryptography.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
Sorry for the slow response here. Part of the reason we've taken a while to reply is that the PQC methods are starting to cause non-trivial divergence in the APIs of OpenSSL and its forks (boring, libre, and aws-lc) so we shy away from even thinking about it on occasion.

`SSL_get0_group_name` returns a `char *` of the negotiated group name, but while it's not officially documented looking at the code it appears to be the group name as defined by the TLS specs. I would be okay with that being exposed here. Eventually this binding would also need to live in [rust-openssl](https://github.com/sfackler/rust-openssl) since we're migrating that direction over time as well, but we can land it here first.

Before we merge here we'd like to see the PR opened on the pyOpenSSL side though (knowing all tests will fail of course) so we can agree on the API and see how the binding will be consumed.

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
I did some work a few weeks ago on a similar feature to this in the Python standard library's SSL module. See https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/136306 for details. More specifically, it added the ability to get a list of all supported groups for a given TLS version range and to choose the set of groups to try and use as methods on an SSLContext object, and then later query the group selected on using a method on an SSLSocket object once the handshake is complete. The specific OpenSSL functions used are `SSL_CTX_get0_implemented_groups()`, `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()`, and `SSL_get0_group_name()` (which you mention here).

I'm in the middle of working on adding the ability to select TLS 1.3 cipher suites and to set and get client and server TLS 1.2/1.3 signature algorithms.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body:
@reaperhulk Thanks for the thoughtful response! Acknowledging that this will also need to live in the `rust-openssl` eventually but will start here. I've just opened a PR https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13384 for the change, and will start on the corresponding one for pyOpenSSL per your comment. 

@ronf I wasn't aware, thanks for sharing! I'm only exposing `SSL_get0_group_name` in my first PR, but may also want to expose the other two OpenSSL group functions in the near future.

comments.author: toddabrams
comments.body: @reaperhulk Here is the corresponding (draft) PR in pyOpenSSL clarifying the API and how the binding will be consumed: [pyca/pyopenssl#1442](https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/pull/1442)

comments.author: ronf
comments.body: In addition to https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/136306, I've finished the other work I mentioned above and the changes have all been merged into python:main. The related issues are https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/137197 and https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/138252. You can also see a summary of all these changes at https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#ssl.

comments.body:
Thanks for all the support, @reaperhulk, looks like both PRs have been merged!
* https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/13384
* https://github.com/pyca/pyopenssl/pull/1442

I can next look into what's needed to add support for getting the group in [rust-openssl](https://github.com/sfackler/rust-openssl).

title: CryptographyDeprecationWarning when parsing certifi bundle
security_topic: deprecation timeline for certificate parsing warnings
qa_summary: The deprecation warning for certificates with non‑positive serial numbers will stay until those CAs are removed from certifi, and you can suppress or filter it via Python’s warnings system (see https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html#warnings.filterwarnings).

comments.author: Rogdham
comments.body:
When running the following code:
```py
import certifi
from cryptography.x509 import load_pem_x509_certificates

load_pem_x509_certificates(certifi.contents().encode())
```

…the following warning is raised:
```
CryptographyDeprecationWarning: Parsed a serial number which wasn't positive (i.e., it was negative or zero), which is disallowed by RFC 5280. Loading this certificate will cause an exception in a future release of cryptography.
```

I believe this was introduced in #12853.

I'm opening this issue because I think you would like to get the feedback, because parsing CAs included in `certifi` seems like a reasonable use case. But I understand that this may not be an issue in `cryptography` per se, so feel free to redirect me elsewhere.

---

Versions used:
```
$ uv pip freeze
certifi==2025.8.3
cffi==1.17.1
cryptography==45.0.6
idna==3.10
pycparser==2.22
```

comments.author: alex

title: Since 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` allows arbitrary garbage after `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----`
security_topic: PEM parsing permissiveness for trailing data
qa_summary: The developer asked whether accepting arbitrary data after the PEM END line is a security issue, and the maintainer answered that RFC 7468 permits such data (see RFC 7468 §2).

comments.author: bluetech
comments.body:
Since version 45.0, `load_pem_private_key` accepts arbitrary "garbage" after the `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----` line. Previous versions would fail with the error below. Maybe it's intentional, but it feels like something that *might* not have been intentional so I'm reporting it (can't hurt). It doesn't affect me personally, I only noticed it because I have a test case which tries to make a PEM private key input invalid by appending `b"xxx"` to it which no longer fails (though I should note that it seems adding `b"\nxxx"` doesn't fail in previous versions either).

Example code:

```py
import os

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization


PRIVATE_KEY = b"""-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIGHAgEAMBMGByqGSM49AgEGCCqGSM49AwEHBG0wawIBAQQglcJB9Do845/R18ef
ButMVXFbRqmo/F9kdsIbgTSbDUWhRANCAAR+OeTq+FCd8eRNt9IU16kP3SZ5W8Pj
dS0YwItKLwTyDA4zTupEPWWqAikmw7Xv9DAgiDVFLbzP3C+3mjYmvUkL
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----"""

# OK
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY, password=None)

# Previously would fail, now passes
serialization.load_pem_private_key(PRIVATE_KEY + os.urandom(1000), password=None)
```

Error in 44:

```
ValueError: ('Could not deserialize key data. The data may be in an incorrect format, the provided password may be incorrect, it may be encrypted with an unsupported algorithm, or it may be an unsupported key type (e.g. EC curves with explicit parameters).', [<OpenSSLError(code=503841036, lib=60, reason=524556, reason_text=unsupported)>])
```

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Hmm, interesting -- I'm surprised that garbage was previously rejected. Historically most of the bugs we've gotten are that we've been _too strict_, and we specifically loosened PEM parsing as a result of that.

comments.author: bluetech
comments.body:
Yes I thought it might be intentional.

I was thinking about suggesting a "strict" mode but it isn't worth it IMO.

Either way, it's a bad idea to store or forward user PEM inputs directly, instead should load+serialize and store that instead (preferably in DER format).

comments.author: nbastin
comments.body: As a person who every once in a while pops up to be one of the squeaky wheels here, the current behaviour is (arguably) correct.  RFC 7468 (which is more of a reflection of reality at the time than an actual spec, which never existed during the time when many of these systems were built) makes clear that _any_ data before encapsulation boundaries is permitted (and states parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing such data - [section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7468#section-2)).  It is ambiguous as to whether data is "before" an encapsulation boundary if you never find another `BEGIN`, but plenty of systems generate such files and thus failing to parse them puts a burden on users.

MAY   This word, or the adjective "OPTIONAL", mean that an item is

   particular marketplace requires it or because the vendor feels that

The whole RFC is written in a confusing way. Unless there's a clear reason our behavior either a) violates the spec, b) harms interoperability, c) is a security issue, I'd be inclined to leave it as is.

title: [Feature request] Allow to define tag length for object AESGCM
security_topic: setting custom AES-GCM tag length in cryptography library
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to configure a 12-byte GCM authentication tag in the cryptography library, and the answer referenced the cryptography.io GCM mode documentation as the concrete source.

comments.author: braquino
comments.body:
Hello,

I'm working with DLMS protocol: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEC_62056

It uses AES GCM 128 encryption for secure comunication.
I would like to use cryptography lib to decrypt those DLMS payloads, but it's not possible, because when I create a `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM` object, I'm not allowed to set the tag length to 12 bytes, it uses hard coded 16 bytes.
(12 bytes is defined on DLMS standard)

Looking at the Rust code, seems that the Rust struct allows the length setting, but the python wrapper doesn't.

As a workaround I'm using pycryptodome:

``` python
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce, mac_len=12)
```

But would be nice not having to manage two cryptography libs.

Thank you in advance.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Tag lengths can be set using the more flexible https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/symmetric-encryption/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.modes.GCM API. While the one-shot AEAD is preferrable where possible, this API si more general.

comments.author: braquino
comments.body:
Ok, thank you, it works
```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import (
  Cipher, algorithms, modes
)
decryptor = Cipher(
    algorithms.AES(key),
    modes.GCM(nonce, gcm_tag, min_tag_length=12),
).decryptor()

decryptor.authenticate_additional_data(aad)
plain = decryptor.update(ciphertext) + decryptor.finalize()
```

human_note: Accepted because the question is a valid cryptographic configuration issue and the answer correctly provides the appropriate lower-level API workaround.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
The issue here is that you have a PKCS#8 key and the PEM headers are `BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY`, however PKCS#8 keys are supposed to have a `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` header. https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/12993 is a similar issue.

How was this PEM generated? Is there some library you used, or was it constructed "manually"

comments.author: joshdcu
comments.body:

comments.body: No problem! @alex, would this be considered a regression that will be fixed in an upcoming release or are users expected to modify their private keys so that the headers match what is expected by PKCS#8?

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Strictly speaking this is part of the PKCS#8 RFC, so we don't really
consider it a bug -- if this was _super_ widespread we might add a

title: Can adding some bindings (for OpenSSL-3.x) enable support for SM2?
security_topic: SM2 algorithm support in cryptography library
qa_summary: The developer asked if adding OpenSSL‑3.x bindings could enable SM2 support, and the maintainer replied that it requires explicit implementation, pointing to the proposed API in PR #5894 as the concrete reference.

comments.author: xiaoge1001
comments.body: At https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/commit/c28bfb352ab1f390900ef92856a9570aadd5fe2c, we can use EVP_PKEY_set_alias_type  API to using SM2 algorithms. However, the latest version has removed these APIs. Is there any other way to make cryptography support the SM2 algorithm?

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
We no longer have workarounds for using unsupported features like this. To use SM2 in cryptography we'd need to implement support explicitly. It would likely look like the API proposed in https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/5894 but using the rust-openssl bindings like we do in our current codebase. If you want to contribute a PR I'd be willing to review, but there are a few things we'll require:
* SM2 keys should **not** be allowed to be used with ECDSA and should instead only use a `sign` method on their objects that supports `SM2Sign`. I want to see a concrete use case before allowing ECDSA signing. These keys should not be registered against the EC key types.
* SM2 signing should only work with SM3 hashing per spec.

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
There wouldn't be any serialization in decap. The current API proposal isn't stateless, it expects you will have loaded an `MLKEM768DecapKey` and then called `decap` on it with the ciphertext.

There is a strong desire to not expose expanded decap keys as a serializable type for a variety of reasons (see: https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/122/materials/slides-122-pquip-the-great-private-key-war-of-25-00 for a bit of context), so I'm interested in what the SSH protocol's requirements are for this. I'm guessing you need to be able to obtain encapsulation keys as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, but what else?

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
SSH requires access to the public key as bytes (1184 bytes long for mlkem768x25519-sha256), along with the 32 byte X25519 public key. It concatenates these and encodes the combination as an SSH string (4 bytes of length followed by concatenated raw key bytes) and sends this public key data in an MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT message

When the server receives the INIT message, it extracts the public keys and calls encaps() on the PQ public key bytes and gets back a random secret and cipher text. The cipher text (1088 bytes) is combined with X25519 shared bytes (32 bytes) and sent as a concatenated SSH string in a MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY message.

The client decrypts the cipher text with decaps() using its private key and creates a shared key made of the random secret and EC shared bytes concatenated and passed into a SHA-256 hash. The server has the same secret bytes and EC shared bytes, and it does the same. There's some other stuff here related to signing with the SSH server's host key, but that's not relevant for this discussion.

I have to admit I don't know the exact formatting of the ML-KEM public key bytes in liboqs, but whatever liboqs returns from its keypair() function is exactly what SSH needed to put on the wire.

* LibreSSL will be using the boring implementation, but as of 4.1.0 their release notes say `Imported ML-KEM 768 and 1024 from BoringSSL (not yet public API).`

I had a sync with @simo5 - I believe he was in some earlier discussions, and he conveyed (at a high level) some of the expectations in this project.  These include:

In terms of which additional backend(s), does the project have any preference?

3. 100% code coverage.

For Red Hat, ML-DSA is the higher priority and I want to work toward delivering that first.  (I did not see a github issue for ML-DSA so I will make a new one).  Is addition of ML-DSA separately and prior to ML-KEM acceptable for you?  (ML-KEM design discussion can proceed in any case).

Fraser

comments.author: reaperhulk
comments.body:
That is an immense diff (+8000). I appreciate that it contains roughly everything, but let's strip this down to bare essentials to start reviewing and potentially landing more effectively.

Looking at it a bit, the APIs you've defined for MLDSA are similar to what we did for Edwards curves. However, it is an explicit non-goal of this project to use expanded forms of MLDSA or MLKEM keys -- we will support seed only. Hence, `private_bytes_raw` is not an API we want to support unless it outputs the bare seed. In the proposed API for MLKEM in this thread we have `from_seed_bytes`, which I think you're trying to match with `from_private_bytes`, but due to the expanded vs seed ambiguity I'd prefer the former name for MLDSA as well.

To make some forward progress here I'd suggest the following. Let's pick MLDSA, strip it down to a single key size, and land that. Doing that has this ordering of PRs:
1) Vectors for ML-DSA testing
2) Land impl for boring or aws-lc + docs + tests
3) Followups for other impls.

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
I just did an interoperability test between this ML-KEM support (using BoringSSL) and a prior implementation I had done on top of liboqs. Everything looks good. The public_bytes_raw() call on the public key is exactly what was needed on the wire by SSH, and so was the ciphertext returned from the encap call. I confirmed that I could exchange the 32-byte secret successfully in both directions.

As expected, there was no requirement to serialize the private key data. So, the fact that this API operates only on the seed and not the expanded key will not be a problem.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Excellent. I think this is all benefitting from teh fact that ML-KEM's cryptographic API is much better designed (with the exception of seed vs. expanded form) and has way fewer parameters than previous cryptographic algorithms (e.g., no multiple representations of signature like ECDSA, or 19 different parameters like RSA PSS).

comments.author: ronf
comments.body:
Agreed!

On that note, has there been any consideration for adding SNTRUP support to PyCA? It has basically an identical API, and it has been providing quantum-resistant crypto in SSH since OpenSSH 8.0 released in 2019, dating back to before ML-KEM was selected as the new standard. Both SNTRUP and ML-KEM are supported by liboqs, so I'm actually sharing a wrapper between those today in AsyncSSH, but at some point it would be nice to drop liboqs as an additional dependency.

comments.author: alex
comments.body: No plan for SNTRUP ATM. My sense is that ML-KEM has won at this point and nothing is likely to use SNTRUP for anythign new.

title: Cryptography parsed a CRL file with the authorityCertSerialNumber set to 0.
security_topic: validation of authorityCertSerialNumber zero value in CRL parsing
qa_summary: The developer asked whether parsing an authorityCertSerialNumber of 0 violates RFC5280 and constitutes a bug, and the maintainer replied it is intentional and allowed, referencing issue #10247.

comments.author: onepeople158
comments.body:
Version:
cryptography-44.0.2

Hello Developer:
I have a CRL file where the authorityCertSerialNumber field in the AKI extension is set to 0. Cryptography successfully parsed the authorityCertSerialNumber field without any errors. However, according to RFC5280, the authorityCertSerialNumber field stores the certificate serial number, which must be a positive integer.So, is this a bug?

Code:
```
from cryptography.x509 import load_pem_x509_crl, load_der_x509_crl
from cryptography.x509 import ExtensionNotFound
import sys

def load_crl(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
        crl_data = f.read()
    try:
        crl = load_pem_x509_crl(crl_data)
    except ValueError:
        crl = load_der_x509_crl(crl_data)
    return crl

def print_crl_issuer(file_path):
    crl=load_crl(file_path)
    aki_extension = None
    try:
        for ext in crl.extensions:
             if ext.oid == x509.oid.ExtensionOID.AUTHORITY_KEY_IDENTIFIER:
                    aki=ext.value
                    print(aki.authority_cert_issuer)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error parsing CRL: {e}")

file_path = 'crl_aki_serial_0.der'
print_crl_issuer(file_path)
```
Test Case:

[crl_aki_serial_0.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/19668466/crl_aki_serial_0.zip)

comments.author: alex
comments.body: Yes, it's fairly intentional. We also allow negative serial numbers (both there, and for certificate's serial numbers), as a result of a large number of certs in the ecosystem still. See #10247.

security_topic: estimate for adding post-quantum cryptography support
qa_summary: The developer asked for an estimate on when post‑quantum algorithm support (e.g., ML‑KEM) will be added, and the maintainer responded that there is no timeline but expressed hope for ML‑KEM in the next release and referenced https://cryptography.io/en/latest/statements/state-of-openssl/ as a source.

comments.author: h-vetinari
comments.body:
This is a continuation of #9795 for newer versions. The points here are simply harvested from the feature list in openssl's [`NEWS.md`](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/NEWS.md), not all of them are necessarily applicable to cryptography (but I don't know how to make that determination, so I opted to err on the side of completeness). Please feel free to prune/edit/expand the list as you see fit.

* OpenSSL v3.3
  * [x] Added a new EVP_DigestSqueeze() API. This allows SHAKE to squeeze multiple times with different output sizes.
  * [x] New atexit configuration switch, which controls whether the OPENSSL_cleanup is registered when libcrypto is unloaded.

* OpenSSL v3.4

* OpenSSL v3.5
  * [ ] Support for PQC algorithms
    * [ ] ML-KEM (#12824)
    * [ ] ML-DSA
    * [ ] SLH-DSA
  * [ ] Support added for opaque symmetric key objects (EVP_SKEY).

comments.author: deivse
comments.body:
For examples on how the ExtensionPolicy API can be used, you can reference the tests, for example this one:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/5e899038809a0895f75423524dcb832a580b77de/tests/x509/verification/test_verification.py#L383

### There are two main differences between a ClientVerifier and a ServerVerifier:
1. A ServerVerifier is built with a specific `subject`, and the verification will fail if the certificate doesn't contain a SAN extension which matches the `subject` specified in `build_server_verifier`. So this is intended to be used when you know who the certificate must belong to, which is the case when connecting to a server via https. In many other cases you don't know the subject in advance. Then ClientVerifier can be used, which doesn't require that the SAN extension contains a specific value.
Despite not knowing the exact subject, you may still have eg. a whitelist of possible subjects, and after calling `ClientVerifier.verify`, you can access the subjects from the SAN extension via `VerifiedClient.subjects`.

2. The default EE extension policies check the EKU extension. For ClientVerifier, it is required to have the ClientAuth EKU, and for ServerVerifier, ServerAuth. The EKU is not currently user configurable (although this may be exposed later via a method on PolicyBuilder), however you can create a custom extension validator callback and use a custom extension policy that will constrain the EKU in any way you want.

### Why some properties are on `Policy` but not on `PolicyBuilder` 
The current `Policy` class is basically a direct mapping to python from a rust struct that contains context required for chain building and certificate verification/validation. The main purpose of the `Policy` class is to expose this context to python extension validation callbacks (as set by `ExtensionPolicy.may_be_present` and similar methods) so that the callbacks can express complex constraints based on these parameters. There wasn't really a per-property decision process on whether to include something there or not, but I don't think it hurts to have extra stuff there since we can't envision every use case. Some of these properties, for example, EKU, as you have noted, can not yet be configured by the user. However they can still be useful, for example you might want to write a verification callback for another extension that makes a decision based on what EKU value is required by the policy.

You are right that this might be a bit confusing currently, and there is a slight leakage of implementation details into the public API. However this could not be reasonably avoided currently I would say, and I would err on the side of the `Policy` class providing access to extra properties rather than trying to predict every use case. Maybe there's something to be said about the naming - there is a clear parallel between `PolicyBuilder` and `Policy`, but, as @loewexy said, not all properties configurable via the builder are accessible on `Policy` and vice versa. I don't have any good ideas on how to improve this currently, but maybe we _can_ come up with a better name for `Policy`

comments.author: deivse
comments.body:
Oh yeah, and regarding having the extension policies or the store as properties on `Policy`:
1. For the extension policies, I don't see a strong use case currently, and it would require creating a mapping from rust to python (which currently is only the other way around), which is not something you want to do, trust me 😄
2. The store is not really part of the `Policy`, since it's potentially specific to verifying a single certificate, whereas a policy (conceptually here, not necessarily the `Policy` class) can be used to verify any number of certificates issued by different CAs.

That second point brings me to a renaming idea, which might actually make sense, but it's a breaking change unfortunately - instead of renaming `Policy` it would maybe make more sense to rename `PolicyBuilder` to something like `VerifierBuilder`. It sounds worse, but does make more sense conceptually imo, since what you actually build with it are verifiers, not policies, and you can also set things that are not part of the policy - the certificate store. Any thoughts on this, @alex, @reaperhulk?

DISCLAIMER: I sound pretty confident about some of these things here, but I'm not a core contributor here, so take what I say with a small grain of salt 😄 I just happened to work on this feature.

comments.author: deivse
comments.body: And @loewexy, I think this would indeed benefit from a guide-style documentation entry, so if you will be able to take some of the stuff I laid out here and convert it to that format, that would be a great contribution!

qa_summary: The developer asked whether using the PKCS#7 bindings to verify CMS messages is safe, and the maintainer replied that it is not recommended and referenced PR #12267 which tracks proper support.

comments.author: lgcCerti
comments.body:
Hello,

Currently I'm attempting to implement a portion of the [OpenSSL cms](https://docs.openssl.org/3.1/man1/openssl-cms/) command line application in pure python to avoid calling subprocess in my software to validate some CMS messages. Basically, the following command:

```
echo veryCoolCMSdata | openssl cms -verify -binary -inform der -CAfile ./mychain.pem 
```

 I saw wider CMS support was "dropped" with https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/924

From there I've taken notice of the cryptography module and how it implemented OpenSSL bindings. This was used to advise someone to verify using a modified version of a "_pkcs7_verify" helper in the codebase on https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/issues/6413 which called the backend functions directly. While the OP of that thread claimed it worked for his CMS case, I haven't managed to reproduce the success.

_In my attempts, I've noticed the bindings for functions such as CMS_verify and d2i_CMS_bio in the OpenSSL Backend don't seem to exist._

Currently I'm a bit concerned whether attempting the procedure with the PKCS7 bindings is advisable for validating CMS, even if there's a good PR for verifying PKCS7 at https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/12267. Is it safe to do? I have a lack of experience with this.

Thanks

comments.author: alex
comments.body: We definitely do not recommend using the PKCS#7 bindings directly at this point. #12267 tracks adding proper support, and is being actively worked on, so I'm going to close this as a duplicate of that.

title: verify_directly_issued_by compares encoded subjects rather than subject values
security_topic: policy on distinguished name comparison in certificate verification
qa_summary: The developer asked whether verify_directly_issued_by should compare issuer/subject values using StringPrep per RFC 5280 rather than ASN.1 encoding, and the maintainer answered that the library follows the CABF Baseline Requirements (section 7.1.4.1) and RFC 5280, confirming the current behavior and indicating a bias against implementing StringPrep.

comments.author: wkral-netlync
comments.body:
In a certificate being verified the issuer name attributes are encoded using PRINTABLESTRING, while the issuer cert encodes it's subject name attributes with UTF8STRING. When using `verify_directly_issued_by` an exception is thrown:
```
ValueError: Issuer certificate subject does not match certificate issuer.
```

The comparison is done with the ANS.1 encoded values:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/blob/ad537914d55373f00c1be3eb7aaea1851859d042/src/rust/src/x509/certificate.rs#L331-L339

I think that the comparison should follow the rules outlined in [RFC 5280 Section 7.1 Internationalized Names in Distinguished Names](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5280#section-7.1) which would ignore the ASN.1 encoding and compare the values.

The cause of the exception was difficult to find since two `x509.Certificate` objects subjects do compare positively in python:

```python
untrusted.issuer == issuer.subject  # True
```

comments.author: alex
comments.body: The behavior we have there matches what's in the CABF BRs https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/TLSBRv2.0.4.pdf at 7.1.4.1

comments.author: wkral-netlync
comments.body:
Reading through that portion of the CABF spec the relevant section seems to be:

>For each CA Certificate in the Certification Path, the encoded content of the Subject
>Distinguished Name field of a Certificate SHALL be byte‐for‐byte identical among all
>Certificates whose Subject Distinguished Names can be compared as equal according to RFC
>5280, Section 7.1, and including expired and revoked Certificates.

It clearly says byte-for-byte identical, but I find it slightly odd that it points to the same portion of the RFC that I did which states:

> Conforming implementations MUST use the LDAP StringPrep profile
> (including insignificant space handling), as specified in [[RFC4518](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4518)],
> as the basis for comparison of distinguished name attributes encoded
> in either PrintableString or UTF8String.

It seems a bit contradictory to me.

The CABF spec seems to only cover TLS Server Certificates, but there are many other x509 certificate chain use cases, and the reason I've been trying to use `verify_directly_issued_by` is because the `x509.verification` API only covers server certs and client certs and checks for the key usage attributes. I'm working with JWS [RFC 7515](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515) and CMS [RFC 5652](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5652) and I think there are probably several other cases. It would be useful if cryptography could be used more generally for certificate chain verification without having to go deep into the hazmat portion of the library. This is especially true with PyOpenSSL having deprecated all of the x509 portions of it's library in favour of cryptography.

comments.author: alex
comments.body:

StringPrep behavior is _extremely_ disfavored at this point, so we're going
to have a strong bias against implementing that.

I understand and sympathize with that position and if I was able to control the certs being verified I'd author them with consistent encoding. Unfortunately these are production certificates in the wild and there are millions of them in this form.

title: Missing not_valid_after_utc property.
security_topic: regression of certificate attribute availability in cryptography library
qa_summary: The developer asked whether the `not_valid_after_utc` property was intentionally removed in Cryptography 44.0.0 and how to handle it; the maintainer confirmed the property still exists in version 44.0.0, citing a REPL demonstration showing the attribute.

comments.author: vog
comments.body:
It seems that Cryptography 44.0.0 introduced a regression by replacing `not_valid_after_utc`/`not_valid_before_utc` properties with their non-"utc" suffixed counterparts.

Background:

Not long ago the Cryptography library deprecated the `not_valid_after` property and encouraged everyone to switch to `not_valid_after_utc`:

* #9186
* #9667

This is what we in requests_pkcs12, as downstream library, also did:

* m-click/requests_pkcs12#51
* m-click/requests_pkcs12#52

Now with Cryptography 44.0.0,  the `not_valid_after_utc` suddenly vanished and only `not_valid_after` remained:

* m-click/requests_pkcs12#58

Questions:

* Is this change back to a deprecated properties intentional?
  * If so, how are downstream libraries like `requests_pkcs12` supposed to deal with that in a backwards compatible way?

title: Wrong type annotation for is_signature_valid
security_topic: type annotation mismatch for cryptography public key validation
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that the type signature for `CertificateRevocationList.is_signature_valid` is correct because a certificate can contain a public key not valid for issuing, and they should refer to the Cryptography library’s `CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes` documentation (https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes).

comments.author: userappgate
comments.body:
See this example code:

```python3
from cryptography import x509

def is_signature_valid(crl: bytes, ca_cert: bytes) -> bool:
    crl_object = x509.load_pem_x509_crl(crl)

    ca_cert_object = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(ca_cert)

    return crl_object.is_signature_valid(ca_cert_object.public_key())
```

mypy fails with

```
test.py:8: error: Argument 1 to "is_signature_valid" of "CertificateRevocationList" has incompatible type "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey | X25519PublicKey | X448PublicKey"; expected "DSAPublicKey | RSAPublicKey | EllipticCurvePublicKey | Ed25519PublicKey | Ed448PublicKey"  [arg-type]
```

I noticed that while migrating the codebast on ubuntu noble (that uses 41.0.7-4ubuntu0.1), while on ubuntu jammy (that uses 3.4.8-1ubuntu2.2) mypy does not complain.

The codebase is quite different, but the code seems to work on both versions so I think the mistake is in the type annotations (unless I am doing something wrong, of course).

Thanks

comments.author: alex
comments.body:
Unfortunately, that's correct.

A certificate can _carry_ a public key that's not valid for issuing certificates, and the type signatures reflect this.

You can use https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/asymmetric/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.types.CertificateIssuerPrivateKeyTypes to check for this (either with `typing.cast()` or an `isinstance` check.)

title: Thread-safety: data race in ImagingDefaultArena block cache (memory_get_block / memory_return_block)
security_topic: thread-safety of Pillow's block cache in multi-threaded usage
qa_summary: The developer asked if the ImagingDefaultArena data race is a security vulnerability and whether a fix exists; the maintainer answered that Pillow 11.0.0 (see issue #8238) includes threading fixes, so upgrading resolves it.

comments.author: ctkhanhly
comments.body:
### What did you do?

Used `asyncio.to_thread()` / `ThreadPoolExecutor` to offload PIL Image operations (create, load, resize, encode) to multiple threads concurrently.

### What did you expect to happen?

Thread-safe access to PIL Image allocation/deallocation, or documentation stating that multi-threaded usage requires `set_blocks_max(0)`.

### What actually happened?

`ImagingDefaultArena` in `src/libImaging/Storage.c` uses shared mutable state (`blocks_cached`, `blocks_pool`) without any synchronization. When multiple threads call `memory_get_block` / `memory_return_block` concurrently (which happens when PIL's GIL-releasing C operations run in parallel), data races can occur:

```c
// memory_get_block (line 310) — no lock
if (arena->blocks_cached > 0) {
    arena->blocks_cached -= 1;                          // ← read-modify-write, no lock
    block = arena->blocks_pool[arena->blocks_cached];   // ← concurrent read, no lock
}

// memory_return_block (line 347) — no lock
if (arena->blocks_cached < arena->blocks_max) {
    arena->blocks_pool[arena->blocks_cached] = block;   // ← concurrent write, no lock
    arena->blocks_cached += 1;                          // ← read-modify-write, no lock
} else {
    free(block.ptr);
}
```

**Race scenario** (two threads returning blocks simultaneously):
```
Thread A: reads blocks_cached = 19 (< blocks_max 20)
Thread B: reads blocks_cached = 19 (same stale value — no lock)
Thread A: writes blocks_pool[19] = block_A, increments to 20
Thread B: writes blocks_pool[19] = block_B (OVERWRITES block_A)

Result: block_A.ptr is permanently lost — malloc'd, never free'd.
```

Similarly, `memory_get_block` can hand the same cached block to two threads simultaneously (use-after-free / double-free risk).

The race window is narrow under the GIL (requires concurrent C-level execution during GIL-released operations like resize/encode), making it hard to reproduce in simple tests. Under sustained high-concurrency production workloads with longer GIL-released operations, the race triggers more frequently.

**Workaround:** `Image.core.set_blocks_max(0)` disables the cache entirely, eliminating the shared mutable state.

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS: Linux x86_64
* Python: 3.12
* Pillow: 10.4.0

```python
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from PIL import Image

# This triggers concurrent access to ImagingDefaultArena from multiple threads.
# The race is probabilistic and more likely under sustained production load
# with longer GIL-released operations (resize, encode).
async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    loop.set_default_executor(ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20))

    resolutions = [(512, 512), (1024, 1024), (1536, 1536), (2048, 2048)]

    async def process(res):
        def _work():
            img = Image.new("RGB", res)
            img.load()
        await asyncio.to_thread(_work)

    for _ in range(1000):
        await asyncio.gather(*[process(resolutions[i % 4]) for i in range(20)])

asyncio.run(main())
```

**Additional context:**

PIL's C extensions release the GIL during image operations, enabling true parallelism in thread pools. However, `ImagingDefaultArena` is a process-global struct with no mutex or atomic operations protecting its state. When `asyncio.to_thread` dispatches PIL work to a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, multiple threads can call `memory_get_block` / `memory_return_block` concurrently during the GIL-released portions of operations like `Image.resize()` or `Image.save()`.

This is particularly relevant for:
- Python's increasing use of `asyncio.to_thread` for GIL-releasing C extensions
- The upcoming free-threaded CPython (PEP 703), which will remove the GIL entirely and make this race trivially triggerable

**Suggested fixes:**
1. Add a `pthread_mutex` around `blocks_cached` / `blocks_pool` access in `memory_get_block` and `memory_return_block`
2. Or use per-thread arenas (eliminates contention)
3. Or document that the block cache is not thread-safe and recommend `set_blocks_max(0)` for multi-threaded usage

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
You have said that you are using Pillow 10.4.0. Is there any particular reason you are not using the latest version of Pillow?

#8238 helped threading in Storage.c in Pillow 11.0.0, so would you be interested in testing a more recent version?

Any fix for this issue will be applied only to new Pillow releases. https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/index.html
> Please use the latest version of Pillow. Functionality and security fixes should not be expected to be backported to earlier versions.

comments.author: wiredfool
comments.body:
Do you have a specific test case/code path where you've got a provable issue here, or is this a theoretical issue from reading/llming the code?

1) You're testing a version from before free-threading support. Newer versions have explicit handling for this for free threaded builds. (using `PyMutex_Lock/UnLock`, which compiles to a noop for GIL builds)

2) We do release the GIL for long running operations, but the GIL releases are generally around tight loops or calls out to third party library calls (e.g. `webpAnimDecoderGetNext`). A quick scan of the code isn't showing any mallocs or similar in any of the locations where we're releasing the GIL. (in the code, anywhere where `ImagingSectionEnter/Leave` are called). 

Specifically looking at the code for resize, the GIL is dropped in the `ImagingResampleHorizontal* and ImagingResampleVertical*` methods of `Resample.c`, all of which take in `imIn` and `imOut`. (e.g. https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/Resample.c#L543)

The other fork of the code calls `ImagingTransform`, passing in an `imOut`, and these operations only drop the GIL around the tight loops. (e.g. https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/Geometry.c#L1010)

> It could have been a good idea if we were starting Pillow from scratch, but for a library concerned with backwards compatibility, I don't think it can be achieved without rewrites that seem excessive.

title: Security concerns when loading user-provided fonts: Can they contain malware?

qa_summary: The developer asked whether loading user‑provided fonts with ImageFont.truetype could be a security risk, and the maintainer answered by referencing Pillow’s OSS‑Fuzz font fuzzing and the specific fix documented in the Pillow 8.2.0 release notes (memory DoS in ImageFont).

comments.author: daeeros
comments.body:
Hello! I have a question regarding the security of using user-provided fonts in Pillow.

I'm implementing a feature where a font uploaded by a user is loaded as a byte stream and then used in `ImageFont.truetype`. The loading and usage look like this:

```python
font_22 = None

if creator_profile.quote_font_file_id is not None:
    downloaded_font = await pl.app.backend._get_file(creator_profile.quote_font_file_id)
    if downloaded_font:
        font_22 = ImageFont.truetype(BytesIO(downloaded_font.content), 22)
```

My question:
How safe is it to accept fonts as byte streams and load them through ImageFont.truetype? Is there a risk that malicious fonts could contain viruses or otherwise disrupt the application? Are there any known vulnerabilities with font handling in Pillow or best practices for validating fonts before use?

Thank you very much in advance for any guidance!

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Hi. This is a security problem that we consider when developing Pillow.

[One](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/actions/workflows/cifuzz.yml) of our GitHub Actions uses [OSS-Fuzz](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz) to check for security problems that may occur when [opening and using random font data](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5bff2f3b2894ec6923c590d0c37b18177d0634bd/Tests/oss-fuzz/fuzzers.py#L31-L43).

When a problem in Pillow is found, we endeavour to fix it. You can see and example of a problem that was found and fixed in the past at https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/8.2.0.html#fix-memory-dos-in-imagefont

As far as what you should be doing as a user, https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/index.html
> Please use the latest version of Pillow. Functionality and security fixes should not be expected to be backported to earlier versions.

If you do not use our pre-built wheels, and instead compile Pillow from source, I would also suggest using the latest version of dependencies - in this case, FreeType.

additional information that I may have forgotten to mention is that `zPug_3.heic` is three images (or frames) in one file:

```
<pillow_heif.as_plugin.HeifImageFile image mode=RGB size=64x64>
<pillow_heif.as_plugin.HeifImageFile image mode=L size=64x64>
<pillow_heif.as_plugin.HeifImageFile image mode=RGB size=96x64>
```

> git bisect points to [84e275d](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/84e275d90629bfdf508f81a1142eddd5d5ea46e4) from PR #8390:

thanks, very good finding

comments.author: bigcat88
comments.body:
It turns out that when the second frame has a different mode, a new `Image.core.new` is not created after that commit, and the mode does not change, therefore, in pillow_heif, the wrong **stride** is calculated based on wrong mode(RGB vs L), and the `libde265` decoder crashes as it expects more data.

Edit: the reason is correct(wrong mode for `Image.core`), and it crashes here:

https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/51c577df825cee6917bd55912f6cb1c9b8df5f84/src/PIL/Image.py#L887


Can we revert this commit https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/84e275d90629bfdf508f81a1142eddd5d5ea46e4 ?

comments.author: wiredfool
comments.body:
History says that this hasn't changed since the PIL fork, except for the most recent batch of changes. I can see where we could get multi image container formats (gif or webpanim or tiff) where the frame type could change, esp something like rgb->rgba, though our internal decoders might handle that directly.  Obviously at least one external decoder has been relying on this. 

I'd say revert, but finding a good test case for this might be the hardest bit.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
My commit was inspired by @homm's comment that he considered it a bug [when an image changed size after it was loaded.](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8341#discussion_r1760807429)

I think `load()` is a method that many users are probably not even aware of, and so they might the behaviour unexpected if it is internally called and the mode changes.
```python
from PIL import Image
im = Image.open(...)
print(im.mode)  # L
print(im.copy().mode)  # RGB
```

When I made the mode change, none of our internal plugins had to be updated to handle it. GifImagePlugin changes modes between frames, sure, but the the core image can be reset before loading, in its own `load_prepare()`. TiffImagePlugin creates a new core image at the end of `seek()`. It doesn't look like WebP does change modes between frames.

@bigcat88 a few questions - do you disagree with my idea in theory? Do you think pillow_heif could be updated handle this new way of doing things? Is the problem simply that this change was made suddenly, and you would prefer a deprecation?

comments.author: bigcat88
comments.body:
> When I made the mode change, none of our internal plugins had to be updated to handle it.

I don't know how common it is that frames have different modes.
I know that in modern formats like AVIF or HEIF this is supported, and this can happen.
*But I do never see real world examples of this, and not custom crafted images*


> @bigcat88 a few questions - do you disagree with my idea in theory? Do you think pillow_heif could be updated handle this new way of doing things? Is the problem simply that this change was made suddenly, and you would prefer a deprecation?

I don't mind updating "pillow_heif", that's why I created issue to determine the way to do it, knowing that here everyone can always get an answer to the question of what is best


> TiffImagePlugin creates a new core image at the end of `seek()`

After receiving a hint that TiffImagePlugin does this in the seek method, in theory it should be done the same way.

Like this:

```python3
    def seek(self, frame: int):
        if not self._seek_check(frame):
            return
        self.__frame = frame
        self._init_from_heif_file(frame)  # this fills  `self._size` and `self._mode` with new frame info

        if pil_version[:3] != "10.":
            # Pillow 11.0+
            # We need to create a new core image object on second and
            # subsequent frames in the image. Image may be different size/mode.
            # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/8439
            self.im = Image.core.new(self._mode, self._size)

        _exif = getattr(self, "_exif", None)  # Pillow 9.2+ do no reload exif between frames.
        if _exif is not None and getattr(_exif, "_loaded", None):
            _exif._loaded = False  # pylint: disable=protected-access
```

It seems to work and tests passed successfully, many thanks to everyone for help.

 I think the issue can be closed?

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
I still think it's better to revert this, especially now, when we realise not only TiffImagePlugin relies on this behaviour.
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8390/files#r1764864935

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Reverted and deprecated?

I think the ideal behaviour when changing modes between frames is actually to set `self._im = None` at the end of seek - https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/8392. I think `load()` shouldn't change the image mode, and in theory at least, `load()` doesn't have to be called after `seek()`, so if there's a core image with the wrong mode hanging around, it can be discarded.

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
> is actually to set self._im = None

This will lead to unnecessary memory allocation if all frames have the same size and mode. The previous implementation of `load_prepare` was straightforward: it prepared `self.im` with the correct mode and size, so there was no need to worry about handling `self.im` in the plugins.

> I think load() shouldn't change the image mode

I fully agree, just like with size changes, which I also tried to fix, as you might remember. But I don't quite understand how this would happen if we return to the previous `load_prepare` behavior.

> load() doesn't have to be called after seek()

Possibly. But I'm specifically talking about `load_prepare`, which I believe is the correct API for managing the `self.im` object.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Returning to the previous `load_prepare` behaviour wouldn't cause a problem, no. I was sort of trying to enforce the core image to either be `None` or the correct mode/size before calling `load()`, to allow for the core image to be dropped if it theoretically became unnecessary. However, once I take on board your comment about unnecessary memory allocation, that's hard to do simply. I've created #8450 to try - at the end of `seek()`, an external plugin could call `super().seek()`, and if the mode or size has changed, then `self._im` is set to `None`.

If you're not a fan of that suggestion though, then I'm happy to just revert the `load_prepare()` change.

comments.author: homm
comments.body:
> I was sort of trying to enforce the core image to either be None or the correct mode/size before calling load()

Good point. I'll take a look.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Hi. You are hitting a limit when opening images.

https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/plugins.html#PIL.PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK
> PIL.PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK = 1048576
> Maximum decompressed size for a iTXt or zTXt chunk. Eliminates decompression bombs where compressed chunks can expand 1000x. See [Text in PNG File Format](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/handbook/image-file-formats.html#png-text).

You can increase this in your script like so.
```python
from PIL import Image, PngImagePlugin
PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK = 2 * 1024 * 1024
Image.open('001041.png')
```

comments.author: robonrrd
comments.body:
That fixes my proximate issue (I can now open this image), thank you.

However, I would still claim this is a bug. It was a PNG generated by Pillow and the naive user (me!) would expect Pillow to also be able to open it.  Further, OpenCV (and GIMP and qiv, etc.) can open it with no adjustment of internal constants.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
The problematic part of the image is the ICC profile, which is just over 1mb. We are raising an error to try and prevent decompression bombs, where compressed data becomes excessively large when expanded.

Without a self-contained example, it's hard to go into further detail, but it would appear that something external to Pillow is providing a large ICC profile. I think there is an expectation that Pillow saves exactly the data that it is given. I considered splitting it into multiple iCCP chunks, but http://www.libpng.org/pub/png/spec/1.2/PNG-Chunks.html#C.iCCP doesn't say anything about concatenating.

We could raise an error when saving a large ICC profile, but I don't think you would find that helpful.

If there was a self-contained example, we could try and figure out where the ICC profile comes from, but otherwise, I don't think there is anything for us to do here.

comments.author: robonrrd
comments.body:
I still feel that this is a bug, or at least a bad preset that causes problems.  My reasoning is that Pillow is the only image manipulation library I use which has a problem with this image and, further, the error message is not instructive and the fix is non-intuitive.  I would never have been able to diagnose this without your help.  

Perhaps the easiest solution is to kick the can down the road and increase the default maximum decompressed size?   If you think changing the default max size is bad, perhaps change the error message to suggest that the user increase the size.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
I've created #8391. That will change the error message to "Decompressed data too large for PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK".

If a user sees that, and searches our docs for "PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK", they will find https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/handbook/image-file-formats.html#png-opening
> Individual compressed chunks are limited to a decompressed size of [PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/plugins.html#PIL.PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK), by default 1MB, to prevent decompression bombs.

title: Is Pillow affected by WebP vulnerability?
security_topic: applicability of CVE-2023-4863 to Pillow versions
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if Pillow is vulnerable to CVE‑2023‑4863 and whether upgrading libwebp (instead of Pillow) mitigates the issue, with the answer citing Pillow 10.0.1 and newer libwebp versions as anchors.

comments.author: afk42
comments.body:
Being aware that CVE-2023-4863 was already fixed in Pillow 10.0.1 and as I'm unable to update to that version at the moment, I want to understand if Pillow really uses any of the functionality where the issue resides or if the CVE can be whitelisted since use of this vulnerable library is excluded by the functional design of Pillow.

Thank you

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS: 
* Python: 
* Pillow:  < 10.0.1

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Pillow calls WebPAnimDecoderGetNext, which calls WebPDecode, calling DecodeInto, calling VP8LDecodeHeader, calling DecodeImageStream, calling ReadHuffmanCodes, calling ReadHuffmanCode, calling VP8LBuildHuffmanTable, calling BuildHuffmanTable - so I don't see why we wouldn't be vulnerable.

You might also be interested in this distinction - the source code of Pillow itself did not really change in 10.0.1 to address this situation. 10.0.1 was released to provide new wheels to those who do not compile Pillow from source. You could use an earlier version of Pillow with a recent version of libwebp and not be vulnerable.

comments.author: afk42
comments.body:
Thank you for your answer. @radarhere 
So if I understood correctly I can just bump up the version of libwebp and maintain compatibility with <10.0.1 versions.

title: Provide a documented way to turn off EPS handling via Ghostscript
security_topic: disable EPS handling to mitigate Ghostscript RCE risk
qa_summary: The developer needed a way to disable Ghostscript/EPS handling to mitigate RCE vulnerabilities, and the answer provides the concrete solution of setting EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False (see PR #7392 and the documented API change).

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body:
Pillow parses EPS files through ghostscript.

Ghostscript is troubled with regular security issues of critical impact, such as remote code execution. There has been [this one](https://github.com/farisv/PIL-RCE-Ghostscript-CVE-2018-16509), two CVEs this year already, and there is another one [just coming up](https://git.ghostscript.com/?p=ghostpdl.git;a=commit;h=e59216049cac290fb437a04c4f41ea46826cfba5) with the patch not yet included in any release.

We do not need EPS handling and we can turn it off in our code using `Image.open(…, formats=["JPG", "PNG", …])`. However, we use third-party components that also use Pillow (such as `reportlab`) and we'd like to make sure they also don't accidentally open EPS files and we can't modify the code.

From what I can tell, we can accomplish this with:

```python
from PIL import Image

if "EPS" in Image.ID:
    Image.ID.remove("EPS")
```

However, that seems to be undocumented and feels like unclean monkeypatching. I think it would be worth it providing a documented API to turn off third-party backends like ghostscript globally.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body: Hi. See what you think of #7392. It adds `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary`, so that setting `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False` would result in `OSError: Unable to locate Ghostscript on paths` when trying to load an EPS image.

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body: Wow, that was fast! Not sure if I read the code exactly, but wouldn't this trigger OSError from line 72 whenever I set it to `False` and import the module?

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
No, the `Ghostscript` function is only called when an image is loaded.
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/a84a43528ebf8756369a3b7248312c4122ef3bc9/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py#L383-L386

With the workaround that you posted above, an EPS file won't be identified. In my suggestion, it will be identified. `Image.open` will complete successfully. It will just raise an OSError once `load()` is called on it (which many Pillow operations call internally).

comments.author: raphaelm
comments.body: Ah sorry, I've mistaken `Ghostscript` to be a class. My bad! Yes, sounds good then. (A note in the docs about it would be great to make it "official" so I can somehow expect it to continue to work in future versions.)

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Sure. I've added a commit to the PR. You can see the preview at https://pillow--7392.org.readthedocs.build/en/7392/handbook/image-file-formats.html#eps
> To use Ghostscript, Pillow searches for the “gs” executable. On Windows, it also searches for “gswin32c” and “gswin64c”. If you would like to customise this behaviour, `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gswin64"` will set the name of the executable to use. `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = False` will prevent Ghostscript from being used altogether.

title: Automate build and release to PyPI
security_topic: process for securely uploading release artifacts to PyPI via Trusted Publishers
qa_summary: The developer asked how to securely upload release artifacts to PyPI using Trusted Publishers, and the answer pointed to a concrete CI run showing the upload step (see actions run https://github.com/radarhere/Pillow/actions/runs/7329629479/job/19960359962#step:4:1008).

comments.author: hugovk
comments.body:
Currently the [release process](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/RELEASING.md) has many steps, including preparing things in this repo, and then starting a build in https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-wheels, before downloading the sdist + wheel artifacts to disk, and manually uploading them to PyPI using twine.

I'd like us to move towards more automated releases, including using the new Trusted Publishers to upload wheels directly from the CI to PyPI, which is more secure:

* https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2023-04-20-introducing-trusted-publishers/

We can do this in a phased manner, not all of these things would need to be done at once, to ensure we can still make releases with just some of them completed.

We could potentially deal with the Travis CI wheels later, and tackle GitHub Actions first as they're a bigger win and we don't know when Travis CI will go away.

Big picture:

* Prepare release
* Push a tag
* The CI builds release artifacts
* The CI uploads artifacts to PyPI

I'd suggest something along these lines:

1. Move Linux and macOS https://github.com/python-pillow/pillow-wheels to this repo https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow. We already have Windows wheels build here.
   * We'll need to add [`paths:` / `paths-ignore`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#onpushpull_requestpull_request_targetpathspaths-ignore) to workflows so we only trigger the main test workflows for "normal" code changes, and only trigger the wheel workflow for things like release and modifying its config
   * Upload wheels as GitHub artifacts in this repo instead

2. Add automation to download artifacts and upload them to PyPI via Trusted Publishing
   * This may need refactoring to move all the wheel building to the same workflow (but separate jobs), and then a final job that runs when the wheels have all been built, that builds sdist, checks and uploads them all.
   * See https://github.com/ultrajson/ultrajson/blob/main/.github/workflows/deploy.yml and https://github.com/ultrajson/ultrajson/actions/workflows/deploy.yml for examples.
   * We also have https://test.pypi.org/project/Pillow/ which we can use to verify the upload machinery is working smoothly before release. For example, we can upload for non-tagged wheel builds.

Thoughts?

comments.author: hugovk

title: "close" syscall run twice on same file descriptor when loading binary LZW-compressed TIFF
security_topic: race condition causing double file descriptor close in Pillow TIFF handling
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the double‑close race condition constitutes a security risk and which fix resolves it; the issue is addressed by PR #7199 (and later PR #8458) which modifies TiffImagePlugin to prevent the duplicate file‑pointer close.

comments.author: philip-bl
comments.body:
If I open an LZW-compressed binary TIFF file using pillow and load its data, pillow calls the "close" syscall on one of the two relevant file descriptors twice. The second call results in a "EBADF (Bad file descriptor)" error. The program doesn't crash and everything seems to work ok. But if multithreading is used and a race condition happens, this might crash the program.

In this example, the expected behaviour would be that there is only one "close" syscall on each of the two relevant file descriptors and that there is no "EBADF" error. Below, I show how to reproduce the problem.

```console

#!/usr/bin/env python

import numpy as np
import PIL.Image as Image

Image.fromarray(np.random.rand(500, 600) > 0.9) \
    .save("example.tif", format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")
$ cat read_tiff_file.py
#!/usr/bin/env python

import PIL.Image as Image

print("Right before the with-block", flush=True)
with Image.open("example.tif") as mask:
    print("Right in the beginning of the with-block", flush=True)
    mask.load()
    print("Right after load()", flush=True)

comments.author: nurumaik
comments.body:
### Updated example that actually leads to bugs

create_tiff_file.py

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python

import numpy as np
import PIL.Image as Image

# Create really big file so it will take time to load. But even bigger file will cause libtiff to complain that we are trying to zip-bomb it
Image.fromarray(np.random.rand(5000, 30000) > 0.9) \  
    .save("example.tif", format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")
```

reproduce.py
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python
from threading import Thread
import os
from collections import deque

finish = False

def load_files():
    descriptors = deque()
    while not finish:
        try:
            fd = os.open("test", os.O_RDONLY)
            descriptors.append(fd)
        except:  # in case of too many descriptors
            os.close(descriptors.pop())
    
    for d in descriptors:
        os.close(d)
    
    print("success")


t = Thread(target=load_files)

import PIL.Image as Image

print("Right before the with-block", flush=True)

with Image.open("example.tif") as mask:
    print("Right in the beginning of the with-block", flush=True)
    t.start()
    mask.load()  # replace it with time.sleep(10) and it works just fine without exceptions
    print("Right after load()", flush=True)
print("Right after the with-block", flush=True)
finish = True
t.join()
```


Steps to reproduce:

```sh
touch test
./create_tiff_file.py
./reproduce.py
```

_Note: you need to delete example.tif and test before every iteration of running this. otherwise the OS might cache the files and thus the problem won't reproduce because libtiff will load file too fast_

Expected behavior:
`load_files` outputs "success"

Actual behavior:
```
Right in the beginning of the with-block
Right after load()
Right after the with-block
Exception in thread Thread-1 (load_files):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 1016, in _bootstrap_inner
    self.run()
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/threading.py", line 953, in run
    self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)
  File "reproduce.py", line 17, in load_files
    os.close(d)
OSError: [Errno 9] Bad file descriptor
```

### Cause of bug

1. tiff loader creates file duplicate of file descriptor for use in external c library code
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1256

2. As comments say "[libtiff closes the file descriptor, so pass in a dup.](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1254)", libtiff probably closes `fp` after decoding here
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1298

3. Pillow closes `fp` again
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/5832362215f5fa661fa05ad31e6c97aab87d410a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1308

If another thread decides to open new file between steps 2 and 3 (like `load_files` in example), it may get file descriptor that was just closed by libtiff. Then, in step 3, pillow closes this file, making descriptor invalid

comments.author: nurumaik
comments.body:
I reproduced the problem with this fix. Unfortunately, reproduction code doesn't work in all cases, and I don't know how to make a better version without hooking something in libtiff. I can only suggest storing file "test" on some very slow drive to ensure read is really slow

How this can still lead to a bug:
1. We call `os.dup` on `self.fd` and get descriptor, let's say 4
2. decode finishes and calls `close(4)`
3. Other thread opens another file, and os gives it the same number 4 as descriptor, since it's already freed
4. We call `os.read(4, 0)` on file descriptor and it successfully reads that other file
5. We close file that doesn't belong to us

I checked libtiff code and it should always close the descriptor after performing decode. It will stay open only if libtiff contains a bug (but this will probably lead to much more serious errors anyway)

https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/main/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c#L723

If libtiff may not close the fd in some cases, the proper fix would be to either:
1. Somehow report back if it closed fd or not
2. Disable fd closing in libtiff

comments.author: wiredfool
comments.body:
As to why we're duping the file pointer in the firster place,  I think the original logic was:
* Libtiff always closes the pointer when read on an image is complete.
* If we have a multiple frames in an image, we're looping over calls into libtiff to decode individual frames. If libtiff closes on the first frame, we don't get subsequent frames
* Our original source for the file pointer may be one of a filename, tempfile, or open file like object. We can't necessarily re-open a file once it's been closed. 

One option was to use python/our code for all the byte shuffling at the file level. IIRC there was a pretty decent performance and complexity improvement for cases when we did have a file pointer to be able to send that into libtiff and let it manage all of that. 


(edit: yeah, that's definitely my comment style)

title: PPM "Channel value too large" error
security_topic: resource consumption vulnerability due to half-token handling in PPM decoder
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether the PPM parsing bug was a security issue and how it would be fixed; the maintainer identified it as a resource‑consumption vulnerability and provided PR #7052, which will be included in Pillow 9.5.0 as the concrete fix.

comments.author: GauthierDa
comments.body:
<!--
Thank you for reporting an issue.

Follow these guidelines to ensure your issue is handled properly.

If you have a ...

1.  General question: consider asking the question on Stack Overflow
    with the python-imaging-library tag:

    Bug reports which follow these guidelines are easier to diagnose,
    and are often handled much more quickly.

3.  Feature request: do a quick search of existing issues
    to make sure this has not been asked before.

We know asking good questions takes effort, and we appreciate your time.
Thank you.
-->

### What did you do?

We are using PIL for reading PPM images of 1280x1024 or 1920x1080 pixels in RGB 24 bits with maxval of 255 in the header.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expect the PPM to open correctly.

### What actually happened?

The opening of PPM images failed due to a maxval error "Channel value too large for this mode"

### What are your OS, Python and Pillow versions?

* OS: Windows 10
* Python: 3.9
* Pillow: 9.4.0

<!--
Please include **code** that reproduces the issue and whenever possible, an **image** that demonstrates the issue. Please upload images to GitHub, not to third-party file hosting sites. If necessary, add the image to a zip or tar archive.

The best reproductions are self-contained scripts with minimal dependencies. If you are using a framework such as Plone, Django, or Buildout, try to replicate the issue just using Pillow.
-->

When I first try to load my PPM, PIL return the channel value too large error with the value of 20458 with a maxval of 255. Then I searched in my PPM this value and there is no data higher than 255.
After investigated the issue, I saw that the concatenation of the half_block and the next block block give this:
-> end of previus block: ... 204 ]
-> half_block + block:    [20458 ...
-> expected:                   [204 58 ...

I fixed the issue locally by changing line 239:
```python
if half_token:
    block = half_token + block  # stitch half_token to new block
```
By
```python
if half_token:
    block = half_token + b' ' + block  # stitch half_token to new block
    half_token = False
```
