comments.body:
After searching a little bit more, my issue was because I create my PPM image in a C program using LF at the end of each line but then I launch the program with Windows so the EOL became CRLF and then pillow crash when I wanted to use show or save method.
I don't know if this CRLF is handle by pillow.

**Edit**
I have the same issue. Because my PPM file is internal to my company, I can't share it but I will try to replicate the bug with another PPM tomorrow.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Hmm. I don't think the issue should be CRLF. I would have thought that
https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/8cc5396659c7a728eb4e50bc6671571df86cd346/src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py#L241
splits CRLF without a problem.

comments.author: GauthierDa
comments.body:
[output.zip](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/files/10821798/output.zip)

Here my PPM images. First one, "mignon.ppm" can be open and show without any issue. The second one, "mignon1280.ppm" is the same image resize to 1280x1024 by Paint Shop Pro and can't be shown.

Code use to test:
```python
# Python39
from PIL import Image
im = Image.open("mignon1280.ppm")
im.show()
```

comments.author: GauthierDa
comments.body: Amazing, did you have any idea how can we make a local fix because we use pillow to convert PPM images to PNG and we can’t really wait one month. If you don’t know, we will find another way make it !

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
This should serve as a temporary workaround.
```python
from PIL.PpmImagePlugin import PpmPlainDecoder
PpmPlainDecoder._read_block = lambda self: self.fd.read()

from PIL import Image
im = Image.open("mignon1280.ppm")
im.show()
```

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
I've created PR #7052 to resolve this. It should be part of Pillow 9.5.0, due out in the next day or so.

Normally I would have created the PR earlier, but investigating your problem, I found that it was actually also a security issue. The half token that was sticking around could be used to consume unexpected resources, by continuously providing data to fill any size that the image might claim itself to be.

title: Pip audit reporting security vulnerability OSV-2022-715
security_topic: resolution of reported vulnerability OSV-2022-715 in Pillow
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the OSV-2022-715 vulnerability reported for Pillow 9.2.0 was a false positive and which version resolves it; the answer states it is fixed in Pillow 9.3.0 (see release notes https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/9.3.0.html#decode-jpeg-compressed-blp1-data-in-original-mode).

comments.author: jrzerr
comments.body:
We run pip-audit and just this week started reporting a security vulnerability with 9.2.0, we are running python 3.10.8.

https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2022-715

When you follow the References link in the issue, it says something about being fixed.

https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=50217

But yet `pip-audit` is still flagging.

Should we be treating this as a false flag?  Problem is with `pip-audit` and it's source of vulnerabilities?  Or is this something that needs to be investigated?

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
My conclusion is that the security vulnerability was only detected intermittently. A later test didn't detect the vulnerability, so the automatic software marked it as fixed, believing that something we'd done in the meantime had resolved the matter.

Since then, #6678 has merged a proper fix for this.

We plan to release Pillow 9.3.0 with that fix very soon. Follow #6460 for updates.

comments.author: radarhere
comments.body:
Pillow 9.3.0 has now been released.

This security problem is mentioned in the release notes at https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/9.3.0.html#decode-jpeg-compressed-blp1-data-in-original-mode

I've created https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz-vulns/pull/21 to try and sort this out.

title: Accessing the key generator in an initializer silently changes the hash digest class for the entire application
security_topic: unexpected hash algorithm downgrade due to early key_generator access
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that accessing Rails.key_generator before setting config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class can downgrade the hash algorithm to insecure SHA1, and that this was fixed in PR #56746 which now raises a RuntimeError to prevent the misconfiguration.

comments.author: ankane
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

Create a new Rails application and add `config/initializers/repro.rb` with:

```ruby
Rails.application.key_generator
```

And run:

```sh
rails runner "p Rails.application.key_generator.instance_variable_get(:@key_generator).instance_variable_get(:@hash_digest_class)"
```

### Expected behavior

`OpenSSL::Digest::SHA256`, which is the output without the initializer.

### Actual behavior

`OpenSSL::Digest::SHA1`

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.1.2

**Ruby version**: 3.4.8

### Additional notes

turbo-rails was [affected by this](https://github.com/hotwired/turbo-rails/blob/v8.0.21/UPGRADING.md#key-digest-changes-in-111) and made a change to initialization to workaround it.

A few ideas to address this would be:

- apply `config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class` earlier in initialization
- warn or raise if `Rails.application.key_generator` is already cached when applying `config.active_support.key_generator_hash_digest_class`
- include the hash digest as part of the cache key in `Rails.application.key_generator`

comments.author: 6temes
comments.body:
I've opened a PR to address this: #56746

The fix raises a `RuntimeError` when `key_generator` is accessed before the `key_generator_hash_digest_class` configuration has been applied. This turns the silent misconfiguration into an immediate, actionable error.

Apps that don't configure `key_generator_hash_digest_class` (pre-7.0 defaults) are unaffected.

title: `ActiveRecord::Rollback` is silenced in nested transactions - including ApplicationRecord callbacks
security_topic: silencing of rollback errors in nested transactions leading to potential data inconsistency
qa_summary: The developer needed to know that raising ActiveRecord::Rollback in a nested transaction is intentionally swallowed by Rails (as documented in the Rails transaction docs), see https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionAdapters/DatabaseStatements.html#method-i-transaction

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->
[Full script
](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/e442ccaf22657b2457ce50981c11a305)

```ruby
    user = User.create!(name: "john")

    assert_equal true, user.active
    assert_equal true, user.email.active

    User.transaction do
      user.active = false

      Email.transaction do
        email = user.email
        email.active = false
        email.save

        raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
      end
    end

    user.reload

    # Both are committed to the database even though an ActiveRecord::Rollback was raised
    assert_equal true, user.active, "Expect that the whole transaction fails and the user is not saved"
    assert_equal true, user.email.active, "Expect that the email is not updated"
```

### Expected behavior

This is related to the issue reported in [this PR](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44518). The error should bubble up and not be silenced by Rails.

Raising an error should always have an effect, swallowing it is error-prone and can easily throw people off.
Based on [this GitHub search](https://github.com/search?q=%2Fraise%5B%5C%28%5Cs%5Cn%5D*ActiveRecord%3A%3ARollback%2F+-org%3Ashop+language%3ARuby+-org%3AShopify+-path%3Aspec%2F+-path%3A_test.rb&type=code), it looks like people seem to be raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback` errors.

if the idea is that developers should not be manually raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback`, then the documentation should be clear about it (even better if people are blocked from raising it).

### Actual behavior

Raising the error in nested transaction is a no-op. This means that ApplicationRecord callbacks will also silence `ActiveRecord::Rollback` errors. Example (also include in the [full test](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/e442ccaf22657b2457ce50981c11a305)):

```ruby
# definition
class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  after_create :create_email_for_user

  private

  def create_email_for_user
    email = build_email(email_address: "#{name}@example.com")

    unless email.save
      errors.add(:base, email.errors.full_messages.first || "Email creation failed")
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end
  end
end

# usage
user = User.new(name: "john")
saved = User.transaction do
  # This will attempt to create an email with `john@example.com` which already exists
  # and raise an ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid error in `create_email_for_user`
  user.save
end

user.reload

# user is successfully saved, this fails:
refute user.persisted?, "User should not be persisted since create_email_for_user raised an ActiveRecord::Rollback error"
```


### System configuration

**Rails version**:  Latest from main

**Ruby version**: `3.4.4`

comments.author: eglitobias
comments.body:
This is expected behavior and well documented, not a bug:
https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionAdapters/DatabaseStatements.html#method-i-transaction

Nested transactions in Rails are joinable by default. That means the inner transaction does not start a new database transaction, so raising `ActiveRecord::Rollback` there does not issue a SQL `ROLLBACK`. The exception is intentionally swallowed, and the outer transaction can still commit.

At the SQL level, most databases don’t support true nested `BEGIN/COMMIT`. There is only one transaction per connection. To roll back part of a transaction, SQL uses SAVEPOINTS, not nested `BEGIN`s:
```
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO posts ...;          -- first
  SAVEPOINT sp1;
    INSERT INTO posts ...;        -- second
    ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;    -- undo only inner work
COMMIT;
```
Rails maps this explicitly via ^requires_new: true`:
```
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  Post.create!(title: "first")
  ActiveRecord::Base.transaction(requires_new: true) do
    Post.create!(title: "second")
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end
end
```

Without `requires_new`, there is no SQL boundary to roll back so the behavior is correct by design.

Changing this would be a significant backward-compatibility change, so it’s likely outside the scope of a bugfix. As already discovered, this is being discussed in more depth in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44518, which seems like the appropriate place for exploring a broader proposal or deprecation path.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
Thanks for taking a look into this @eglitobias . I was aware of it being documented, but I was expecting this decision could be re-evaluated.

I cannot see a scenario where a developer would expect that raising a `ActiveRecord::Rollback` would **not** rollback. I think this is misleading and very likely a source of bugs and corrupt data. I understand changing it at this stage would be complex since this would be a breaking change.


From some conversation with @matthewd and @rafaelfranca , it looks like the recommendation would be to not manually raise `ActiveRecord::Rollback` if you have an application that is too complex with many layers of nested transactions.

For this particular issue, what about just reporting when these rollbacks are silenced and the transactions is committed? This could, at least, give insight that something fishy might've happened running the application.

[Example of changes](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

comments.author: zzak
comments.body:
Just a thought but here instead of trying to keep track of all the rollback errors, we just emit a notification when swallowing them:
https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks#diff-88e231c48eb5559ac3be58a024b019e86f7c74d388f5d49fac3f4e47bf851cc6R435

That way the behavior is the same but we can at least be aware of such a case should it occur and observe it.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
> Just a thought but here instead of trying to keep track of all the rollback errors, we just emit a notification when swallowing them: [main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks#diff-88e231c48eb5559ac3be58a024b019e86f7c74d388f5d49fac3f4e47bf851cc6R435](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks#diff-88e231c48eb5559ac3be58a024b019e86f7c74d388f5d49fac3f4e47bf851cc6R435)
> 
> That way the behavior is the same but we can at least be aware of such a case should it occur and observe it.

That's a good point. This will be less resource intensive and make it simpler, the only thing thought, is that it will not be too assertive. One pattern that I see in code is something like this (simplified here for clarity, usually happens in several layers of classes):


```ruby
def delete_user
  User.transaction do # <-- top-level transaction
    user = User.find(1)
  
    User.transaction do
      # ...
      destroy_addresses(user)
      # ...
    end

    user.destroy

    # The rollback from the nested transaction is silenced, but the parent transaction is still rolledback:
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if user.errors.any?    
  end
  # ...
end

def destroy_addresses(user)
  unless AddressService.destroy_user_addresses(user)
    user.errors.add(:base, "Failed to destroy addresses") unless user.addresses.destroy_all
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
  end
end
```

I'll add an alternative implementation and get some feedback to see which one would make more sense in Rails. For my particular use case, being more assertive (ie. making sure a `rollback` was raised as part of a transaction that was indeed committed) would be more helpful, otherwise it would generate too much noise.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
## Proposed mitigations

Given changing the existing behavior of silencing rollbacks in nested transaction would be a breaking change, and given @zzak suggestion above, I would like to propose just "bringing awareness" to the issue. I understand this is documented, but we still have the fact that a rollback error should rollback.

### 1) Instrument when rollback is silenced **and transaction is committed** [Preferred IMHO]

This approach will capture all silenced rollbacks in nested transactions, and, if the `RealTransaction` is committed, it will send an `ActiveSupport::Notification`.

[Implementation](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:instrument-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

Code example:

```ruby
ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe("transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors") do |event|
  rollback_errors = event.payload[:errors]

  # rollback_errors will have an array with error silenced in the nested transaction(s)
end

def trigger_notification_with_silecend_rollback
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)
    User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback # < -- silenced rollback
    end
  
    user.destroy
  end # <-- when transaction commits, transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors will be emitted
end

def do_not_trigger_notification
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)

    operation_result = User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback # <-- silenced rollback
    end
  
    # Propagate silenced rollback and perform a real rollback ✅
    # This will NOT emit transaction.active_record.silenced_rollback_errors
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if operation_result.nil?

    user.destroy
  end
end
```

### 2) Instrument when rollback is silenced, even if the real transaction is also rolled back

This approach is simpler as it will always send an `ActiveSupport::Notification` whenever a rollback is silenced in a nested transaction. This can lead to false positives though, since the real transaction might also be rolled back.

[Implementation](https://github.com/rails/rails/compare/main...ipvalverde:rails:instrument-possible-silenced-ar-rollbacks)

Code example:

```ruby
ActiveSupport::Notifications.subscribe("silenced_rollback.active_record") do |event|
  rollback_error = event.payload[:error]

  # rollback_error will have the error raised in the nested transaction below
end

def trigger_notification_with_silecend_rollback
  User.transaction do
    user = User.lock.find(1)

    operation_result = User.transaction do
      user.addresses.destroy_all
      raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
    end # <-- The rescue for the transaction will immediately emit the 'silenced_rollback.active_record' notification

    # Even if the actual transaction is rolled back, the notification will be sent
    raise ActiveRecord::Rollback if operation_result.nil?

    user.destroy
  end
end
```

title: Deadlocked transactions are still seen as "usable" for MySQL (trilogy / mysql2)
security_topic: transaction state misreporting after deadlock leading to unintended writes
qa_summary: The issue asks if deadlocked MySQL transactions incorrectly remain marked as usable, allowing writes outside a transaction, and the answer points to a concrete fix in PR #44127 that restores the invalidated transaction state.

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce

<!-- (Guidelines for creating a bug report are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->

[Full reproduction script gist](https://gist.github.com/ipvalverde/2d2f6b91d593e09b89a86a7c61a3ca5b). Important bit:

```ruby
Account.transaction do
  Account.create!(name: "Account in top-level transaction", balance: 50)

  begin
    puts "1) Is transaction open? #{Account.connection.transaction_open?}"

    # consider the logic in here will raise a deadlock:
    Account.lock.find(1).update!(balance: 10)
    Account.lock.find(2).update!(balance: 20)

  rescue ActiveRecord::Deadlocked => e
    puts "2) Is transaction open? #{Account.connection.transaction_open?}"

    # Everything up to this point is DISCARDED from the Database perspective.
    # No account being created, no accounts being updated.
    
  end

  # This will write directly to the database - no valid transactions in here.
  Account.create!(name: "Last account in top-level transaction", balance: 999)

  # this will be a no-op since there's no transaction open
  raise ActiveRecord::Rollback
end
```

### Expected behavior

Any database write operations (or maybe also read?) that happens in a code that is intended to run within a transaction should fail if there's no transaction open. Currently it misleads you, where you might think there is a transaction but there isn't.

This works as expected in postgres, but it looks like it's because postgres, when attempting to create an account after the deadlock will raise an error:

```
ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: PG::InFailedSqlTransaction: ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
```

### Actual behavior

After the transaction is deadlocked it gets killed, if that error is swallowed, any code that runs within a transaction block will write directly to the database!


### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.1.1

**Ruby version**: 3.4.4

comments.author: ipvalverde
comments.body:
I did a bit more digging.

It looks like [this fix](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/44127) changed how the transaction state works, now an `invaldiated` transaction that is rolled back has its state also going from `invalidated -> rolledback`, which means it will still look like a healthy transaction even though it is not.

I'll propose a PR to fix that transaction state issue and preserve the `invalidated` state without fully invalidating the connection.

title: Migration token with uniq generate more than one unique
security_topic: duplicate unique index generation for token columns in Rails migrations
qa_summary: The developer needed to know why the Rails migration generator creates duplicate `unique: true` indexes for a `token` column, potentially compromising token uniqueness security, and the answer cites the `create_table_migration.rb.tt` template and a new test in `migration_generator_test.rb` as concrete sources.

comments.author: valenciaj
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce
I run this command from CLI:
```bash
bin/rails generate model account identifier:string{32}:uniq name:string{255} join_token:token:uniq
```

> [!NOTE]
> Yes, I use `uniq` on token column definition... Sorry.

and I get this migration file:
```ruby
class CreateAccounts < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.1]
  def change
    create_table :accounts do |t|
      t.string :identifier, limit: 32, null: false
      t.string :name, limit: 255, null: false
      t.string :join_token, limit: 32, null: false

      t.timestamps
    end
    add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true, unique: true
    add_index :accounts, :identifier, unique: true
    add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true
  end
end
```

> [!NOTE]
> `limit` argument on `join_token` column is touched by myself

> [!WARNING]
> `join_token` has twice `unique` arguments and additional index

### Expected behavior

The command must generate a migration like this:

```ruby
class CreateAccounts < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.1]
  def change
    create_table :accounts do |t|
      t.string :identifier, limit: 32, null: false
      t.string :name, limit: 255, null: false
      t.string :join_token, limit: 32, null: false

      t.timestamps
    end
    add_index :accounts, :identifier, unique: true
    add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true
  end
end
```

### Actual behavior

Redundant `join_token` index definition with redundant `unique` argument.

```ruby
class CreateAccounts < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.1]
  def change
    create_table :accounts do |t|
      t.string :identifier, limit: 32, null: false
      t.string :name, limit: 255, null: false
      t.string :join_token, limit: 32, null: false

      t.timestamps
    end
    add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true, unique: true
    add_index :accounts, :identifier, unique: true
    add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true
  end
end
```

### System configuration

ruby 3.4.7

Rails 8.1.1

comments.author: dancristianb
comments.body:
Hey @valenciaj 👋 Thanks for the detailed description! 

I've had a look and I think I understand where this is coming from. It looks like in [create_table_migration.rb.tt](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/activerecord/lib/rails/generators/active_record/migration/templates/create_table_migration.rb.tt#L23) if the `attribute` type is a `token` we will include both the [Rails::Generators::GeneratedAttribute#inject_index_options](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/railties/lib/rails/generators/generated_attribute.rb#L232) return and the `, unique: true` hardcoded string. That's how we end up with the `add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true, unique: true` line.

Later in the template [on line 26](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/activerecord/lib/rails/generators/active_record/migration/templates/create_table_migration.rb.tt#L26) we go through all `attributes_with_index`. The return will include the `token` attribute due to how `Rails::Generators::GeneratedAttribute#has_index?` [is computed](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/railties/lib/rails/generators/generated_attribute.rb#L117). This will lead to the `add_index :accounts, :join_token, unique: true` line we see in the migration.

I've added a new test that surfaces the issue in [migration_generator_test.rb](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/railties/test/generators/migration_generator_test.rb#L385)

```
  def test_create_table_migration_with_uniq_token_option
    run_generator ["create_users", "token:token:uniq"]
    assert_migration "db/migrate/create_users.rb" do |content|

      assert_method :change, content do |change|
        occurrences = content.scan("unique: true").count
        assert_equal 1, occurrences, "Should only have unique: true present once"
      end
    end
  end
```

```
$ bin/test test/generators/migration_generator_test.rb -n test_create_table_migration_with_uniq_token_option
Run options: -n test_create_table_migration_with_uniq_token_option --seed 12882

# Running:

F

Failure:
MigrationGeneratorTest#test_create_table_migration_with_uniq_token_option [test/generators/migration_generator_test.rb:400]:
Should only have unique: true present once.
Expected: 1
  Actual: 3
```

I think we'll need some additional changes in the [migration.rb.tt](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/main/activerecord/lib/rails/generators/active_record/migration/templates/migration.rb.tt#L9) template file too. I'll get back with a PR with the full details.

title: SSL certificate verification fails on macOS (OpenSSL 3.6 + Ruby 3.4) due to CRL check
security_topic: SSL verification failure due to CRL check on macOS with OpenSSL 3.6
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to fix SSL certificate verification failures caused by OpenSSL 3.6 CRL checking on macOS, and the answer references ruby/openssl issue #949 (and PR #950) recommending adding the openssl gem or rebuilding Ruby with a compatible OpenSSL version.

comments.author: fitterfly-jainam-parikh
comments.body:
When running any HTTPS requests (e.g., through Net::HTTP, ActiveStorage::Service::S3Service, or AWS SDK) on macOS with Ruby 3.4.x and OpenSSL 3.6, SSL handshakes fail with the error:

```bash
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError:
  SSL_connect returned=1 errno=0 peeraddr=1xx.1xx.6x.1xx:443 state=error:
  certificate verify failed (unable to get certificate CRL)
```

This occurs on a clean macOS (M2) setup using Homebrew OpenSSL@3 and rbenv.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On macOS (Apple Silicon):
```bash
brew install openssl@3 ca-certificates rbenv ruby-build
RUBY_CONFIGURE_OPTS="--with-openssl-dir=$(brew --prefix openssl@3)" rbenv install 3.4.1
rbenv global 3.4.1
```

2. Run inside IRB:
```bash
require 'net/http'
Net::HTTP.get(URI('https://aws.amazon.com'))
```

3. Observe the error:
```bash
SSL_connect ... certificate verify failed (unable to get certificate CRL)
```

### Expected behavior
Ruby (and by extension, Rails apps using Net::HTTP or ActiveStorage) should complete HTTPS requests successfully without manual CRL configuration.

### Actual behavior
The SSL handshake fails because OpenSSL’s default verification flags include V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK and V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK_ALL.
macOS’s OpenSSL build does not provide a CRL bundle, so verification fails even though the certificate chain is valid.

### Workarounds
Disabling CRL checking resolves the issue:
```bash
# config/initializers/ssl_fix.rb
require 'openssl'
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::DEFAULT_PARAMS[:verify_mode] = OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_PEER
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::DEFAULT_PARAMS[:verify_flags] &=
  ~(OpenSSL::X509::V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK_ALL | OpenSSL::X509::V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK)
```

title: Migrations that alter SQLite table structure can cause data loss
security_topic: proper handling of SQLite foreign key enforcement during migrations to prevent data loss
qa_summary: The developer needed to know the correct sequence for disabling and re‑enabling SQLite foreign key enforcement during migrations to prevent data loss, as documented in the SQLite PRAGMA foreign_keys and foreign_key_check specifications (see SQLite docs and the related Rails commit).

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
[A mere add_foreign_key can wipe out your whole Rails+SQLite production table](https://kyrylo.org/software/2025/09/27/a-mere-add-foreign-key-can-wipe-out-your-whole-rails-sqlite-production-table.html)

We likely should be disabling and re-enabling the `foreign_keys` PRAGMA before/after the transaction to change the table per the [sqlite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_altertable.html#otheralter).

Edit: actually it looks like we already do that since https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/45881b0a64b4039e3b0d27e2c4d959dc2d744b9d

Edit2: Ah, this is complex. We currently do

```
transaction do
  disable_referential_integrity do
```

but it should be

```
disable_pragma_foreign_keys do
  transaction do
    enable_defer_foreign_keys do
```

because `PRAGMA foreign_keys`

> is a no-op within a transaction; foreign key constraint enforcement may only be enabled or disabled when there is no pending [BEGIN](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html) or [SAVEPOINT](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_savepoint.html).

per [doc](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_foreign_keys), and "`PRAGMA foreign_keys` before `TRANSACTION`" is the order recommended in the first sqlite doc link above. However, `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys` is [set _per transaction_](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_defer_foreign_keys) so it has to be inside the transaction block.

comments.author: ruyrocha
comments.body:
The fix is ready for reviews. It disables foreign key enforcement before the table recreation process, and re-enables it afterwards. Since `PRAGMA foreign_keys` cannot be modified inside a transaction in SQLite, the operations are sequenced as:

1. Disable foreign keys (outside transaction)
2. Perform table recreation (inside transaction for atomicity)
3. Re-enable foreign keys
4. Validate schema integrity with `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`

title: ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector sets cookies on asset requests
security_topic: asset requests setting cookies unexpectedly
qa_summary: The developer asked whether asset requests should set a session cookie, and the maintainer replied that it’s a bug in Propshaft, pointing to the Propshaft railtie file at commit e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc as evidence.

comments.author: EmilioCristalli
comments.body:
Not sure if this is a bug, but noticed that when using the automatic DB switching ([docs](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_multiple_databases.html#activating-automatic-role-switching)), with the default resolver `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver` and context `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session`, it seems like requests for assets are getting a cookie sent back in the response.

Noticed this while investigating issues with system tests not rendering flash messages correctly, and it looks like it was happening because of race conditions between redirect requests and asset requests, causing it to override the cookie and remove the flash message. This might be a different issue on our side (that we are not properly waiting for asset requests to finish before submitting a form or something like that), but it made me wonder if it's correct for asset requests to respond with a cookie.

I don't know too much about the session and cookie management, but from what I could debug, it seems like this is happening because the `ActiveRecord::Middleware::DatabaseSelector::Resolver::Session` middleware reads `request.session[:last_write]`, so it's like it makes it load the session, and maybe this makes `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` send the cookie back in the response?

### Steps to reproduce
Created [this repo](https://github.com/EmilioCristalli/test_db_selector) to reproduce the issue. Has a few commits with the steps to create the app, but it's a normal Rails app with scaffold for one model (Post). 

The last commit in main has the automatic db switching enabled, but moving one commit back (to `9232d6768d`) should disable it to see the difference.

Can open the root page (which loads posts#index) and observe any asset requests (like http://localhost:3000/assets/application-bfcdf840.js) in the developer tools to see the `Set-Cookie` header in the response.

### Expected behavior
The asset requests shouldn't have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

(not 100% sure this is the expected behavior, but it looks like it's what happens when automatic DB switching is not enabled)

### Actual behavior
Asset requests have a `set-cookie` header in the response.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: 8.0.2.1
**Ruby version**: 3.4.5

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
This IMO is a bug in propshaft. It's mounted inside the Rails routes: https://github.com/rails/propshaft/blob/e49a9de659ff27462015e54dd832e86e762a6ddc/lib/propshaft/railtie.rb#L48-L50

So it's invoked after all rack middlewares.

Instead, it should probably be early in the rack middleware chain, likely right after `ActionDispatch::Static`.

Now the good news is that this is a development only setup (should be fixed regardless).

title: Handle links and other safe content inside translations
security_topic: safe interpolation of HTML in i18n translations to prevent XSS
qa_summary: The developer needed a secure method to interpolate HTML‑safe strings into I18n translations without introducing XSS, and the answer provides a concrete implementation in a Gist (https://gist.github.com/henrik/f6619f298de3b6f59dfba589fa5476d7).

comments.author: runephilosof-abtion
comments.body: Currently, if I want to put a link into a translation, I have to do ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` However, the `text_html` translation should not have to know whether the `insert` contains html or not. ~Also, the `insert` translation cannot have unescaped html content, because it is used as content inside another `_html` translation.~ The rails i18n guide does not mention how to do this nicely. The best would be if rails-i18n could handle it automatically by being aware of SafeBuffer. ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` Rails-i18n should handle safe joining the above example. `link_to` returns a `html_safe` string, so this should output ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ```

comments.author: runephilosof-abtion
comments.body: Related issue in https://github.com/svenfuchs/rails-i18n/issues/1147, which was closed with a suggestion of implementing it in Rails.

comments.author: dari-us
comments.body: I'm not sure I understand the use case for this. What prevents you from putting the `` directly into the translation YAML file? ``` text_html: 'Some >< text with a link, properly escaping ><' ``` Yes, you have to escape the content of the `` yourself in this case, but isn't it static anyway? If you really need this grade of freedom for the `insert`, the second option seems totally fine to me. However, the first one calling `t` with the non-HTML I18n key and then making it `html_safe` is super ugly.

You might consider translations to be untrusted user input, except `_html` ones, which would be more expensive to maintain. 3. Rails already has the concept of SafeBuffer, so why throw that information away when translating.

title: Authentication generator missing rate limiting on PasswordsController despite ActionMailer being available
security_topic: missing rate limiting on password reset endpoint
qa_summary: The missing rate‑limiting protection is addressed by commit e87af0f3235ca555f7864de9bb44da1d464d012d, which will be included in the upcoming Rails 8.1 release.

comments.author: sebasfourn
comments.body:
# Authentication generator missing rate limiting on PasswordsController

## Description

The Rails 8 authentication generator is missing rate limiting on the `PasswordsController` despite ActionMailer being available. This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
# Create a new Rails application
rails new test_app
cd test_app

# Verify ActionMailer is available
rails runner "puts defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie)"
# Output: "constant"

# Generate authentication
rails generate authentication

# Check the generated PasswordsController
cat app/controllers/passwords_controller.rb
```

## Expected behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` should include rate limiting on the `create` action when ActionMailer is available:

```ruby
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
```

This protection is essential to prevent abuse of the password reset email functionality.

## Actual behavior

The generated `PasswordsController` is missing the rate limiting line, despite ActionMailer being available. The controller includes the `create` action that sends password reset emails, but lacks the rate limiting protection that should be conditionally included when `ActionMailer::Railtie` is defined.

This leaves the password reset endpoint vulnerable to abuse for email spam attacks.

## System configuration
- **Rails version**: 8.0.0
- **Ruby version**: 3.2.0

## Additional context

The authentication generator template appears to have an ERB conditional that should include rate limiting when ActionMailer is available:

```erb
<%- if defined?(ActionMailer::Railtie) -%>
rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { redirect_to new_password_path, alert: "Try again later." }
<%- end -%>
```

However, this conditional is not evaluating correctly during template generation, resulting in missing rate limiting protection.

comments.author: fatkodima
comments.body:
Was added in https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e87af0f3235ca555f7864de9bb44da1d464d012d

It works only on `main` and will be available in the next rails minor (8.1 probably) release.

title: ActiveRecord call `.lease_connection` inside `.transaction` cause connection leak
security_topic: connection leak causing resource exhaustion in ActiveRecord transactions
qa_summary: The developer needed to know how to prevent the ActiveRecord connection leak (a potential availability/security risk) when using lease_connection inside a transaction, and the answer cites the Rails API docs and PR #51192, recommending calling release_connection or using with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true).

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
### Steps to reproduce
1. rails c
2. run code:
```ruby
puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  ActiveRecord::Base.lease_connection
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```
### Expected behavior
```
Before:
After: 
```

### Actual behavior
```
Before:
After: #<ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter>
```

#### Explanation
When .lease_connection called in .transaction, connection is not released when exiting from .with_connection. So connection is leaked(or stuck) to current thread

#### Why it is a problem
Our application send mixed db queries with http requests, which much slower than db queries so. And we faced with connection limit on mysql server side. So we have to release(return back to process pool) all obtained db connections before start execute http requests

#### When we faced with it
1. Our legacy have dirty call db queries(.connection.execute) inside transaction, but nested in several methods. So refactor(to forward connection from .transaction yield) is complicated
2. When we added after_commit_everywhere 1.6.0 to application(rails 7.2.2.1 only) to use Sidekiq.transactional_push!. And following code cause connection leak:
```ruby
class MyWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker
  sidekiq_options queue: :default

  def perform; end
end

puts "Before: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  MyWorker.perform_async
end
puts "After: #{ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.active_connection?}"
```

Connection leak because next trace:
https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/blob/v6.5.12/lib/sidekiq/transaction_aware_client.rb#L16
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L100
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L111
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L144
https://github.com/Envek/after_commit_everywhere/blob/v1.6.0/lib/after_commit_everywhere.rb#L172

### System configuration
rails 7.2.2.1 with ruby 3.3.2
rails 8.0.2 with ruby 3.4.4

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
Isn't this by design? The API docs say

> The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until [release_connection](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionHandling.html#method-i-release_connection) is called.

So if you want the connection returned to the pool you must use `release_connection` after `lease_connection`

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
@skipkayhil So how i can easily receive connection without this behaviour in complicated, nested code? 
For example:
```ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end

def do_call
  # ActiveRecord::Base.connection or something else that will release connection after #transaction block
end
```

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
```ruby
# call `release_connection` when you're done with a connection
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  do_call
end
ActiveRecore::Base.release_connection

# or only checkout connections where you need them (nesting with_connection always gives you the same connection)
def do_call
  Base.with_connection do |c|
  end
end
```

comments.author: tevvi
comments.body:
@skipkayhil So next step to rewrite all code(application and gems) which use ActiveRecore::Base.lease_connection. I think it is a complicated solution

Easier solution is return back previous logic. Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.) and rewrite lease_connection to release connection after with_connection block

comments.author: skipkayhil
comments.body:
> Add method sticky_connection with new behaviour(The connection will remain leased for the entire duration of the request or job, or until release_connection is called.)

This is how `ActiveRecord::Base.connection` has always worked (1 connection per request/job). `with_connection`/`release_connection` _is_ the new behavior that allows you to not have a single connection checked out for a whole request/job.

comments.author: byroot
comments.body:
What @skipkayhil said, this was done by design to not break code that had expectations about the connection being sticky: https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/51192

You can manually call `release_connection` after, or wrap the whole thing in `.with_connection(prevent_permanent_checkout: true)`.

human_note: ActiveRecord connection leaks are a resource exhaustion vulnerability affecting application availability, and the answer provides correct mitigation patterns

title: ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError with bidirectional foreign key
security_topic: modifying ActiveStorage blob key security implications
qa_summary: The developer asked if they could safely modify an ActiveStorage blob’s key to include the user ID, and the maintainer answered that the key is a secure token generated automatically and must not be changed, citing the ActiveStorage::Blob key implementation and documentation.

comments.author: zzak
comments.body:
I don't think this has anything special to do with your associations, but modifying the `key` directly like this is not supported.

The key is a secure token designed to be unique and generated automatically:
https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/ce359806416550c3b1b790c116aee5f0f9a182d4/activestorage/app/models/active_storage/blob.rb#L22

See also: https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html#method-i-key

> The key is the secure-token format from Rails in lower case. So it’ll look like: xtapjjcjiudrlk3tmwyjgpuobabd. This key is not intended to be revealed directly to the user. Always refer to blobs using the [signed_id](https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html#method-i-signed_id) or a verified form of the key.

And: https://edgeapi.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveStorage/Blob.html

> Blobs are intended to be immutable in as-so-far as their reference to a specific file goes. You’re allowed to update a blob’s metadata on a subsequent pass, but you should not update the key or change the uploaded file. If you need to create a derivative or otherwise change the blob, simply create a new blob and purge the old one.

Does this match your understanding or am I missing something?

comments.body:
If I were to change the code to edit the blob's `filename` instead of the blob's `key`, I'll still end up with the same bug though.

For example:

```ruby
class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one_attached :profile
  belongs_to :post
  after_save :override_blob_filename

  def override_blob_filename
    profile.blob.filename = "#{id}_#{(Time.now.to_f * 1000).to_i}"
  end
end
```

The original intent of modifying the `key` was because I would like to have my files in the remote storage (i.e. Amazon S3) to be easily findable and also contains the information of the `user.id`. And I'm quite not sure if there are any other ways of achieving that intent.

https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/active-storage-provide-filename-for-use-where-file-is-actually-stored/86081/2

title: "on_rotation" callback is not called for ActiveRecord Signed Id
security_topic: on_rotation callback support for Signed Ids
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if the `on_rotation` callback is supposed to be invoked for Signed Id key rotation, and the answer cites the intended API and fixes in PR #44179 (and related PR #54362/54422) confirming the bug and the required implementation.

comments.author: AliSepehri
comments.body:
`on_rotation` is supported by `MessageVerifier`, but the Signed Id implementation does not pass it through. This feature is very useful for secret-key rotation and monitoring the usage of old keys.

### Steps to reproduce

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  ActiveRecord::Base.signed_id_verifier_secret = "new_secret"
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def test_association_stuff
    Post.create! id: 1

    on_rotation_is_called = false

    # signed Id of "1" with "old_secret"
    signed_id_with_old_secret = "eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MSwicHVyIjoicG9zdCJ9fQ--e3c0118ae573077a32264dc32acc63800352323c41039b0e096af64bd6ecc28b"

    Post.signed_id_verifier.rotate "old_secret", on_rotation: -> { on_rotation_is_called = true }
    assert Post.find_signed!(signed_id_with_old_secret, on_rotation: -> { on_rotation_is_called = true })

    assert on_rotation_is_called
  end
end
```

### Expected Behavior
`on_rotation` should be called, and `on_rotation_is_called` should become true.

### Actual Behavior
The `on_rotation` method from `rotate` or `find_signed!` is not called, leaving `on_rotation_is_called` as false.

### Suggestions
1. Call `on_rotation` when it is set using the `rotate` method. This would require updating the `read_message` method in `activesupport/lib/active_support/messages/rotator.rb` file.

2. Call `on_rotation` when it is set using `find_signed`/`find_signed!`. These methods would need to accept `on_rotation` as an optional argument.

3. Implement both solutions.

title: `./bin/rails assets:precompile` is loading ActiveStorage s3 configuration after upgrading from Rails 7.1 -> 7.2 or 8.0
security_topic: unexpected loading of ActiveStorage configuration during asset precompilation
qa_summary: The issue was caused by commit 8bf1353cae which loads ActiveStorage::Blob during boot, causing assets:precompile to load S3 credentials and potentially expose them; fixing or awaiting the patch resolves the problem.

comments.author: michaelroudnitski
comments.body:
## Current behavior

Hi, I hope this is the right place to report this.

I spent some time debugging an error I encountered after starting my Rails 7.1 -> 8.0 upgrade.

I was able to reproduce it with a new rails 8 app, installing devise and configuring ActiveStorage to use S3. It seems like when you run `RAILS_ENV=production rails assets:precompile`, it is now loading ActiveStorage attachments on the User model from the devise routes.rb entrypoint, which is undesired.

This was not the case on Rails 7.1 and seems to be reproducable after upgrading to Rails 7.2. I was not able to find anything obvious from the [ActiveStorage 7.2 changelog](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/7-2-stable/activestorage/CHANGELOG.md#rails-720-august-09-2024). I would guess something changed with autoloading that causes routes.rb to get picked up and evaluated during the precompile task?

### To reproduce:

1. create a new rails 8 app
2. run `bundle add devise` and setup devise as normal on a User model
3. add an attachment to the User model
```ruby
# app/models/user.rb
class User < ApplicationRecord
  # Include default devise modules. Others available are:
  # :confirmable, :lockable, :timeoutable, :trackable and :omniauthable
  devise :database_authenticatable, :registerable,
         :recoverable, :rememberable, :validatable
  has_one_attached :display_picture
end
```
4. configure ActiveStorage to use the S3 service in `production.rb`,
```ruby
# config/storage.yml
s3:
  service: S3
  public: true
  access_key_id: "123"
  secret_access_key: "123"
  endpoint: "https://s3.example.cloud"
  region: null # purposely set to null to mimic secrets not being available in a docker build stage
  bucket: "bucket"

# config/environments/production.rb
config.active_storage.service = :s3
```
5. run `RAILS_ENV=production SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 ./bin/rails assets:precompile --trace` and observe an error from our ActiveStorage setup not having a configuration set
```
RAILS_ENV=production SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 ./bin/rails assets:precompile --trace
** Invoke assets:precompile (first_time)
** Invoke environment (first_time)
** Execute environment
bin/rails aborted!
Aws::Errors::MissingRegionError: No region was provided. Configure the `:region` option or export the region name to ENV['AWS_REGION'] (Aws::Errors::MissingRegionError)

        raise Errors::MissingRegionError if region.nil? || region == ''

comments.author: rafaelfranca
comments.body:
`RAILS_ENV=production rails assets:precompile` always loaded all the application code, including routes and models. This wasn't the behavior that changed. You can check that in Rails 7.1 by raising on the top of the user model if you want.

I don't know why you didn't get that error on Rails 7.1, but you should.

Can you confirm adding `raise` on top of `user.rb` causes the application to also fail on Rails 7.1?

comments.author: michaelroudnitski
comments.body:
@rafaelfranca yes you're right, adding `raise` to the top of `user.rb` also causes it to fail on Rails 7.1.

worth noting: on rails 7.1 with `raise` at the top of the user model, removing `devise_for :users` from `routes.rb` results in `precompile` succeeding

> I don't know why you didn't get that error on Rails 7.1, but you should.

I thought it could be another gem I upgraded in the process, but even following my same reproduction steps for a new Rails 7.1 app `rails _7.1_ new 7_1-app`, running `assets:precompile` is successful

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile

comments.author: Kishan-Talaviya-TBS
comments.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

**Issue Description**

Hello Stripe team 👋,

We are currently using the Stripe Node SDK and noticed that it pulls in a vulnerable version of the qs package as a transitive dependency.

The qs versions < 6.14.1 are affected by CVE-2025-15284 / GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p, where the arrayLimit option can be bypassed using bracket notation (a[]=x), allowing unbounded array creation and leading to potential Denial of Service via memory exhaustion.

**Affected Dependency Chain**
stripe → qs@^6.11.0

This version range resolves to a vulnerable qs release.

**Impact**

Even when applications configure arrayLimit in qs.parse(), the limit is ignored for bracket notation (a[]=value), which makes it possible for an attacker to submit a single crafted request that consumes excessive memory.

This issue is particularly impactful for applications parsing user-controlled query strings or request bodies.

### Describe the solution you'd like

**Suggested Fix**

Upgrade the qs dependency to the patched version:

qs >= 6.14.1

This version includes the upstream fix that enforces arrayLimit consistently for both indexed and bracket notation, resolving CVE-2025-15284.

**References**

CVE-2025-15284
GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p
[References link](https://github.com/ljharb/qs/security/advisories/GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p)

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body:
First off, I would strongly recommend using the PaymentMethod API instead as we rebuilt our ACH Debit integration entirely. Please carefully read https://stripe.com/docs/payments/ach-debit and related docs which go over how to do this in details. It also encourages you to collect bank account details **client-side** securely instead of having access to those server-side which is dangerous and increases your security burden (and PCI compliance burden if you do the same for cards).

Ultimately though the code you have works just fine, it's just old and discouraged. There are no types for this, both because it's deprecated and because we discourage passing raw bank account details server-side. If you want to move forward with that approach, you will have to explicitly suppress the type errors on that code.

I'm going to close this out as this is more an integration support question and not really a bug with the library. If you have follow up questions, please work with our support team directly: https://support.stripe.com/contact

comments.author: ItsWendell
comments.body:
I would love to propose better support for [Web-interoperable Runtimes](https://wintercg.org/) like Cloudflare Workers and Deno. After a lot of hassle, I got this library working on Cloudflare Workers, but that required adding a lot of polyfills for Node APIs, which added 500kb+- to my bundle size.

The Node APIs in question I get issues for are: `crypto`, `http`, `https`, `events`. Some build systems allow you to build for multiple runtimes like Preconstruct recently [added functionality for this.](https://preconstruct.tools/configuration#exports).

I've used `esbuild` here to bundle this, not the native build tool in Wrangler or Webpack. The example in the `stripe-examples` also uses webpack to include polyfills, I personally think that using Polyfills is more of a workaround, than an actual solution.

title: PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData does not support 'card' type
security_topic: PCI compliance rationale for API type definitions
qa_summary: The developer asked if using a token with payment_method_data type='card' is safe and why the TypeScript interface lacks the 'card' type, and the maintainer explained that raw card details require higher PCI compliance, referencing Stripe’s security guide, and confirmed that casting to any is the supported workaround.

comments.author: willbt
comments.body:
Hello, 

I used the payment_method attribute in the paymentIntents.create function and received this error: 

`A token may not be passed in as a PaymentMethod. Instead, use payment_method_data with type=card and card[token]=tok_xxxx"`


So I tried to use the payment_method_data and set the type as 'card' as below: 
payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxxx' } },

However, with TypeScript this doesn't work as the interface  PaymentIntentCreateParams.PaymentMethodData does not support the 'card' type.  

I solved by casting to any before passing to .paymentIntents.create and it works. 



```
const stripeRequest = {
      amount: request.amount,
      currency: request.currency_code,
      application_fee_amount: 0,
      payment_method_types: ['card'],
      confirm: true,
      capture_method: 'manual',
      payment_method_data: { type: 'card', card: { token: 'tok_xxxx' } },
    };

    const res = await this._stripe.paymentIntents.create(stripeRequest as any);
```

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body: @willbt Thanks for the report. We avoid typing the `card` hash because it'd also contain types for passing raw card details server-side which requires a higher level of [PCI compliance](https://stripe.com/docs/security/guide#validating-pci-compliance). Passing a Token id (tok_123) like you do is definitely supported but it's seen more as a temporary migration path than a canonical integration path as you should be confirming the PaymentIntent client-side instead of server-side on creation. We don't have plans to add types for that scenario but casting as any should solve the issue as you found!

Hi,

My client side code sends a request to the server to validate a basket. The server checks all the pricing is correct then creates a PaymentIntent object on the server side using a POST fetch. The response from that fetch is the full Stripe.PaymentIntent type (for example, including the `metadata` field in the response JSON). Returning this response back to the client will expose too much info, so I'm using the reducer function below to strip out the fields that are not available for publishable key.

```

// But Stripe.PaymentIntent is incompatible with @stripe/stripe-js version of PaymentIntent.
// The below code results in Typescript error.

function reduceStripePIToPublishableKeyPermissions(pi: Stripe.PaymentIntent): PaymentIntent {
    return {

        payment_method_types: pi.payment_method_types,
        receipt_email: pi.receipt_email,
        setup_future_usage: pi.setup_future_usage,
        shipping: pi.shipping,
        status: pi.status,
        object: pi.object,
        canceled_at: pi.canceled_at,
        cancellation_reason: pi.cancellation_reason,
        capture_method: pi.capture_method,
        confirmation_method: pi.confirmation_method,

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body: @imdavidmin Thanks for the extra details. Just to make sure I understand, the issue here is unrelated to stripe-node and its types and is instead related to Stripe.js, our client-side library, and its own types? And you get an error because you are doing your own logic to truncate/redact the JSON yourself server-side, unrelated to stripe-node?

comments.author: imdavidmin
remi-stripe
comments.body:
@imdavidmin From what I can tell, the problem is that server-side the `customer` property on `PaymentMethod` can be a `string` **or** a `Customer` object. This is due to the [Expand feature](https://stripe.com/docs/expand) which can be used server-side (and not client-side).

So when you retrieve the `PaymentIntent`, the `last_payment_error` can have the `PaymentMethod` object in it, and that could technically have the whole `Customer` object in `customer` because the types are identical to the top-level `PaymentMethod` object which it describes. This is reflected by the types in `stripe-node` for that reason [here](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-node/blob/master/types/2020-08-27/PaymentIntents.d.ts#L273)

Client-side though, the `customer` property can never be anything else than a `string` on `PaymentMethod` since it can't be expanded for security reasons. This means that inside `last_payment_error`, the type definition points to a `PaymentMethod` too but that one only supports `string` as defined [here](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-js/blob/master/types/api/PaymentMethods.d.ts#L30)

This does mean that, since you're the one turning a server-side PaymentIntent into a client-side PaymentIntent, you'll need to force the type for that specific part of the JSON (and possibly others) explicitly. You could also ignore `last_payment_error` in the returned property since it could have sensitive information such as the entire `Charge` object.

comments.author: imdavidmin
comments.body:
Thanks @remi-stripe 

I had a further read and seems like for most operations on the front-end, the client only needs the client secret, and not other attributes in a PaymentIntent. I'm trying to use the PaymentIntent object as a single source of truth so that the displayed amount, currency etc on the UI matches what the PI will charge. 

In this case, I guess Stripe's preferred way is for me to pass from the server the client secret only, and then the client makes additional queries to Stripe's server as needed? There is no built in redaction function on the stripe-node library, I assume?

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body:
Correct, there's no built-in redaction in stripe-node and it's not something we would add for now unfortunately. You could retrieve the PaymentIntent server-side with the publishable key I guess though it'd be the same as doing it client-side after passing the client_secret back.

I do understand wanting to pass more than just `client_secret`, like amount/currency, but I'd recommend doing this as your own object instead between your server-side code and client-side code.

I'm going to close as we've resolved the confusion. Don't hesitate to ask for help from developers on our Discord server: https://stripe.com/go/developer-chat

@yilmazbingo This is by design on our end. Sending raw card details server-side changes your PCI compliance requirements and are harmful to the vast majority of developers and businesses out there. Ultimately though, this works if you are already meeting the higher [PCI compliance requirements](https://stripe.com/docs/security/guide#validating-pci-compliance) and you can pass card details, it will just be untyped to avoid mistaken adoption by developers.

title: Consider retrying on 429 Too Many Requests?
security_topic: automatic retry on rate limit (429) errors
qa_summary: The developer asked whether the SDK should automatically retry on 429 Too Many Requests (a rate‑limit security control), and the maintainer answered that it does not retry to avoid hiding underlying problems, citing Stripe’s rate‑limit documentation (https://stripe.com/docs/rate-limits).

comments.author: jli
comments.body:
I expected that setting `maxNetworkRetries` would result in retries when rate limited (429 Too Many Requests errors), but in testing, I noticed this isn't the case. Would the team consider adding 429 as a condition that gets retried automatically (e.g. [here, in _shouldRetry](https://github.com/stripe/stripe-node/blob/v8.131.1/lib/StripeResource.js#L251))?

I think the typical "right" thing to do when rate limited is automatic retries with exponential backoff, which is why it would be nice to have it be part of the built-in retry mechanism (though having a higher max delay than 2s might also be nice in this particular use case as well).

Thanks!

comments.author: paulasjes-stripe
comments.body:
The reason we don't automatically retry on 429 errors is that getting that error usually means there's something up with your application. It's actually quite difficult to reach Stripe's rate limit with normal traffic, so getting that error usually means you need to review your application to make sure you aren't making unnecessary requests.

Getting rate limited shouldn't be solved by automatically retrying within the SDK, as that will obfuscate the actual underlying problem.

comments.author: jli
comments.body:
Thanks @paulasjes-stripe, that makes sense!

FWIW, what prompted this is that my team gets alerted for errors in our staging environment which uses the Stripe test environment, which I know has lower rate limits[1]. (The error occasionally gets triggered during server startup, when many processes spin up at the same time and make a Stripe API call as part of initialization.)

I guess I'll find some other workaround for our staging environment. Thanks!


[1] per the Stripe error message: `Testmode request rate limit exceeded, the rate limits in testmode are lower than livemode. You can learn more about rate limits here https://stripe.com/docs/rate-limits.`

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body:
@jli The way we approach rate limits is that we expect the vast majority of integrations to never hit this, even at scale. In Test mode the rate limits are 25 requests per second which is extremely high overall for a test suite. If we were retrying the requests automatically for you, you might not even notice that your test suite is making that many requests to our API per second (which is a pretty high load for our servers and yours).

In this world, we would expect no test integrations to go over a few of rps other than random peaks. Otherwise you should actively look into adding mocks to your tests and not hit the API directly in test suites!

comments.author: theredcat
comments.body: @remi-stripe @paulasjes-stripe IMHO You should at least provide an option `retryOnRateLimit` because you have small clients, but you have big clients too : @ work we can trigger 1000+ payment in a few seconds because we are doing time-limited auctions and our clients often program all their items to end at a specific time (often Sunday evening)

comments.author: remi-stripe
comments.body: @theredcat the large clients are even more reasons not to retry automatically or provide that option in my opinion. Rate limits are something you need to handle carefully and how to handle them depends on your own approach and business models and a "permanent retry" for all your requests is likely a bad idea. We implement various logic in rate limiting, dropping reads before writes for example and prioritizing some requests over others internally and most advanced/large users should do the same on their end when they start hitting rate limits, on top of alerting for it.
